Commentary on the *Zhao Lun*, Scroll One (Including Preface).
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Zunshe of Lanruo Hermitage at Yaofeng, Gusu.
Indeed, the myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by a single Dharma-seal, which is what is called the "mind. This mind is tranquil and profound, vast and harmoniously integrated;
it is without cessation and without arising, remaining unchanged throughout the three periods of time. It is neither large nor small, and its form cannot be measured throughout the ten directions.
It shines alone with perfect luminosity, yet is without fixed location; it is pure, true, and eternal, yet possesses a presence. Although it is spiritual...

Spiritual transcendence is beyond dependence; its随缘 (suiyuan) manifestations of form and appearance are a thousandfold, yet in its profound stillness it is beyond words. Its universal responses in sound and resonance are myriad, like the ten thousand pipes.

Thus, the myriad things of both form and mind each attain their proper place—this is what is meant by "attaining this. The myriad practices of sages and worthies each reach their respective destinations—this is what is meant by "arriving at this.
Sentient beings are deluded regarding this and thus revolve in saṃsāra without ceasing; sages realize this and [attain liberation].
Perfect Quiescence and Sublime Permanence: thus we know that were it not for the One Mind, the myriad dharmas would not exist; yet the dharmas are not the mind.

Were it not for the myriad dharmas, the One Mind would not be manifested; yet the mind is not the dharmas. Therefore, when the Tathāgata appears, he takes on form out of compassion for sentient beings;

his clouds of bodies respond to their perceptions, while his boundless essence remains free from increase or decrease. His perfect voice accords with their vows to pervade everywhere, for its principle transcends all names.
It is said: "Formless yet possessing form, like the moon reflected in a clear pool; unspeakable yet spoken, like an echo in a deep valley.
Thus, the great causes and conditions of the Deer Park and the Crane Forest were brought to completion; the teachings of the Three Periods circulated throughout the Five Indias and China.
Sages and worthies arose in succession, and the tradition was transmitted through antiquity and the present. During the Eastern Jin dynasty, there was a Great Dharma Master whose name was...

Sengzhao was born during the Qin dynasty; his fame resounded throughout distant lands. In his youth, he studied non-Buddhist scriptures, but later he attained enlightenment through the teachings of Śākyamuni.
He resolved his doubts under Kumārajīva of Kucha and resided for a long time at the Xiaoyao Translation Hall, where he established the five chapters of the *Zhonglun* (Treatise on the Middle).

Thus, he assisted in the singular transformation of the Tathāgata. Behold his magnificent talent, vast and unimpeded; his subtle understanding penetrated the core of the doctrine, and his profound principles were brilliantly illuminated.

Profound wisdom exhausts the boundaries of principle. Yet, regarding the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions, phenomena possess a thousand variations; while the true mark (dharmatā) is fundamentally non-existent, the principle is of a single flavor.

However, because each person’s faculties reflect differently, the two truths remain unmerged. How could one know that waves and water are not distinct, or that a gold ring is no different from its source?

For this reason, many names are enumerated to highlight their differences, while a single meaning is established to bring them into harmony, thereby constructing the doctrine of the "unshared" (asādhāraṇa).

This reveals the profound essence [of the teachings] and manifests the ultimate pinnacle of the Mahāyāna. Thus, there is no mundane reality distinct from the real; the conventional truth that is identical with the real is immutable.
There is no reality distinct from the mundane; the true emptiness that is identical with the mundane is manifest.

Reality and conventionality are non-dual, and phenomena and principle are mutually integrated. Without *prajñā* (wisdom), one cannot accord with the real; without *upāya* (skillful means), one cannot engage with the mundane. To enter [this state]...

While conventional reality prevails, the true source remains ever manifest. The provisional mind must necessarily possess the ultimate mind; by acceding to the truth, conventional affairs do not shift. Ultimate wisdom must necessarily rely upon provisional wisdom.
When the provisional and ultimate minds operate in tandem, the Middle Way is perfectly integrated. The realms of the true and the conventional exist simultaneously;

the single truth is still and silent. Sentiment ceases and conceptual understanding vanishes. As the contemplation of the truths becomes thoroughly fused, one returns to the fundamental and reverts to the source. [This is] forcefully...

This is titled *The Treatise on Realizing the Path*. The profound purport of this treatise and its systematic thread of reasoning are as follows. Nevertheless, commentaries and sub-commentaries produced by scholars of both ancient and modern times are numerous;
yet, in their pursuit of meaning and phrasing, each followed their own particular views. As for establishing a definitive school or determining the teaching, not a single such tradition has emerged.

Consequently, students have become confused by the literal text and lost the essential purpose of the path. Since my youth, I, Zunshi, have followed my teacher’s instruction, emptying myself to seek the fundamental source. Later, through the process of study...
Regarding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, I have constantly studied the commentaries and exegeses of Qingliang, which fully elucidate the five teachings.

Following the ancient masters, I have found a definitive point for the principles of the provisional and the real, and a direction toward which the gates of practice and understanding may be turned. I have always regretted that once these treatises are lost to humanity, they will be difficult to recover, thereby allowing the profound doctrine to fall into many erroneous paths.
Now, having investigated with meticulous thought and exhausted my ignorance by reciting this three times, I can only feel shame at the prospect of its dissemination.
This work was composed at my humble request. On the thirteenth day of the second month of the year Jiayin (1074) of the Xining era, the preface at the West Hermitage on Nanfeng states:
I bow my head to the Truly Responsive, Equal, and Perfectly Awakened One, The Dharma-nature’s boundless gateway of wisdom.
May the noble sages who practice according to reality grant their secret assistance in explaining the profound meaning.

Now, in order to explain this treatise, I shall briefly open four gates: first, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, its inclusion within the scriptural collections (*piṭaka*) and the vehicles of teaching;
third, the general and specific thematic purports (*abhiprāya*); and fourth, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text.

△ First: Now, when sages and worthies establish their treatises, they must have a specific basis. Herein, we clarify the causes and conditions for the inception of this teaching, briefly analyzing them through two gates:
first, a general clarification of various treatises; second, a specific exposition of this particular text. Regarding the general clarification of various treatises:

there are two types of treatises. The first is called *zong-lun* (doctrinal treatises); the second is called *shi-lun* (commentarial treatises). A *shi-lun* explains the text according to its wording.
Regarding the meaning: there is no other cause or condition; it is simply initiated because the fundamental meaning is profound and mysterious.

As for those who engage in sectarian debate: the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is deep and vast, difficult to measure. Its provisional and ultimate teachings have many gates, and its principles are not uniform.

If the Perfect Sound were to preach all at once, beings of different dispositions would each hear it differently, and thus there would be no need for treatises. However, after the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa, the inclinations and preferences of sentient beings were not [uniform].

[The teachings are] equal [in essence]. (Whether they be Sūtras or Śāstras, they delight in both the Real and the Expedient. The conditions for receiving and understanding them differ: (if one has a karmic affinity with the Buddha, Sūtras are appropriate;

if one has a karmic affinity with Bodhisattvas, Śāstras are appropriate. Although there are many Sūtras, some are unable to achieve realization. Therefore, various schools establish Śāstras, each suited to the capacities of sentient beings.

This is to enable people to know the school through the Śāstra and to attain the ultimate goal through the school. Thus, there are Śāstras of the Hīnayāna, Śāstras of the Triyāna, and Śāstras of the Ekayāna.

Introduction. Part Two: A Specific Explanation of This Text. This section further divides into two parts: first, a general clarification; second, a specific explanation. Regarding the general clarification:

if one traces the original purpose for which the Buddha appeared in the world, it was fundamentally for a single matter and condition; however, due to the differences in the capacities of sentient beings, there are variations in what they see and hear.
Although the teaching employs the three vehicles, its ultimate aim is solely the One Vehicle. Failing to understand this principle, many remain stuck at the provisional gates of transformation.
To enable them to trace back to the source and grasp the Buddha’s original intent, this treatise is composed.

Second, the specific exposition has two parts: first, refutation; second, establishment. Refutation refers to the refutation of the provisional; establishment refers to the establishment of the real. The purpose of this refutation and establishment is fourfold.

The treatise consists of four gates: 1. **Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya)**: It refutes the two inversions of permanence and impermanence, establishing that movement and stillness are mutually identical.
2. **Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya)**: It refutes the two views of existence and non-existence, establishing that the principles of the ultimate and the conventional are one. 3. **Prajñā**:

It refutes the existence or non-existence of illumination and function, establishing that the provisional and the real are of the same essence. 4. **Nirvāṇa**: It refutes delusion regarding the ultimate and attachment to the responsive, establishing...

Because the Real and the Responsive are non-dual, this process of refutation and establishment reveals the mutual integration of the ultimate and the conventional, the interpenetration of the provisional and the real, the profound union of wisdom and its object, and the dissolution of mind and境 (the objective realm).
Therefore, the single principle is established as the central tenet to exhaustively realize the ultimate, profound intent.
Although there are many intermediate conditions, they do not exceed this general meaning.
△ Regarding that which is subsumed within the two collections of teachings: it is subsumed within the Abhidharma Piṭaka among the three collections;
it is subsumed within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka among the two collections; and it is subsumed within the definitive teaching (nītārtha) among the provisional and definitive teachings.

However, the principles of the provisional and definitive are manifold. For now, following Master Xianshou’s classification of the teachings by way of their meaning, there are five categories of teaching. First:
1. The Hīnayāna Teaching; 2. The Initial Teaching of Mahāyāna, also called the "Teaching of Distinctions"; 3. The Final Teaching of Mahāyāna, also called the "Teaching of Reality";

4. The Sudden Teaching of Mahāyāna; 5. The Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Regarding these five in relation to one another, each preceding stage is provisional while each succeeding stage is real.
However, according to the fundamental tenets of each school’s own system, each allows that its own teaching is real and others are provisional. Now, as for what is said here...

Regarding the provisional (*neyārtha*) and the ultimate (*nītārtha*), they are distinguished according to their beginning and end. The first two [teachings] are both provisional, as they explain what is not yet final.

The latter three are all ultimate, as they universally explain the one mind (*ekacitta*). Within these provisional and ultimate [teachings], the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-dharma*) comprises two schools: the Dharma-character (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and the Refutation of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇāpavāda*).
Now, by contrasting these with the Final Ultimate, I shall briefly set forth ten points; through this, one will know that the meaning of the treatise’s discourse is complete.
Regarding what is subsumed under the teachings: first, the Dharma-characteristics (Hossō) school establishes that the three vehicles (tri-yāna) are definitively distinct;

the True Teaching (Shōkyō) establishes the one vehicle (eka-yāna), asserting that there are no three. As the lower treatise states: "Truly, the One is true and without differentiation," and again: "The primary Great Way has no duality.

Second, the Dharma-characteristics school speaks of the distinctions between the five natures (pañca-gotra)—namely, the three vehicles, along with the natureless (agotra) and the indeterminate (aniyata) natures—whereas the True Teaching discusses the single nature as universally equal. As the lower [treatise] states: "Thereupon the nine streams converge, and the myriad sages meet in profound harmony. Third...

In the Dharma-characteristics (Hossō) school, the two truths are established as distinct and separate (the conventional exists while the ultimate is non-existent). In the True Teaching (Shōgyō), the ultimate and the conventional are mutually identical. As it says below: "When speaking of the real, it has never existed; when speaking of the false, it has never been non-existent.

These two expressions have never been one, yet these two principles have never been different. Regarding the four dharmas, the Dharma-characteristics school asserts that they are realized sequentially (fundamental wisdom realizes the ultimate, and subsequently attained wisdom reaches the conventional).

The True Teaching speaks of the two wisdoms as being mutually illuminating. As it says below: "One contemplates emptiness without realizing [extinction], and dwells in existence without being defiled. Regarding the five dharmas, the Dharma-characteristics school... [text ends].
1. Regarding the sequence of the four characteristics (*catvāri lakṣaṇāni*): arising belongs to the past; abiding, change, and cessation belong to the present; and cessation belongs to the future.

In the *Real Teaching* (*saddharma*), it is revealed that arising and cessation are simultaneous (as stated below: "All sentient beings are the very mark of quiescent extinction"). 2. Regarding the six dharmas, the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* school asserts a distinction between wisdom and principle (*jñāna* and *tattva*), holding that conditioned wisdom realizes unconditioned principle.

The *Real Teaching* clarifies the seamless fusion of the subject and object (as stated below: "This and that are quiescently extinguished; things and self are darkly one; in this state of silent tracelessness, it is called *nirvāṇa*"). 3. Regarding the seven dharmas, the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* school speaks of *tathatā*.

1. Quiescence (*nirābhāsa*): The Real Teaching (*shijiao*) reveals the wondrous function of following conditions (*suiyuan*). (As it says below: "Without moving from the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), one establishes the locus for all phenomena.

And again: "The Dharma-body has no form; it takes shape in response to things. 2. The refutation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bhañjana*) teaches that true wisdom realizes emptiness. The Real Teaching clarifies that numinous awareness is fundamentally quiescent. (As it says below: "One knows all day long, yet never knows. And again:

"Wisdom possesses the mirror-like discernment of the profound mysteries, yet there is no knowing. 3. The refutation of characteristics teaches that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). (That which lacks intrinsic nature is *tathatā*.)

The teachings of the definitive vehicle (niyata-yāna) state that the fundamental nature is truly eternal. As it says below: "The Way of Nirvāṇa is as vast as the great void and is everlasting. It further states: "It is quiescent extinction and eternal peace; it has no beginning and no end."

"Profound as empty space" (10): This refutes the teaching of the marks [of the Buddha], asserting that even the Buddha’s virtues are empty. "The knowledge of all modes of knowledge is also pure": The True Teaching clarifies that the Tathāgata is endowed with all virtues.

As it says below: "There is no principle with which he does not accord; thus, the myriad virtues are extensively manifested. It further states: "The Buddha is like empty space, neither going nor coming; he appears in response to conditions, yet has no fixed location.

By comparing these two perspectives, the provisional and the real are clearly distinguished. Although there are extensive thematic categories for this, fearing prolixity, they are not set forth here. This concludes the exposition of the meaning of this treatise.

What is truly gathered therein leaves no room for doubt regarding principle. Within this, there are occasional explanations of provisional meaning (*upāya*), the intent of which lies in returning to the ultimate convergence.

(As it says below: "Prajñā is empty and profound; this is the pinnacle of the Three Vehicles. It is truly the undifferentiated One Reality. Without engaging the gate of the provisional, how could one be said to reach the final reality? Furthermore, it also suddenly clarifies the *dharmatā*.
(As it says below: "Those who speak lose its truth," and again: "Śākyamuni closed his chamber in Magadha; Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth in Vaiśālī. This directly reveals [the ultimate].

"True and eternal" (zhenchang) encompasses both the Sudden (dun) and the Gradual (jian). However, it does not clarify the meaning of the inexhaustible interdependence of the principal and the attendant within the ocean-like nature of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) and its unimpeded dependent origination;

thus, it is not subsumed under the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao). If one considers the deep to encompass the shallow and the fundamental to include the derivative, then the Perfect Teaching also includes this;
therefore, it is said to be "subsumed under the Real Teaching" (shijiao).

△ Third, regarding the general and specific aspects of the tenets (*siddhānta*) and their ultimate goals (*gati*): that which expresses what is esteemed is called a "tenet" (*siddhānta*); the destination to which the tenet leads is called the "goal" (*gati*). These also have general and specific aspects.

Generally, the single principle of "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) is the tenet, and the non-duality of the ultimate and conventional truths, wherein wisdom and phenomena are seamlessly integrated, is the goal.
Specifically, there are four gates. First, the mutual identity of the ultimate and conventional truths is the tenet; the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is the goal.

1. The ultimate goal (*yāna*) is the mutual possession of the provisional and the real as the central tenet (*siddhānta*). 2. The ultimate goal is the non-existence of cognitive objects (*jñeya*) as the tenet.

3. The ultimate goal is the non-duality of principle and wisdom (*prajñā*) as the tenet; the non-duality of principle and wisdom is the ultimate goal. 4. The ultimate goal is the transcendence of understanding, cultivation, and realization as the tenet;

the elucidation of the meaning of the teachings is the tenet. Through these tenets and goals, one knows that the four treatises progress from shallow to deep: the specific does not exceed the general.
△ Fourth, the explanation of the meaning according to the text. The text has three parts. First, the general title.

"Zhao Lun" (Treatise by Zhao): "Zhao" is the name of the person, and "Lun" (treatise) is the teaching. By using the person to encompass the teaching, the teaching follows the person; thus, it is the "Treatise by Zhao."

Therefore, while the *Śāstra* (treatise) applies universally across all treatises, Sengzhao selects from the specific text in order to distinguish the particular from the universal. Generally, there are many ways to establish a title:
namely, a single person, a single dharma, or a single metaphor. When these three are combined, they are called "person and dharma," "dharma and metaphor," and "person and metaphor."

Alternatively, "complete" (or "endowed with") refers here to a single individual. The commentator Xianshou says: "A treatise (*śāstra*) consists of words that are established, definitive, and conformable to the rules;
it judges and explains the principles of the profound characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Based on this meaning of definitive judgment, it is called a 'treatise'."

Furthermore, it is said that "treatise" (*śāstra*) refers to the gathering of discussions on the Dharma. This means establishing a proponent and an opponent to engage in a back-and-forth analysis and investigation to deliberate upon correct principles.
Thus, there are two types of treatises composed: first, *siddhānta-śāstra* (doctrinal treatises), and second, *vyākhyāna-śāstra* (commentaries).

The present work is a *siddhānta-śāstra*. Furthermore, *siddhānta-śāstra* is of two kinds: first, those that establish the textual meaning and principles of the scriptures, such as the *Mahāyāna-śata-dharma-viśada-śāstra*.
Regarding the *Menlun* (Treatise on the Gates): second, it establishes its own school (*svamata*) by means of both sūtras and śāstras, as seen in the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
The present treatise possesses these two characteristics. The first chapter, "The Fundamental Tenet" (*Zongben*), is that which is established by the author himself;

the subsequent four treatises each take sūtras and śāstras as their tenets. Therefore, this work has scriptural authority and its meaning has a doctrinal basis. It is thus subsumed under the category of "Tenet Treatises" (*Zonglun*). However, this...
The general title and the detailed examination of what has been established show that this was not composed by the Master himself.

Furthermore, among the two traditions of Confucianism and Buddhism here in China and in the Western Regions, we have never heard of an author using his own name as the title of his work. Moreover, observing the structure of the following five chapters, they were not composed in sequential order.
Once the composition was complete, its systematic threads were clearly woven; it circulated within the realm, and all people held it in high esteem.

It is so. Although each section is individually designated by its subject matter (*dharma*), they collectively follow the text of the author; therefore, it is titled with the author’s name as a general designation.
△ Second, the author reveals his name.
Composed by Shi Sengzhao of Chang’an during the Later Qin dynasty.
"Later Qin" is the dynastic name; it was established during the reign of Emperor Yao’s second ruler, whose taboo name was Xing. It flourished during the Hongshi era.

This precisely coincided with the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin dynasty. At that time, the Master was born in Qin; Chang'an City was the name of the capital, which was the ancient region of Yongzhou.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* states: "Śramaṇa Sengzhao was a native of Jingzhao; his religious conduct is as recorded in his original biography."

Based on this, it should be shown that the presentation of names follows the thematic titles. Since ancient masters have already established general titles and presented the specific names beneath them, there is no contradiction here.
△ Third, the formal explanation of the main text consists of five chapters, which are divided into two major sections. The first establishes the doctrine and sets forth the core tenet; the latter...
The treatise is composed based on four reliances. The initial section is divided into two parts. First, the title indicating the subject matter. Regarding the term "zong" (宗):

that which is esteemed within the teachings of the fundamental meaning is called *zong* (tenet); that upon which speech relies is called *ben* (basis). It is like the root being the basis of a tree, or a source [of a river].
Water is the fundamental source. Now, taking "meaning" (*yi*) as the basis upon which one relies, it becomes the doctrine (*zong*) that is esteemed.

The doctrine is itself the foundation. "Meaning" signifies what is appropriate. Since the teaching that relies upon and esteems [the meaning] must necessarily accord with the meaning and intent that it relies upon and esteems, meaning is thus the foundation of the doctrine. Someone may ask: "I do not yet know by what the doctrine is established."
Question: What is meant by "the fundamental" (*ben*)? Answer: It refers to the single meaning revealed in this chapter, which is the fundamental principle and the basis of our school's tenets.

The five subsequent names and the four treatises are the teachings that constitute the tenets and depend upon that basis. Therefore, it is known that the tenets of name and teaching are rooted in the meaning;
thus, meaning serves as the fundamental principle of name and teaching.

△ Next, the formal establishment of the doctrine (*siddhānta*). This section has two parts: first, the general establishment of the fundamental doctrine; second, the specific opening of the thematic gates.
Now, regarding the single chapter on the fundamental tenet (*mūla-siddhānta*), there are both general and specific aspects. When the general is opened into the specific, the four treatises differ;

when the specific is subsumed into the general, they equally manifest a single meaning. Now, for the first part, it is divided into three: first, the enumeration of names; second, the establishment of the doctrine; third, the analytical explanation. Now...
Among the five names listed at the beginning, the commentary divides them into five sections for explanation. Now, wishing to explain these names, one must discuss their signification.

Among the five, the first four signify principle (*li*), while "the convergence of conditions" (*yuanhui*) signifies phenomena (*shi*). This means that although phenomena consist of a thousand variations, they are all subsumed within the convergence of conditions;
and although principles have varying depths, the four names collectively encompass them. Now, I wish to clarify the single meaning of the non-duality of principle and phenomena.
The primary purpose [of this section] is first to explain that principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) are not identical. Regarding the five types of names, some may ask:

"Upon what dharma-substance does the Master establish this doctrinal position? The answer is: according to the tenets of this school, it is necessarily established based on the single mind-dharma (*ekacitta-dharma*).

That is to say, among the five names, the upper three express the essence of the mind, while the lower two express the functions of the mind; this is because the essence and function of the single mind exist simultaneously.
The meaning of the five names is one. If that is so, why does the treatise not indicate a single mind? There are two reasons for not indicating it:
first, because mental factors can only be reached through realized wisdom (*pratyātmajñāna*) and are beyond the reach of verbal teaching.
Now, this is revealed solely through meaning and not demonstrated by words. This is like Śākyamuni’s “closing the room” and Vimalakīrti’s silence;

it is the separate transmission outside the teachings, where one loses the expression to attain the essential meaning—all of which share this intent. Second, regarding principle and phenomena, essence and function:

the various schools and sections of the Three Vehicles do not speak of their mutual fusion; it is only in the ultimate discourse of the Mahāyāna that non-duality is clarified. Such is the purport of this treatise.

Because it intends to lead from the provisional into the ultimate reality, it specifically enumerates five names; because it seeks to harmonize these into a single meaning, it does not first designate the "one mind" as the fundamental dharma.
This is analogous to how, within the Vimalakīrti chamber, five thousand great bodhisattvas each first expounded two dharmas before entering the gate of non-duality.
From these two points of comparison, one can know that this treatise is largely identical to the *Awakening of Faith*.

There is not a slight difference. This is truly because [the former] involves returning to the ultimate by means of the provisional, proceeding from the beginning to the end; whereas [the latter] involves directly accessing the nature of mind.
Since their capacities for the Dharma differ in terms of superiority and inferiority, the teachings established for them are accordingly different.

"Fundamentally non-existent" (*benwu*). This term has two interpretations. First, "fundamental" (*ben*) means "from the beginning," and "non-existence" (*wu*) means "quiescence. This refers to the essence of the single true mind, which is serene throughout the three periods of time.
As it says below: "It is not that one pushes it so as to make it non-existent"; therefore, it is called "fundamentally non-existent. Second, "fundamental" (*ben*) means...

The source: when there is no [source], all is extinguished. This means that as the myriad streams return to the source, names and characteristics are thereby extinguished. Regarding the two previous interpretations:
the former holds that it is originally non-existent by nature, while the latter holds that the source is revealed through non-existence.

Only the fourth treatise elucidates this point, clarifying the meaning of the two nirvāṇas—non-conditioned cessation and extinction—wherein the equality of sentient beings and Buddhas brings the aspects of wisdom and principle to mutual extinction. Only then...
The *niṣyanda* (outflow) is fundamentally non-existent.

"Real aspect" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) means that "real" refers to the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*), while "aspect" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to its phenomenal form. That which is the true reality is itself the signless (*alakṣaṇa*). This also constitutes two [aspects].
Explanation: First, the true mind is fundamentally devoid of all marks; because it is the truth that transcends marks, it is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
As stated below: "The true mark is itself non-existent; the quiescence of the marks of the ten thousand dharmas is precisely the true mark.

Regarding these two explanations, the former directly discusses marks in relation to the essence of the dharma-body, while the latter thoroughly investigates the reality by means of the various dharmas. Reality is attained because the essence and its marks are fundamentally true.
All phenomena (*dharmas*) are real; furthermore, it is precisely by seeing reality within phenomena that one comes to know that every phenomenon is entirely true.

[The principles of] "Non-Deviation" (*apracāra*), "Not Non-Emptiness" (*a-tattva-śūnyatā*), and "Prajñā Without Cognition" (*ajñāna-prajñā*)—these three treatises (*Tri-svabhāva-śāstra*)—all uniformly employ these names regarding their expressed meaning (*abhidheya*).

Regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*), they fuse the ultimate and the conventional to manifest the *dharmatā*. Regarding wisdom (*jñāna*), they fuse the provisional and the ultimate to manifest the *dharmatā*. Practice...

In this regard, it appears that for human beings, the traces of subject and object have not yet been extinguished; therefore, it is only upon reaching *nirvāṇa* that these are fundamentally non-existent.
If one considers the four treatises as distinct gateways, then only through *prajñā* can one reach this state.

Because both provisional and ultimate wisdoms arise together from the reality-mark (*dharmatā*), which is the essence of the *dharmadhātu*, and because the nature of this essence is eternally quiescent, it is called *prajñā*.
Ignorance. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

"Phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to the rules and the sustaining power; "nature" (*tā*) refers to their seamless integration and unchanging state. The true, eternal body of phenomena is tranquil and profound.
It is profound, unchanging across the three periods of time, and enables sentient beings to understand it; therefore, it receives the name "Dharma" (the Teaching).
Although it is pervasive throughout all phenomena, it does not lose its indivisibility; therefore, it receives the name "Nature" (dharmatā). As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The nature of phenomena is omnipresent in all places, yet no form or characteristic can be apprehended. It continues below: "The nature of phenomena is thus. If Xianshou [Fazang] were to arise...
The *Xinshu* states: "Dharmatā (the nature of phenomena) clarifies the meaning of the true essence being universally pervasive.

It penetrates and serves as the nature of all phenomena, thereby manifesting that True Suchness (*tathatā*) pervades both the defiled and the pure, and encompasses both the sentient and the insentient.

Here, 'phenomena' (*dharma*) refers to the myriad dharmas that follow conditions, while 'nature' (*svabhāva*) refers to the unchanging aspect of True Suchness. This also accords with the explanation provided here; however, it does not [employ] the term 'phenomena'..."

Regarding the single character: it is explained directly according to its meaning as "upholding the true track. If one uses "following conditions" (*suiyuan*) to explain "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*), one is utterly deluded;
[the nature] is empty.

"Nature" (*xing*) refers to the nature of all phenomena arising and ceasing in dependence upon conditions. "Emptiness" (*kong*) means that they are provisional and lack substantial reality. This also has two interpretations:
First, by investigating all phenomena through the fourfold nature (*caturvidha-svabhāva*), one finds that they do not arise from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without cause;

thus, there is not a single thing that possesses substantial reality. As the subsequent treatise states: "Because their nature is eternally empty of itself. Second, the nature and characteristics of all phenomena appear as such to the deluded mind.

They exist [conventionally], yet in reality they do not. It is like seeing a rope at night and fearing it is a snake; while the nature and characteristics of a snake were never present from the start, sentient beings—if they were to abandon their pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) and realize that phenomena (*dharma*) based on others (*paratantra*) lack a real nature—would find that this treatise, "On Non-True Emptiness" (*Asatyatva-śūnyatā-śāstra*), takes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as its gateway.
This name is precisely aligned with that. If, however, one refers to the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as it is revealed, then it expresses the ultimate reality itself.
Regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*):

conditions (*pratyaya*) are those that provide indirect assistance; causes (*hetu*) are those that directly produce [an effect]. "Convergence" (*samāgama*) means union or aggregation. This is a general discussion of the Buddha.

The teachings on the various schools of causes and conditions exhaustively investigate the origins by which all phenomena arise; they directly refute the non-causality and false causality of the heterodox paths.
Thus, the True Teaching (Dharmatā-yāna) points to the single mind as the source, while the School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇa-yāna) clarifies that [phenomena] exist by virtue of seeds.
Now, speaking merely from the perspective of conventional truth, it is said that through the convergence of various conditions, the various phenomena of form and mind manifest distinctly.
However, the "Treatise on the Non-Transmigration of Phenomena" takes conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as its gateway and employs these names solely for the sake of conventional designation.

Since it does not exhaustively investigate the source from which all phenomena arise within the framework of conventional truth, it simply uses the name "convergence of conditions" to encompass all phenomena in their entirety.

The text below states: "All dharmas arise through the convergence of conditions. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* likewise says: "All dharmas arise from conditions," and so forth. Someone might object:
"Since this does not clarify the origin of all dharmas, how can it be considered a discourse that exhausts the principle? The answer is:

If one were to rely on the five names [of the Buddha], they would not be single terms for the convergence of conditions; thus, they would indeed not be names that exhaust the principle. However, in the present case, it is by virtue of a single meaning...

Therefore, the convergence of conditions for all phenomena takes their original lack of real characteristics as the cause; through delusion, they grasp at the true to form the conditioned, and based entirely upon the true, they establish the false.
Thus, the subsequent section employs reverse inference to demonstrate that the convergence of conditions directly reveals the original absence of reality.

Consequently, we know that the truth of the one mind is the direct cause from which all phenomena arise. As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome; it is capable of transforming and giving rise [to them]."
It creates all realms of existence, even unto their arising and ceasing. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates.
Furthermore, some explain that defiled phenomena have ignorance as their cause, while others state in the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Faxiang) school that karmic seeds directly produce them;
both of these refer to the meaning of "conditions" (*pratyaya*) in the present context. Master Qingliang’s commentary states: "Because [beings] do not know that the three realms arise from..."
"In my mind, due to delusion and craving, one wanders through saṃsāra without end. Therefore, I now correctly follow the Mahāyāna, not contradicting its teachings or principles.
Someone asks: "Why does the treatise establish only these five names, neither more nor less? The answer is: "If categorized by their terminology, they are indeed numerous;
yet in exhausting the principles and perfecting human nature, they do not exceed these five. Now, I shall briefly [explain them]..."

The nature and characteristics of the two truths are bound together; thus, the established position is free from the faults of deficiency or excess. The emptiness of the nature of conditioned conjunction clarifies the nature and characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

the real nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) clarifies the nature and characteristics of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Fundamentally non-existent—this single term causes both the nature and characteristics of the true and the conventional to vanish.
Regarding this, there are three layers of fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). First, the fourfold propositions of conventional truth are clarified: first, the characteristic of the conventional.

First, the conventional nature as the convergence of conditions. Second, the conventional nature as the emptiness of intrinsic nature. Third, the conventional nature and its conventional characteristics both exist; this refers to the combination of the two preceding names.
Fourth, the conventional nature and its conventional characteristics both vanish; this refers to original non-existence. Next, the four propositions of the ultimate truth are clarified:
first, the true nature, which is the dharma-nature; second, the true characteristic, which is the real characteristic; third, the true nature and the true characteristic both exist; this refers to...

Combining the two preceding names, the fourth [category] is that in which both true nature (*tathatā*) and phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are simultaneously extinguished; this refers to the state of being fundamentally non-existent. Subsequently, four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are elucidated through the contrast of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*):
1. The nature and characteristics of the conventional: the nature of the convergence of conditions is empty. 2. The nature and characteristics of the ultimate:

the true reality of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). 3. The simultaneous existence of the nature and characteristics of both the ultimate and the conventional: this encompasses the meaning of the following four categories. 4. The simultaneous extinction of the nature and characteristics of both the ultimate and the conventional.

"Vanishing" (mín) means that [phenomena] are fundamentally non-existent. These three sets of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) constitute the perfection of both teaching and principle. Furthermore, each stage—faith, understanding, practice, and realization—must likewise possess these four;
if even one is lacking, it is not truly authentic. Therefore, this name is established as exhausting the full meaning.
It does not exceed five. The preceding section concludes the explanation of the enumeration of names. △ Second, the establishment of the meaning. This consists of a single meaning;
it is the formal establishment of the meaning. Although there are five names listed above, the meaning they express is one. What is called "one meaning" is as follows:
There are also many interpretations. To explain it briefly according to the five names: the first three designate the essence of the mind, while the latter two designate the functions of the mind.

Since these already constitute the single essence and function of one mind, their meaning is one. Furthermore, the first four names designate principle (*li*), while the fifth name designates phenomena (*shi*).
There are no phenomena apart from principle; the essence remains entirely unchanging while responding to conditions. There is no principle apart from phenomena; although...

It accords with conditions without changing; because principle and phenomena are non-dual, their meaning is one. If we rely on the explanations of the "One" meaning in the four treatises that follow, there are three gates.
First, regarding the object (*viṣaya*): the *Wubiquan lun* (Treatise on the Non-transmigration of Things) concerns the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of the convergence of conditions;

the *Buzhenkong lun* (Treatise on the Non-emptiness of Nature) concerns the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the emptiness of nature. By showing the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional, it reveals the fundamental [reality].

The realm of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) devoid of substantial characteristics, is therefore called "one meaning" (*ekārtha*). Second, regarding wisdom:
this refers to the *Prajñā-nirjñāna-śāstra*. It involves the provisional wisdom that engages with existence through conditions, and the real wisdom that contemplates emptiness as empty;

when the provisional and the real are non-dual, it is the wisdom of the Middle Way within the dharma-nature that is fundamentally without substantial characteristics. Therefore, it is called "one meaning. Third, regarding...

This is the realization, namely the *Nirvāṇa-Wu-ming-lun* (Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvāṇa). Because the bodies manifested through transformation do not extinguish the characteristics of principle and phenomena, or of object and wisdom, they are the emptiness of nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) when conditions converge.

Because the true essence does not maintain the duality of subject and object, or of wisdom and its object, the reality-nature (*dharmatā*) and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) are fundamentally non-existent.
Since existence and extinction are unimpeded, and the True and the Responsive are non-dual, it is called "the single meaning. By means of this teaching—
As for the principle [of teaching] being applied to the capacities of beings: it causes those of the three vehicles to return together to the single Buddha-vehicle;

it brings those of the five natures to meet together in the single Buddha-nature. As for practice: compassion and wisdom guide one another. As for the cause: emptiness and existence are cultivated in tandem. As for the mind: quiescence and illumination occur simultaneously.

As for contemplation: principle and phenomena are illuminated equally. Therefore, it is said that within the worlds of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma. Thus, [this doctrine] is established.
The principle of "One" is the core tenet for investigating the great matter of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.

Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* takes non-duality as its core; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is rooted in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* investigates the eternally abiding single mind; and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies the single nature of all sentient beings.
Therefore, one knows that the purport of the meaning of "One" is sufficient to unify the ultimate tenets of the Mahāyāna. Nevertheless...
This is also due to the five names; therefore, they are called "one meaning. Since the names are interpenetrating, the meanings likewise do not constitute a single entity.
Only when one can be both one and five, yet neither one nor five, does one fully exhaust the profound mystery. Thus, a sutra also says:
"Even 'one' is not taken as one, for the purpose of destroying all numerical categories. The general meaning above serves as the fundamental tenet for the four treatises. △ Three.
The analysis and explanation has two parts. First, the analysis. Why is this so?

It is because it is an analysis. Since there are five names, how can they constitute a single meaning? △ Second, the explanation of how they constitute a single meaning, in two parts. First, the indication.
Regarding the two aspects of explaining the convergence of conditions (*pratyaya-samnipāta*): first, it indicates the phenomena (*vastu*) that are explained.
All dharmas are the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). This means they encompass both the mundane and the supramundane; therefore, they are called "all. Each possesses form (*rūpa*).

The mind relies upon the correct [teaching]; therefore, it is called "all dharmas. These are the phenomena (the referents) explained by the names in the passage below, which arise through the conjunction of conditions.

However, the preceding listing of names was based on the principle of deriving the branches from the root—that is, establishing all dharmas from the root of non-abiding. Such is the nature of dharmas.
Now, this explanation establishes the meaning by tracing the branches back to reveal the root. Since the teaching and its underlying principle are thus, the following four...
The treatise elucidates the principle. However, according to the sequence of the teachings, the preceding stages are shallow and the succeeding stages are deep.
This present exposition, however, intends to lead practitioners from the shallow to the deep, so that they may reach the fundamental through the derivative.
For this reason, the order of explanation here specifically reverses that of the preceding section. II. Explaining the Designating Names.
"Arising through the convergence of conditions.

This explains the meaning of the term "convergence of conditions" (*yuanhui*) as it designates phenomena. When defiled conditions converge, the six realms of ordinary beings—both their environments and their bodies—arise.

When pure conditions converge, the four types of noble ones—both their environments and their bodies—manifest. Therefore, the environments and bodies of the ten realms necessarily arise through the convergence of either defiled or pure conditions.
Therefore, when one wishes to explain the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they do not exceed the designation of "the convergence of conditions" mentioned above.

△ Second, revealing the principle to clarify the single meaning, in four parts. First, revealing the principle of the emptiness of nature, divided into two. First, investigating its nature, further divided into three.
First, investigating the emptiness of the prior limit (*pūrvānta*).
They arise through the convergence of conditions;

thus, that which has not yet arisen does not exist. The first phrase restates what preceded; the second phrase provides the formal inference. "Arising" means to emerge. This refers to observing the prior limit of all phenomena:

when conditions have not yet emerged, there is no nature or characteristic of a phenomenon. Therefore, it is said that "that which has not yet arisen does not exist. From this, one can sufficiently know that [phenomena] presently exist.

This certainly belongs to dependent origination. △ Second, the section on inferring the emptiness of the future limit has two parts. First, the actual inference: "When conditions disperse, there is cessation.
Cessation means total extinction.
Furthermore, when one contemplates the future limit of all phenomena, if conditions are dispersed, both their nature and characteristics are extinguished; therefore—
One should exhaust the conditions by dispersing them, thereby realizing that the meeting of conditions is not real. △ Second, the hypothetical extension and subsequent refutation.
"If it were truly real": if it were real, then existence would not cease.
This follows the method of first extending the hypothesis and then refuting it. "If it were" (ru qi) means "if that" (ruo bi). If those matters of the meeting of conditions were truly existent...
If it were so, there would be no cessation at the future limit (*aparānta*). Since there is indeed cessation now, it is certain that it is not real.
△ Third, the correct inference of the emptiness of the present: By inferring in this manner, one knows that although things presently exist, their nature is eternally empty of itself.
This refers to "application. By applying these two limits, one can infer that all phenomena of the present are empty because their self-nature is dependent.
Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I say, are emptiness.

The first phrase belongs to the *Wubian lun* (Treatise on the Non-transmigration of Things), while the second phrase belongs to the *Buzhenkong lun* (Treatise on Non-False Emptiness). Regarding dependent existence (*paratantra*), there are two types: first, [the dependent nature as the basis for error]; second, [the dependent nature as the basis for correct cognition]. One...
There are two types of "otherness" (paratva): otherness in dependence on truth, and otherness in dependence on various conditions, as waves depend upon water and further upon wind.

Here, the latter meaning is taken to reveal that because of the convergence of conditions, all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). △ Second, the conclusion which reveals the emptiness of nature.
The nature is eternally empty of itself; therefore, it is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).

This concludes the formal argument. Because the principle of the emptiness of nature is revealed through phenomena, this emptiness of nature is termed "emptiness of persons" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) in the teachings for those of dull faculties, and "the two emptinesses" in the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*);
yet these have not yet been able to reveal [the nature] by means of phenomena. Now, [it is revealed] through the convergence of conditions.
Thus, the principle of the emptiness of nature manifests; this distinguishes it from the provisional teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. △ Second, revealing the principle of *dharmatā*:
"The *dharmatā* is thus.
This refers to the manifestation of the true *dharmatā* through the emptiness of nature as conditions assemble. "Thus" (*evam*) points back to the aforementioned assembly of conditions.
All phenomena, by virtue of being empty of intrinsic nature, are eternally quiescent in their fundamental nature; such is the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, it is said that what is truly eternal and unchanging is free from faults and transcends all negations; the nature of dharmas possesses this meaning. The intent is to lead one to realize the true reality of things;
therefore, it is said that "the nature of dharmas is thus. Yet, while this involves touching upon phenomena to accord with principle, it is applied according to the capacities of beings.

2. If one realizes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) only after first comprehending that phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, this refers to those of provisional capacity entering the ultimate, which belongs to the gradual approach.
If one directly perceives the nature of phenomena within phenomena themselves, this refers to those of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*) capacity, who enter the ultimate all at once (*sadyas*).
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because all phenomena are entirely true, and because they are all identical to Suchness (*tathatā*). △ 3. Revealing the True Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This is the principle;
hence it is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The former reveals the true nature through phenomena; this [latter] reveals the true appearance through phenomena. It is not merely that the nature arises from the convergence of conditions.

Emptiness is fundamentally the true nature (*dharmatā*). One also realizes that the convergence of conditions is signless and that this very [convergence] is fundamentally the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This is precisely the principle of perceiving the true mark within phenomena. As it says below: "The true mark of all dharmas is called Prajñā. And the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"Livelihood, production, and industry are all not in contradiction with the true mark. Therefore, one directly perceives the emptiness of nature within the convergence of conditions.
The name "true reality" (shixiang) is established; thus it is said, "therefore it is called true reality.

However, the two names "dharma-nature" (faxing) and "true reality" emerge as one, because true nature is without marks and because the nature of true reality is quiescent. △ Fourth, revealing the principle that there is no fundamental [existence].
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is inherently non-existent; it is not made non-existent through deliberation. Therefore, it is called "original non-existence" (*benwu*).

This demonstrates that the principle of original non-existence is revealed through phenomena. Although the true mark is said to be originally non-existent with reference to temporal sequence, in meaning they are simultaneous.
The former merely brings phenomena back to the principle to reveal the true mark; the present clarifies that the principle of the true mark does not arise from deliberation.

As for phenomena, they are seen as non-existent; they have been non-existent from the very beginning. Therefore, it is called "original non-existence" (*benwu*). Previously, there was a principle to which one could return, and phenomena necessarily converged with that principle;
this was the meaning of the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*). Now, it is revealed that the principle is inherently quiescent, and both phenomena and principle are simultaneously extinguished;
this is the meaning of the Sudden Teaching (*dunjiao*). Since this proceeds from the shallow to the deep, reaching the deepest depth, this "original non-existence" specifically steps upon reality.

[These terms] are explained through their characteristics: furthermore, "dharma-nature" (dharmatā) reveals the true nature; "true characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) reveals the true aspect; and "original non-existence" (mūla-abhāva) reveals the true essence. Originally, nature and characteristics are both transcended.
Although these three reveal the principle, there are differences in depth and shallowness. Furthermore, the aforementioned five names pertain to the realization of the convergence of conditions.
Thus, one departs from the parikalpita (imagined nature). By investigating the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one realizes the paratantra (dependent nature).

By revealing that the true mark of the dharma-nature is fundamentally non-existent, one realizes the pariniṣpanna (perfected nature). Guishan said: "Because it exists through conditions, the paratantra lacks intrinsic nature;

this is precisely the pariniṣpanna. Therefore, they share a single meaning. The above analysis of the text on investigation and explanation already shows that the Master merely harmonizes phenomena to reveal the principle.

The meaning of "one" has been explained. The meanings of the remaining "ones" may be sought through one's own understanding; they are all as previously stated. The explanation of the general meaning is complete. II.
Second, the separate opening of the gates of meaning, which has three parts: 1. Revealing the meaning of oneness by simultaneously refuting existence and non-existence with respect to the object; 2.

Revealing the meaning of oneness by simultaneously integrating the provisional and the real with respect to wisdom; 3. Revealing the meaning of oneness by simultaneously dissolving principle and phenomenon with respect to realization. This...

All three sections are derived from the general [principle] and opened out; thus, the whole generality is established as the particulars. These constitute the fundamental tenets of the four subsequent treatises:

namely, the *Wubiquan lun* (Treatise on the Non-transmigration of Things) and the *Buzhenkong lun* (Treatise on the Non-emptiness of Reality) both take the single meaning of the "objective realm" (*jing*) as their tenet. The *Bore wuzhi lun* (Treatise on the Non-cognition of Prajñā) takes the single meaning of "wisdom" (*zhi*) as its tenet.
The *Niepan wuming lun* (Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvāṇa) takes the single meaning of "realization" (*zheng*) as its tenet. Now, for the first [section], the text has two parts. First:
The "citation of the statement" (*jia die wen*) refers to the phrase "neither existent nor non-existent," which cites what was previously said.
Some say: "If one says that because conditions conjoin, the nature of all phenomena is eternally empty by itself, this constitutes [the proof]."

[The interlocutor asks: "There is one meaning [of emptiness]. Why, then, do the Buddha's teachings speak of both 'neither being' and 'not non-being'? Therefore, this [text] now restates [the previous argument].
This merely follows upon the preceding explanation of the middle way, specifically the passage stating: "All dharmas arise through the convergence of conditions...

because their nature is eternally empty of itself," which is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). By provisionally taking this as a basis for inquiry, it opens up the True Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The conventional truth exists and is not non-existent. This serves as the gateway for the two preceding treatises' primary tenets. It reveals the principle that the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual, which is the subject matter elucidated by those two treatises.
Therefore, "not existing" here refers to the aforementioned emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), while "not non-existing" refers to the aforementioned convergence of conditions.

The following section reveals the Middle Way, which is identical to the single meaning mentioned above. The questioner merely relies on the previous difference in terminology. [End of] the preceding section.

The following section is established by the author of the treatise based on the preceding meaning; thus, although it is formulated separately, it does not lose its connection to the general principle.

Since this meaning is not separate from what preceded, it is called a "provisional inquiry. △ Second, the analysis of the principles of truth (*satya*). This section has two parts. First, the elucidation of the two truths (*dvaya-satya*).
The commentary has two parts: first, explaining the intent of the teaching to resolve the question.
It is not a case of "existence" as held by those with views of existence or eternalism, nor of "non-existence" as held by those with false views or nihilistic views.
The two characters "not as" (不如) are used in conjunction across two phrases; they are words capable of refutation, namely the two instances of the character "not" (不) mentioned above.

"Views" refers to false understanding, which is precisely the attachment to be refuted; it consists of the extremes of existence and non-existence. Although the objects of such attachment are numerous, they do not transcend two types:

first, the view of permanence, which clings to existence; and second, the view of annihilation, which clings to non-existence. Furthermore, ordinary persons have not yet realized that things arising through conditions are fundamentally empty;
seeing the existence of various phenomena, they conceive of them as having a permanent nature. Therefore, the Buddha taught that, according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they do not exist.
Therefore, it is said that this is not as good as having the view of the existence of permanence.

Furthermore, because followers of the Hīnayāna and non-Buddhists have not yet been able to accord with reality through phenomena, they mostly exalt emptiness and silence while feeling aversion toward the body and cognition.

Thus, Buddhism treats them by means of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) that things are not non-existent. Therefore, it is said that this is not as good as the "non-existence" of those with wrong views or nihilistic views. This is so.

One should know that in the true teaching of Buddhism, it is said that [things] do not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), yet they are not non-existent from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

This is for the purpose of destroying the two attachments to annihilationism and eternalism; because the Buddha’s correct view does not resemble these two attachments to annihilationism and eternalism, he says "not as such" (*na tathā*) and so forth.

Therefore, I shall first set forth the intended meaning of this teaching: it simply serves to directly negate those two views. II. Establishing the method of concession and refutation (*anujñā-pratiṣedha*) to harmonize with what precedes.
If one takes existence as being existent and non-existence as being nonexistent, this merely follows what was previously stated.

That would be correct. However, in the previous explanation, if one takes the convergence of conditions as existence and likewise takes the emptiness of intrinsic nature as nonexistence, one establishes the dualistic view of existence and nonexistence, which contradicts the Buddha’s teaching.
Since existence does not exist, non-existence also does not exist.
This refutes the previous interpretation that took the meaning loosely to explain the prior sense. "Already" (ji) refers to what has already been established.

In the preceding explanation, it was clarified that the existence of the convergence of conditions is precisely because it is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*) and thus does not exist; one thereby knows that the non-existence of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is precisely because of the convergence of conditions.
It is not non-existent; thus, two names share a single meaning, which accords with the Buddhist teaching on the two truths as being neither existent nor non-existent.
The repeated use of the word "non-existent" signifies that it is not non-existent. This refers to the fact that the two truths can demonstrate the mutual identity of existence and non-existence;
therefore, "neither existent nor non-existent" constitutes a single meaning. The subsequent text will then converge upon this demonstrated meaning of the one reality.

One Meaning. The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "Regarding the truths, there are always two; regarding their understanding, there is always one. △ Second, reconciling the one meaning into two.
First, reconciling the two truths to reveal the one meaning, which has two parts. First, the formal revelation of concealment and illumination.
Now, one who does not rely on non-existence to contemplate phenomena may be said to recognize the true mark (*dharmatā*) of phenomena.
Previously, we relied upon the two truths to take "neither existence nor non-existence" as the gateway; yet this had not yet clearly revealed the actual meaning demonstrated within that gateway.

Now, in this assembly, the ultimate and the conventional converge, revealing the Middle Way, the Supreme Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is precisely the aforementioned conditionality (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

When one realizes that the nature of phenomena is empty and non-dual, the principle of the true reality of the dharma-nature (dharmatā) becomes manifest. Now, the realm of the truths (satya-viṣaya) is discussed by means of no more than four propositions:

The Dual Fusion of the Provisional and the Real to Reveal the Single Meaning (in three parts). 1. Quoting the Question and Briefly Explaining.
"Upāya-prajñā" is a designation for "Great Wisdom.

*Upāya* is a Sanskrit term. According to Master Kang, it is translated as "expedient means" (*fangbian*), which refers to provisional wisdom (*huì*).
*Prajñā* is also a Sanskrit term; its direct translation is "wisdom" (*zhì*). Alternatively, when referring to the cause, it is translated as "wisdom," taking the meaning of "discernment";

when referring to the fruit, it is translated as "knowledge," taking the meaning of "decisive judgment. Here, we take the combination of cause and fruit, meaning that both the cause and the fruit are universally possessed by persons.

This is the wisdom of the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha-jñāna*). Alternatively, *prajñā* is translated generally as "wisdom" (*jñāna*), distinguishing between wisdom as the ultimate (*bhūta*) and insight (*prajñā*) as the provisional (*upāya*).
This distinction is not adopted here either, because the term *upāya-kausalya* (skillful means) already implies provisional insight; as it says below, "provisional insight is complete.

Furthermore, these two types of wisdom are also called "fundamental" and "subsequently attained," "conformity to reality" (*yathābhūta*) and "conformity to the measure" (*yathāmātra*), or "ultimate" (*tattva*) and "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*); all of these are both provisional and ultimate.
These are alternative names [for the title]. The others will be analyzed in the commentary on the title within the main treatise itself. Next, the explanation states:

Regarding the appellation "Mahāmati" (Great Wisdom), it possesses both the provisional and the ultimate; it is the perfection of both compassion and wisdom. Only when one contemplates both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) simultaneously can one be called Mahāmati.

This single meaning of Mahāmati encompasses both *upāya* (skillful means) and *prajñā* (wisdom), which is precisely the contemplation of the Middle Way. It is truly because the provisional and the ultimate are non-dual that it is termed "Great."

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is, in reality, the thorough investigation of principle; it is, in its provisional aspect, the mastery of phenomena. Since that which is illuminated—the phenomena and principle—is already a seamless fusion, that which illuminates—the wisdom—is likewise the mutual identity of the provisional and the real.
Thus, this too does not exceed the manifestation of the single meaning previously mentioned.

Furthermore, from within the ultimate nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and the principle of true reality, the functional illumination of the provisional and the real arises. In its real aspect, it illuminates back toward the principle; in its provisional aspect, it penetrates conditions.

Regarding the convergence of phenomena: provisional and ultimate reality are non-dual, which accords with the single principle of the Middle Way. Thus, one should know that the "single principle" is not separate from the preceding five names;
now, by means of wisdom (*jñāna*), it is opened up as a distinct principle and established as the fundamental tenet of the third treatise, the *Prajñā-aprativijñapti-śāstra*.

△ Second Major Section: Composing the Treatise Based on the School. The treatise consists of four chapters. Ancient commentators mostly divide it into four sections:

the conventional truth, the ultimate truth, clarifying the cause, and manifesting the fruit. While this division may accord with the text, there are differences among the four treatises. Regarding this—
This reasoning is incorrect. Consequently, in the first two cases, the ultimate and conventional truths would not be identical; in the latter two cases, cause and effect would not be integrated.

Furthermore, the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional are not known by those at the stage of the cause, nor are the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real employed by those at the stage of the fruit.

Thus, one knows that while the four treatises exist simultaneously, their explanations appear in a temporal sequence. In this school, if one does not practice, that is one thing; but if one does practice, then—
The two wisdoms operate in unison, and the two objects are observed simultaneously. Although the meanings of object and wisdom differ, they certainly do not possess two distinct essences.
From the stage of an ordinary person to that of a sage, the single path remains thus; only then can it be called the "one meaning. Some of the ancients have said:

"The first two treatises clarify the teaching of the two truths, wherein the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual, thereby revealing the principle; the third concerns practice; and the fourth clarifies the fruit. This interpretation is... [extremely profound].
Furthermore, one must know that these four meanings apply to both cause and fruit. For now, following the primary divisions of our school, we shall treat them in three sections:
first, the first two treatises clarify the non-duality of the ultimate and conventional truths to manifest the unity of the object;

second, the third treatise clarifies the non-duality of essence and function to manifest the unity of wisdom; and finally, the fourth treatise clarifies the non-duality of principle and wisdom to manifest the unity of realization. Now...

The first part is divided into two sections: first, the *Wubiquan lun* (Treatise on the Non-Transmigration of Things) establishes conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); second, the *Buzhenkong lun* (Treatise on Non-True Emptiness) reveals the identity with ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Now, for the first section: the reason this treatise was composed at the outset is to clarify the phenomena of conventional truth. This means that when Buddhism reveals principle, it must do so through phenomena;
if one seeks principle apart from phenomena, or clarifies the ultimate apart from the conventional, then even if one avoids extreme views and heterodoxy, one still...

Because [the previous discussion] leaned toward the provisional and the small [vehicles], I shall now first clarify the phenomena of the conventional level (*saṃvṛti-dharma*). Subsequently, in the "Treatise on Non-Emptiness of Reality" (*Na-zhenkong-lun*), I will manifest the ultimate principle (*tattva*).

Furthermore, ordinary people fail to comprehend the nature and characteristics of conventional truth; seeing only arising and ceasing, existence and non-existence, they claim that things undergo incessant transformation.

I now refute all such views; therefore, I establish this treatise first. This is precisely to investigate the meaning of the term "conditioned co-arising" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as previously mentioned. It is largely in agreement with [the preceding].

The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra opens with the four dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), first clarifying the entities that serve as their substratum. This text consists of two parts; the first is the title. *Wubuqianlun*, Chapter One.
"Object" (*wu*) refers to phenomena (*dharma*).
The mundane world is not apart from the three categories (*triskandha*), and the supramundane does not exceed the two fruits (*phala*). There being only these...

Names and appearances are both designated as "things. Even when speaking of temporal divisions such as past and present, time has no separate substance; names are established in reliance upon appearances.

Thus, one merely understands that within names and appearances there is nothing that is not subsumed. Regarding the statement that "there is no transmigration," "transmigration" means movement—that is, the sense of change and transformation.
Now, within the gateway of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are briefly three meanings by which the myriad things cannot undergo transmutation or change. First:

First, clarifying the nature of things; second, clarifying the characteristics of things; third, clarifying the time of things. That fire is hot, wind is mobile, water is moist, and earth is solid—these are the natures of conditions that cannot be altered.
That heaven is honored and earth is base, mountains are high and waters are clear, the noble are pure and the ordinary are defiled—these are the characteristics of conditions that cannot be altered.
From antiquity to the present, from morning to evening, and through the succession of moments—time simply cannot be altered.

This is easy to understand. Furthermore, at this stage of nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there is the principle that "characteristics arise from meaning and meaning is established by characteristics.

This is precisely what the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* refers to as "dharmas produced through causes and conditions. This properly belongs to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*). According to the Dharma-character school (*Faxiang-zong*), the names and numbers of the hundred dharmas each possess their own essential nature (*svabhāva*);
even such things as True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Nirvāṇa are pure entities that are the fruit of the principle. Thus, one knows [this to be] the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The dharma encompassed by this single gate is likewise exhaustive; therefore, it is said that "things do not migrate. This precisely clarifies that within movement there is stillness, and stillness does not obstruct movement.
One should properly grasp this essential meaning and not confuse it with [the mere notion of] eternal constancy. Someone may ask:

"When an ordinary person transforms a single thought into that of a sage, why do you say there is no migration? The answer is: "It is precisely because there is no migration that transformation is possible."

Why is this? Because the two aspects of defilement and purity each persist; because the two natures of reality and delusion each stand established; because the time of delusive defilement is not the time of true purity;
and because nature, aspect, and temporal division each abide in their own original positions. Thus, one is able to enter from the state of an ordinary being into the state of a sage.
The *Treatise* (Lun) states that "discourse" (*yan-yi*), which refers to investigation and interrogation, comes first; therefore, it is called the "first. As for "things" (*wu*), they are—
"Qiān" (transmigration) is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). "The Treatise on the Non-transmigration of Things" (*Wù bù qiān zhī lùn*) is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound).

△ Second, the treatise itself. This section has two parts: first, the introduction of the intent; second, the main argument. The first part has four sections. First, designating things to demonstrate human sentiments.
Now, birth and death alternate with one another:

"birth" refers to arising, and "death" refers to ceasing. These two are also described as "arising and ceasing. Alternatively, between the moments after arising and before ceasing, they are further analyzed into "arising, abiding, change, and ceasing.
This refers to the nature and characteristics of phenomena: when conditions assemble, they arise. When conditions... [disperse, they cease].
When they are separated, they cease. Therefore, we know that the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of birth and death can encompass the mutual interaction of all things.

"To depart" means to pass away. Birth is necessarily an interaction with death, which is called "birth"; death is necessarily an interaction with birth, which is called "death. Thus, when one is in the midst of living, death is present;
when one is in the midst of dying, life exists. Only then can it be called "interaction. Human sentiment does not understand this principle.
To see the time of birth is called "going toward death"; to see the time of death is called "going toward birth.
Cold and heat alternate and shift;
this refers to the seasons of things by means of cold and heat. The extreme of Yin is called cold; the extreme of Yang is called heat. Now, as for cold...

"Summer" refers to the ultimate limit of the generation of yin and yang. While some divide the year into four seasons—spring for growth, summer for maturation, autumn for decline, and winter for falling—here, instead of mentioning the four seasons, "cold and heat" are used. This is because the four seasons do not transcend yin and yang;
the extremes of yin and yang are termed "cold and heat. Therefore, "cold and heat" are paired with the preceding "birth and death" to form a single syntactic unit.

Therefore, the *Yījīng* says: "One cold and one heat—this is called alternating transition. Furthermore, since birth and death already contain the four phases (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), it follows that cold and heat must also contain the four seasons.
Thus, it is said that among the times of all things, nothing exceeds cold and heat as the general principle.
Whether measured by the three periods or ten periods, or by the moments of mental thought, their duration is indefinite.
"Alternating" (*die*) means reciprocal; "transmigrating" (*qian*) means moving away. When cold alternates with heat, it is called "cold";
when heat alternates with cold, it is called "heat. Since they can alternate, one knows that each exists [independently]. People do not understand this; during the time of summer...
It is said: "Cold shifts. When it is cold, one says that heat has departed.
