There is a thing—namely, the "thing" that encompasses all myriad existents, including birth and death, cold and heat.
Flowing. Water moving is called "flowing. This refers to the constant succession of exchanges and transitions in human affairs, which is the natural condition of humanity.
Human nature clings to movement and is always like this. The above clarifies the attachments that are to be remedied.
Below, it also refutes the non-Buddhist outsiders who hold nihilistic views (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), as they deny cause and effect. II. Stating one’s own understanding based on principle (three parts):
1. Inferring the meaning based on principle.
I, however, maintain that this is not so.
The term "maintain" (wei) here refers to the act of critical evaluation. Regarding the principles of the nature and characteristics of all phenomena as asserted by the proponent himself:
they intersect without yielding to one another and alternate without undergoing transition.
What is meant by this?
What is the meaning of the principle that "the superior and inferior are mutually verified"? Second, citing the sutra to establish the point:
The *Prabhāsa-sūtra* says:
It is one among the eight categories of *prajñāpāramitā*.

Its meaning is "dharma" (*dharma*), defined as "normative rule" (*vidhi*) and "sustenance" (*dhṛti*). Whether true or false, defiled or pure, whether matter or mind, or the environment and its inhabitants, each possesses its own normative rules and is sustained by them; this applies universally.
It receives this name because it is a supreme entity.
It has no coming or going and no movement or transition;
this is what is meant by "non-transmigration. Because birth abides in birth, there is no coming; because death abides in death, there is no going. In the interval...

Cold and heat; youth and vigor each abide in their own state, and thus there is no movement or transformation. Alternatively, "coming and going" refers to time, while "shifting and moving" refers to nature and characteristics (*dharmasvabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
Since the nature and characteristics of dependently arisen phenomena abide in each of the three periods of time, it is said that "there is no transmigration.

If one follows the Prajñā school, which largely sweeps away appearances to reveal emptiness, then from form and mind up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), everything is called "pure. Now, I shall borrow this [textual] passage...
The phrase "designated as proof and trust" does not adopt that [opponent's] intention; this can be seen from the subsequent self-investigation and explanation.
The word "this" (*zhe*) cites the sutra. △ Third, the investigation and explanation of the correct principle.
Now, regarding "seeking" (xún) the "immovable" (bùdòng) action:
"seeking" means to investigate thoroughly. "Now" (*fú*) is a particle. "Immovable" refers to what the Sūtra says: "without going, coming, moving, or shifting.
"Action" (*zuò*) means to investigate. One seeks within the Sūtras for that which is immovable among all phenomena.
How could one abandon movement to seek stillness?
First, I shall refute the erroneous interpretation that seeks stillness by abandoning movement;
one must instead seek stillness within all movements.

This clarifies the true intent of the sutras: one must certainly seek stillness within the multitude of movements; thus, amidst movement, one realizes that nature and characteristics each abide in their own place.
Because one necessarily seeks stillness within all movements, though there is movement, it is eternally still.
The first phrase restates what preceded; the second phrase explains and establishes my own intention.

Since the sutra seeks stillness within movement, I perceive constant stillness amidst the alternating transitions of birth and death and the successive changes of cold and heat; therefore, it is said that [the common view] is not so.
One does not abandon movement in order to seek stillness; therefore, although there is stillness, it is not separate from movement.

This also first restates what preceded, while the following phrase explains and establishes the intent of the sutra. "Although there is stillness" means that phenomena have no coming, going, moving, or shifting.

It is manifested without departing from change and passing away; therefore it is said that "it does not depart from movement. Thus, what is perceived is movement yet stillness, which accords with the Sūtra’s statement that "it is stillness yet movement.
△ Third, clarifying the contradiction between emotional understanding and true realization. This section has four parts. First, a general presentation of delusion and awakening.
Thus, this is a transitional phrase following the preceding section; because it deduces the purport of the scripture,
movement and stillness have never been different from the outset.
When one uses the sūtras to verify one's own intent, it is seen that the nature and characteristics of the arising and ceasing of dharmas produced by conditions are eternally quiescent; thus,
movement and stillness are not different,
yet those who are deluded do not perceive them as such.
Those who are deluded do not see death while they are alive; consequently, they cling to the notion that life is quiescent while death is active, and so forth.
Thus, because movement and stillness are treated as distinct, these conditions cause true words to stagnate in contentious debate.
A "mantra" (zhēnyán) refers to words that accord with reality. "Competitive disputation" (jìngbiàn) refers to contentious speech.

Those who are deluded cling to the notions of difference or non-difference; because their speech contradicts what accords with reality, there arises contentious speech, which causes mantras to become obstructed.
"School and path.
"Path" means the Way. Because the Way, in which movement and stillness are not different, is that which scholars take as their primary reliance, they submit to the preference for novelty.

This refers to being suppressed. Those who are deluded prefer the extraordinary and engage in forced explanations; consequently, they cause the fundamental path to be suppressed by erroneous interpretations.
△ Second, showing that the principle is difficult to express in words.
Therefore, the ultimate limits of stillness and agitation are not easily discussed. "Agitation" refers to movement.
As for the movement and stillness of things, their principle reaches its ultimate point in non-duality.
Because those who are deluded cling to duality and insist on disputing it, this cannot be spoken of in a hasty or superficial manner. △ Third, inferring and explaining its meaning.
Why is this? To elaborate on the meaning of these difficult words:
to discourse on the ultimate truth is to oppose worldly convention; to conform to worldly convention is to deviate from the ultimate truth.
To speak according to reality contradicts worldly convention; to conform to conventional views violates ultimate truth. Therefore, it is not easy to speak of this.
Because they deviate from the Real, they are deluded regarding their nature and fail to return to it.
This is the error of departing from the truth. Human sentiments are long deluded regarding the nature of things; if one follows them, one cannot return to awakening.
Because it runs counter to worldly custom, it is said to be bland and flavorless.
To emerge [from the mundane] is to go against worldly conventions. "Faint" (dàn) means flavorless. To discuss the Truth is to oppose the world;
worldly views do not understand it, and thus there is no meaningful flavor to be gleaned. Hence, it is said that the words are faint. The *Laozi* says: "Music and delicacies cause travelers to stop;
when the Way emerges from the mouth, it is faint and without flavor. △ Fourth, connecting the preceding to the subsequent.

This is the condition for delusion. Those who understand explain that the principles of movement and stillness are identical; those who are confused cling to the notion that movement and stillness differ, which serves as the condition for the delusions of mediocre people.
Ordinary people have not yet distinguished between existence and non-existence;

those of middling faculties may be spoken to regarding the superior, and may likewise be spoken to regarding the inferior. Therefore, they are unable to discern between delusion and awakening, or the heterodox and the orthodox.
Should one preserve the same while discarding the different, or preserve the different while discarding the same? The following discussion is precisely intended for this capacity.
For those of superior capacity already know that movement and stillness are not different.
The inferior person claps his hands and pays no heed;

this refers to those previously mentioned who are deluded. To "clasp the hands" while stubbornly adhering to one's views without turning back and disregarding correct principle is the manner of great laughter.
As the *Daodejing* says, "If it does not provoke laughter, it cannot be considered the Way. These first two phrases are derived from that source.
The *Daodejing*. This text has been slightly revised.
Regarding that which is near yet unknowable:
physical principles are close to human beings, yet they cannot be grasped through the knowledge of those who understand only movement and stillness. As it says below:
Is it not simply the nature of phenomena?
It is "only" (or "solely") so. There is only the nature of the dependent origination of all things; within movement there is constant stillness, and stillness does not obstruct movement.
This principle is most proximate, yet people do not know it. This refers to the single gate of "nature" among the three preceding meanings.

The *Great Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra* discusses non-transmigration (*akṣaya*) in three senses: first, the non-transmigration of that which depends [upon something else], which here refers to the meaning of nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*);

second, the non-transmigration of the basis upon which things depend; and third, the non-transmigration of the basis alone, which clarifies the meaning of the true nature (*tathatā*) as being constantly abiding and unchanging while following conditions, as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*. △ Fourth, the manifestation of the intent for establishing this treatise.
However, following the preceding discourse on its arising, the underlying principle is extremely difficult to express; therefore, one should remain silent.
Yet, because those of mediocre capacity do not understand that the nature of things is thus, it is said below:
Unable to restrain myself (where "yi" means to stop), I shall for the time being entrust my mind to the juncture between movement and stillness.
"Liao" means briefly; "ji" means the boundary. Movement takes stillness as its boundary, and thus one perceives stillness through movement.
Stillness takes movement as its boundary, and thus one perceives movement through stillness. I have briefly entrusted my understanding in this manner; therefore, I say:
It is not that it is necessarily so. Let me attempt to discuss this: "Necessarily" (*bi*) means decisively;
"attempt" (*shi*) means provisionally. How could it mean that it is decisively so? Rather, one uses this to resolve the mind.
This is merely a commentary. △ Second, the main discussion. This section has three parts: first, the direct manifestation of non-transmigration;

second, the reconciliation and explanation of the scriptural intent; third, the conclusion regarding cause and effect and its benefits. Now, the principles of permanence and impermanence regarding all phenomena are fundamentally non-dual.

Although things arise through conditions and perish through conditions, undergoing moment-to-moment succession, arising and ceasing each occupy their own place, and gathering and dispersing occur at different times. Thus it is with the people of the world...
The mind is unable to examine things with clarity; seeing that they momentarily exist, it clings to their persistence, and seeing that they suddenly perish, it clings to their transience.

Both of these states merely bind oneself to the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism. Furthermore, clinging to persistence is easily recognized, whereas being stalled in clinging to transience is difficult to turn back from.

Because of the adherence to the notion of change, one fails to understand that within the gateway of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the nature and characteristics of arising and ceasing each attain their own station, and the beginning and end of the causes and effects of good and evil do not deviate.
Therefore, this treatise first elucidates the correct principle of non-transmigration; next, it reconciles and explains how the two teachings of permanence and impermanence lead to the same goal;
and finally, it concludes by means of cause and effect so as to make known the benefit. The intent of this treatise does not exceed this.
Because of these three [points], we now replace the six categories of the ancients with merely three sections. Regarding the first section, the text has three parts.
First, citing the teachings to establish the school’s tenet; this part has two sections. First, citing the sūtras and śāstras.
The Path-Practitioner says:
"The 'Small Chapter' (Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya) is one enumeration of all dharmas."

These are phenomena (*dharma*). That is to say, form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The six sense organs and the six objects are called the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).
Adding the six consciousnesses makes the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*). Worldly phenomena do not exceed these three categories.

Furthermore, to speak more briefly, they are subsumed under the general categories of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Moreover, bodhi and nirvāṇa are supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*). Now, all [of these] together—
Reflecting upon this, it is said that all phenomena (*dharmas*) fundamentally have nowhere from which they come, and likewise, they have nowhere to which they go; they do not transmigrate.
"Fundamentally" refers to the place from which they arise; "to which they go" refers to the destination where they arrive. This is because of all [phenomena]...
The nature, characteristics, and temporal divisions of phenomena each abide in their own fundamental positions; they have never moved from their origin to arrive at another place.
That is to say, one does not see the fundamental nature coming from the state of ordinary beings to reach the realm of the sages.
Nor does one see it coming from the midst of birth-and-death and afflictions to reach the abode of bodhi and nirvana. Why is this? Because of the identity of the sage and the ordinary being.
Because defilement and purity do not reach one another, and because mundane and supramundane phenomena each abide in their own respective positions;
other cases may be understood by analogy. The *Avataṃsaka* also says: "Each and every thing does not know the others; all phenomena are likewise.

According to the main body of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it primarily elucidates the True Doctrine of signlessness (*animitta*), directly revealing that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and devoid of the characteristics of coming and going. Now...
The texts borrowed here share the same fundamental tenets, yet their underlying intentions differ; this can be seen within the section on "Determining the Tenets" below.
As for *Madhyamaka*, it refers to the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*; I shall now cite it to explain and establish the meaning of the sūtra.
It is said that by observing one knows that another has departed.
"Observing" means seeing. "Directions" refers to the ten directions; for now, let us take the eastern direction as an example. "That person" is a general reference to someone else.
When I observe the eastern direction, I know that such-and-such a person has departed from here.
"The one who goes does not arrive at a destination.

"The one" refers to the person. As the person going to the east has their front step ahead and their back step behind, the characteristic of moving from this place to that destination is not perceived.
Therefore, it is said that "going also has no destination. By reversing [the perspective], one knows [it] from the eastern direction.
Coming to this region, it likewise abides at every step; therefore, it is said that it fundamentally comes from nowhere.
As it is with the eastern direction, so it is with the other nine. Since the person is both in motion and at rest, by analogy all phenomena are both changing and unchanging.
Thus, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* is cited to explain and establish the practice of the Way, thereby founding the central tenet of non-transmigration. △ Next, the central tenet is established.
All of these seek stillness within movement; thus it is clear that things do not transmigrate.
"This" refers to this very point; "all" means they are identical. The aforementioned sutras and treatises likewise seek stillness by means of movement.

Using this as proof, the principle that conditions produce phenomena is established, and the meaning that their nature and characteristics do not transmigrate is already clarified. This section concludes the application of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The Authority of Sacred Teaching (āptāgama). △ Second, destroying delusion to reveal the principle. This section has two parts. First, a comparative analysis of delusion and awakening. This further has two parts.
First, the identity of the object and the difference in views.
Now, that which people call "movement" is—
The statement that "all phenomena are in flux" accords with the common experience of human beings.
Since past things do not persist into the present—just as death alternates with life—the living become past things and the dead become present things; therefore, life does not [persist].
This remains true even to this day.
Therefore it is said that movement is not stillness.

Those who are deluded see that at the time of death there is no birth, and because they believe that birth has already passed away, they cling to the notion that there is only movement and no stillness.
What I call "quiescence" refers back to the preceding [argument], whereas you maintain that it is not so.
Furthermore, because past things do not arrive in the present (as stated above), I say it is quiescent rather than moving.
According to the Master’s interpretation, birth is a thing of the past existing in the past, and death is a thing of the present existing in the present;

therefore, since the past does not reach the present, it is described as "quiescent" rather than "active. By analogy with this, cases such as birth succeeding death, or the alternation of cold and heat, can be understood.
It is movement rather than stillness, because it does not come;
those who are deluded grasp at movement as a vision of what was not here before but is now.
It is stillness rather than movement, because it does not go.

The Master of the Treatise, seeing that [the object] is quiescent, already knows that the former thing abides in its former state and does not depart; this is precisely the resolution of delusions within the preceding introduction.
△ Second, the summary critique of the inverse and the conforming.
Thus, that which is created has never been different;
it is the act of creation itself. Since we see that things of the past do not arrive in the present, the realm reached is no different, yet what is seen has never been the same.
To resolve the confusion regarding what is seen: stillness and movement are not the same.
To act contrary to this is called obstruction; to act in accordance with it is called penetration.

To go against the principle while clinging to movement is what is meant by one who is obstructed and stagnant; to accord with the principle while perceiving stillness is what is meant by one who has penetrating understanding.

As for this, many ancients relied on the Master of the Treatise to explain the principles of the inverse and the direct, or penetration and obstruction; yet such a principle does not exist in reality.
If one truly attains the Way, what further hindrance could there be?
If it is so—that the Way is the principle of phenomena—then once one grasps these principles, there is no movement that is not stillness.
How could there be any delusion or stagnation regarding movement? △ Second, Dispelling Delusion to Reveal Principle (in five parts): First, Lamenting Deluded Attachments.
It is lamentable that human sentiment has been deluded for so long.

People have been deluded by the attachments of their own emotions, remaining unaware from time immemorial; thus, it is a matter for sorrow that they face the Truth before their very eyes yet fail to perceive it.
The "Real" means that past things do not arrive in the present. Although they appear, one clings to movement; thus, though they face one's eyes, one remains unaware of them.
△ Second, the description of deluded sentiments.
Since one knows that past things do not come,
and reiterating that former things do not reach the present— referring to the "past"—
one might then claim that present things can go [to the future].
This is precisely the prior adherence to the view that there is motion and no stillness. "Wang" (往) means to go.

Since one already adheres to the notion that past things do not reach the present as being "motion," one must necessarily claim that present things can likewise migrate and pass away. This is merely a delusion of sentiment.
△ Third, revealing the correct principle. The text has four parts. First, the heading.
In the past, things did not come; now, where would things go? They depart.
Although the deluded understand that things of the past do not come, they do not realize that things of the present do not go.
If one knows that the present thing is in the present and does not go, one will also understand that the thing of the past was in the past and did not go; this is non-transmigration.

This is evident. Thus, that which dwelt in antiquity dwells in antiquity, and that which dwells in the present dwells in the present; the present and the ancient do not come and go between one another.
△ Second, the inference: Why is this so?
An examination of the first two lines. △ Third, the explanation. This section has two parts. First, the explanation of the preceding line:
"Seeking the object of the past within the past; in the past, it was never non-existent. "Past" refers to antiquity.
Seeking the object of antiquity within the time of antiquity, it must have certainly existed then. Therefore, we know that [the self] resided in its ancient position.
If one holds the present object accountable for the present, it has never existed in the present.
If one traces and holds the past object accountable at the present time, the past is not seen in the present;
it has never existed in the present. This clarifies that objects do not come.
We clearly know that things of the past do not arrive in the present;
yet, they have never been absent from the preceding moment. Thus we know that things do not depart.
Because we see the past as it was in the past, we know there is no transition or movement. Why, then, are you deluded into claiming that there is motion and no stillness?
Yes. The above explains that, according to the ancient [teaching], there is no coming or going. △ Next, the subsequent phrase is explained:
"Seeking the present by reversing [the inquiry], the present likewise does not go away.
By repeatedly investigating the present object through this inversion, one knows that the present object exists in the present and does not depart—not only...
It does not go. Since it was known as such in the past and will not head toward the future, it is therefore not in motion.

This above passage explains the meaning of "there is no coming now. One need only transpose the terms from the preceding text: what was called "heading" is here "now," what was "now" is "heading," what was "coming" is "going," and what was "going" is "coming.
This can be seen by reading it thus. It is like a person who has both youth and old age: while youth dwells in the past, old age dwells [in the present].
Nowadays, many people are deluded by this. When they reach old age and decline, no longer seeing their former vigor, they claim that youth has already passed away.
They fail to reflect that during their youth, their skin and tissues were moist and lustrous; thus, they know it existed in the past. Why then do they seek it now?
Having already fallen into confusion and delusion, they further claim it has departed when they cannot find it. Therefore...

Know that this is a profound delusion. One who understands the nature of things realizes that past and present each abide in their own place; there is not even a hair’s breadth that can be altered. △ Fourth, the conclusion:

This is called "the thing of the past abides in the past; it does not come from the present to the past. The thing of the present abides in the present; it does not [come from the past to the present]."
From the past until the present, this can be seen.
△ Fourth, citing Confucian texts, in two parts. First, the direct citation:
Therefore, Zhongni said, "Hui, when you see someone new, their arms crossed with them are not those of the old."
The passage originates from the "Tian Zifang" chapter of the *Outer Chapters* of the *Zhuangzi*. It states:
"Confucius said to Yan Hui, 'I have spent my entire life walking shoulder-to-shoulder with you, yet I have lost you at every turn. Is this not a cause for lamentation? Guo's commentary says:
'Transformation and change cannot be grasped or retained; therefore, even if one holds another’s arm and stays close together, one cannot cause them to remain still. (Master Kang [Kang Falang]...)
The Commentary states: Guo’s annotation is incorrect. He meant that in the brief moment of crossing arms, one has already lost the person before them;
he did not mean that crossing arms or grasping hands cannot cause one to pause. Now, following Master Kang’s explanation of "crossing arms," it is like two arms intersecting.
In this brief interval alone, one has already seen the new supplant the old.
If one were to point to the subsequent passage in the *Lunyu* to clarify the meaning of the new and the old each abiding in their own place, it remains unclear what Confucius’s original intent was.

If Confucius had meant that things do not migrate, why would he have lamented over such matters? If he had meant, "I and you shall remain companions for a lifetime," [then his words would have been different].
In the brief interval of an arm’s movement, that which Guo [Xiang] referred to as "transformation being unable to cause it to remain" captures the essential meaning very well.
The minor revisions in the text of this present treatise merely adopt meanings where Confucianism and Buddhism accord; they do not intend to equate one with the other.
As for the statement regarding seeing the "new," this refers to the fact that the present object exists now by itself and is not the "old"; that is, it is not the former past.

Things have been as they are since antiquity; it has been but a brief moment. If even today and yesterday each abide in their own respective world, how much more so for days, months, years, and kalpas? △ Second, the conclusion.
Thus, it is clear that things do not come and go.
To restate what Confucius said above: the new and the old each abide in their own place; the principle that things have no coming or going is thereby made manifest.
△ Fifth, the Rebuttal of Sentiment:
Since there is not even the slightest trace (*liǎn*) of coming and going, what entity could possibly be moved?
"Coming and going" refers to departing and arriving; "the slightest trace" refers to a minute mark. This is an investigation into the nature, characteristics, and temporal divisions of all phenomena.
If one seeks the traces of coming and going, not even a hair’s breadth can be found. It is unknown what substance the deluded have that they could claim to be "moving" rather than "still.
From the opening of the title through this section of the introduction, the refutation of the view that clings to motion is complete.
△ Third, citing examples to conclude and clarify.
Thus, even as the whirlwind topples the mountains, they remain eternally still.

From the opening chapter onwards, this has fully demonstrated that the myriad phenomena do not transmigrate; therefore, I now cite these points to conclude the argument. "Whirlwind" (*xuānlán*) is also called *bílán*;
according to the *Huáyán yìnyì* (Meanings and Pronunciations of the Avataṃsaka), the correct Sanskrit term is *vairambha*, which translates to [the wind that shakes the world].
"Scattering" (*san*) refers to where it reaches; it is a name for wind. Wherever this wind reaches, there is nothing that is not scattered and destroyed.

Furthermore, it is translated as "not slow. In meaning, it is translated as the "swift and violent wind. "Yanxi" (偃息) means to topple. "Yue" (嶽) means mountain. To topple mountains and peaks is precisely the scattering and destruction wrought by the wind.
Kang [Senghui] said: "Yan" (偃) means to fall prostrate; it also takes on the sense of destruction. He cites the swift and violent wind to illustrate "toppling."
The myriad peaks cease their movement, yet there is no place they do not reach; yet the wind is ultimately not the mountains, and the mountains are ultimately not the wind.
Since they are neither identical nor do they meet, they are said to be eternally still. Thus we know that the nature and characteristics of the wind and the mountains each abide in their own place;
though the wind blows with violent force, it is eternally still. The following three phrases should be understood by this analogy.
The rivers rush forth in competition yet do not flow.
Although the waters race forward, the preceding wave and the succeeding wave do not reach one another; thus, they do not flow.
Furthermore, because they ultimately cannot alter their moist nature, they do not move.
"The wild horse (yema) drifts and billows without moving.
Zhuangzi says it is "the wild horse," and Guo's commentary explains it as "wandering qi.

Because the solar energy is intensely pent-up during the month of the three yangs, one sees wandering qi drifting and billowing; it surges and subsides, remaining distinct in its front and rear positions, and thus does not move.
The sun and moon traverse the heavens but do not complete a full circuit.

"Traverse" means to pass through. The celestial wheel rotates to the left, while the sun and moon revolve to the right; as their respective temporal divisions remain fixed, they traverse the celestial wheel without manifesting the appearance of a complete circumambulation.
Furthermore, what is so strange? "Strange" means extraordinary.
That which moves is immediately still; in all four [states], there is no shifting. How could there be any moving characteristic to be considered strange or extraordinary?

Next, regarding the reconciliation of the meaning of the teaching: in the Buddhist conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are two gates. The first is the gate of permanence (*nitya*). It is peaceful...
Establishing the thesis: The meaning is refuted through the two gates of impermanence. The gate of permanence refutes annihilationism, and the gate of impermanence refutes eternalism.

These two teachings emerge from the same source yet are presented differently. Although the teachings do not stand side-by-side, their attachments must both be eliminated. In principle, they must converge;
the preceding Master [Nāgārjuna] thus used motion to explain stillness, ensuring that stillness does not differ from motion, so as to bring these two teachings into harmony.

The mutual identity [of subject and object] reveals the principle of non-duality. Fearing that practitioners might not understand this intent, he employs an external guest to cite the Buddha’s teachings on impermanence as a point of inquiry.
The purpose is to show that the principle of the non-duality of movement and stillness is no different from the Buddhist doctrine of the non-duality of permanence and impermanence.
The text has two parts. First, citing the teachings to pose a challenge; second, [the response regarding] persons and dharmas. Regarding the first: persons and dharmas...
The two headings are as follows. First, establishing the objection based on doctrine and principle: "Alas!
is an expression of lamenting injustice, for doctrine and principle are in conflict.
"Sage" (shèng rén):
"Sage" means "penetrating. Confucius said to Duke Ai: "A sage is one whose wisdom penetrates the Great Way, responding to changes without end.
Now, in this tradition of the Buddhist school, all point to the Buddha as the Sage; this is because they refer to him according to his manifested traces.

Regarding human relations, whether in times of adversity or success, and in all matters of principle and affairs, there is nothing he does not penetrate; therefore, he is called a "sage" (shengren). The virtues of the Buddha are inconceivable;
for now, I shall explain them according to the meaning of "Right and Universal Knowledge" (Samyak-saṃbuddha).
There is a saying: "The life of a human being passes away with such speed that it is swifter than the flow of a river.
A citation from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Human life does not stop; it passes more swiftly than a mountain stream. I shall now slightly alter the phrasing of this statement.
Regarding "life" (*jīvita*): among the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), there is one dharma called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
This is the essence of the eighth *ālayavijñāna*. It is the sovereign lord of the collective retribution for rebirth; it arrives first at birth and departs last at death.

Upon the substance of this consciousness, there is a function of continuous maintenance that calculates and belongs to the matter and mind of a single lifetime; this is called the life-faculty. It arises and ceases momentarily.
Stop. Like the swift current of a river, this explains the teaching of impermanence and elucidates the principle of impermanence.
△ Second, the fixed refutation regarding practice and fruit:
Thus, the Śrāvakas realize non-eternality to achieve the Way.

The objector fears that although there may be scriptural authority and logical reasoning, they might not necessarily be trustworthy; therefore, the certainty of the scriptural and logical principles is established by means of practice and its results.
A *śrāvaka* (voice-hearer) is one who realizes the Path by hearing the teachings of the voice. One who has realized the Path is one who has realized the nature of partial truth (*pratisaṃvid-satya*).
When a Sage proclaims the teaching of impermanence, the *śrāvaka* hears it and awakens to suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path [leading to its cessation]. Manifesting...
By means of impermanence, they shatter the afflictive obscurations, extinguish the mind of self-clinging, and realize the truth of self-emptiness;
therefore, the eight classes of noble beings are collectively termed Śrāvakas.
The Pratyekabuddha awakens to conditions; by departing from [delusion], he realizes the ultimate reality.

In Sanskrit, he is called *Pratyekabuddha*, which here is translated as "Solitary Awakened One" (*Dujue*). He is also called a "Condition-awakened One" (*Yuanjue*); a Solitary Awakened One is one who attains enlightenment through self-realization.

The term "Pratyekabuddha" (緣覺) refers to one who receives the teaching; here, we take the Pratyekabuddha as the subject. "Condition" (緣) is the object of awakening, namely the twelve links of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time.
"Awakening" (覺) is the wisdom that comprehends this, namely the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (生空觀).

Because they have heard the teachings on impermanence, they awaken to the fact that all phenomena of the three periods of time exist only momentarily through the gathering of conditions, and that when conditions disperse, they are fundamentally empty; thus, it is said that this is "reality" (真). Although their faculties are sharp...

They are superior to the Śrāvakas; however, in breaking through the obstacles of attachment and realizing the truth of self-emptiness (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), there is no distinction. △ Second, restating the previous formal objection:
"If the myriad movements are not transformations (of the Buddha), how can one seek transformation as a means to ascend the Path? (This restates the preceding point.)
That which is not transformed does not migrate. As for the "stages and paths," it is because one realizes the Way through successive stages.

Furthermore, if all phenomena do not migrate, then the doctrinal principles of impermanence would be established in vain. How could the followers of the Two Vehicles seek these teachings on transformation and realize the holy path through successive stages?
Only after the followers of the Two Vehicles have attained the Way do they come to know that the doctrinal principles of impermanence were not in vain. One fears that—

The teachings and principles concerning non-transmigration expounded by the Master of the Treatise cannot yet be accepted with full confidence. △ Second, the explanation and resolution according to principle has two parts.
First, praising the profound depth of the teachings and principles of impermanence.
To re-examine the words of the Sage is called "contemplation" (cintā). To "examine the words of the Sage" refers to the aforementioned teaching on impermanence;
it is subtle, hidden, and difficult to fathom.

This praises the fact that the principle of non-duality within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is difficult to fathom. "Subtle" (*wei*) refers to the wondrous and profound phenomena and dharmas, which cannot be deliberated upon through fixed conceptions of permanence or impermanence.
"Hidden" (*yin*) refers to the secret meaning of non-duality; it lies latent and concealed beneath the teachings.
Therefore, it is difficult to measure or gauge by means of verbal instruction.
If it moves yet remains still, it seems to depart yet stays behind.

According to the aforementioned teachings that explain phenomena, it appears as though movement and departure reside within the nature of things; yet in principle, while it moves, it is eternally still.
To depart while remaining eternally present is the fundamental purport of the Sage’s non-duality. The first phrase clarifies the establishment of the teaching;
the second phrase clarifies the elucidation of phenomena. Therefore, there is this repetition of phrases.
It can be realized through the spirit, but it is difficult to seek through phenomena.

Spiritual understanding can certainly be brought into accord; however, the characteristics of phenomena are inherently difficult to infer or investigate. △ Second, clarifying the profound and subtle doctrinal principles of the permanent and the impermanent;
this section has three parts. First, clarifying that while the teachings differ, their intent is the same; second, one: revealing the differences and similarities based on the fundamental teaching.
Three. First, clarifying the attachment to distinct teachings and their differences, in two parts. First, clarifying the difference:
Therefore, it is said that "going is not necessarily going. This is to set aside people's habitual conceptions; "set aside" (xián) means to prevent.
When the human mind gives rise to the notion of permanence, the sacred teaching speaks of the impermanence of all phenomena to prevent and ward it off.
This does not mean that there is definitely no impermanence.
What is called "abiding" does not necessarily imply remaining static; it is merely an explanation of what people refer to as "passing away.

"Shi" (釋) means to explain or interpret. People cling to the notion of impermanent transition and movement, yet the holy teachings state that all phenomena abide eternally, for the relationship between cause and effect is definitive.
One uses meditative concentration to resolve it, causing one to relinquish what is grasped; this does not mean that concentration is permanent. △ Second, the critique of difference:
How could it be said that what has departed can be sent away, while what remains can be retained?

This can be determined. The two teachings of "departure" and "abiding" are established to shatter the two attachments of annihilationism and eternalism. If these two attachments are eliminated, the teachings no longer need to be fixedly established.
Thus, we know that although the teachings differ, their intent returns to the same point. △ Second, proving that the teachings differ while the intent is the same.
Therefore, the *Chengju* (Siddhārtha) states:
"The *Chengju guangming dingyi jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Light of Accomplishment) says:
'O Bodhisattva...'"
In the Sanskrit language, it is called *bodhisattva*; here, it is translated as "Awakened Being" (*jue youqing*). It is explained according to three meanings, as in the *Vajraśāstra*.
While dwelling amidst those who cling to permanence, he expounds the teaching of impermanence.
Regarding the statement that "Zhengshang says 'going' does not necessarily mean going," this dispels people's ordinary conceptions.
The *Mahāyāna-śāstra* states: "All dharmas are immovable; they have no place from which they come or to which they go.
Zhengshang says that "abiding" does not necessarily mean abiding; this explains what people call "departing. Thus, the above [interpretation] differs from the scriptural teaching. Below...
The underlying intent is the same.
These all serve to guide and lead toward the various quarters.
"Various" means not being one; "quarters" refers to methods. The dharma-gates of the sutras and śāstras are not uniform, yet they all serve to guide and lead those who are attached.
For this reason,
two statements are made:
the gate of permanence speaks of abiding, while the gate of impermanence speaks of departing.
A single convergence.

The principles of permanence and impermanence are unified by this one [convergence]. Why is this? Furthermore, although the myriad dharmas arise and perish without ceasing, each instance of arising and perishing occupies its own position;
yet while these positions are not lost, how could arising and ceasing be permanent? Since movement and stillness are no different, [the two principles are one].

Thus, principle is fundamentally one; this is precisely the purport of the non-duality of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Although it is presented differently according to the capacities of beings, the principle does not vary in its ultimate reach.
This is the profound, subtle, and hidden intent of the Sage, which is difficult to fathom.
How could it be said that Mañjuśrī deviates from its intended meaning?
One cannot claim that because the teachings on the permanent and the impermanent differ, the principle of non-duality itself possesses distinctions.

Therefore, we know that the discourse on the non-transmigration of things is sufficient to exhaustively convey the Sage’s intention regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). △ Third, the conclusion of the non-...
Second: Therefore, it is said that while it is eternal, it does not abide; it is called departing, yet it does not transmigrate.

To speak of eternity and to call it departing constitutes a pair of statements intended as counterpoints to two attachments. Eternity is precisely non-abiding; departure is precisely non-transmigration.
This is because the principles of movement and stillness are one and the same.
Because there is no shifting (repeating the preceding and following phrases), though there is going, it is eternally still;
this is to perceive stillness through movement. It is like perceiving within the cycle of birth and death that birth does not arrive at death; birth and death are each [distinct].
"Abiding. This principle applies to all phenomena as well.
Because they do not abide (restating the preceding phrase), though they are quiescent, they are constantly moving;
thus, one perceives motion within stillness. Although birth and death each appear to abide, birth and death do not cease. These are the following two lines.
These are merely inversions of phrasing; the meaning remains the same.
Because it is quiescent yet constantly proceeding, this restates the preceding point: it is quiescent while moving.
It moves without changing,
thereby manifesting that while it is in motion, it is eternally still.
Because it is eternally still despite its movement, it is still and does not linger.

However, one should infer this by reversing the preceding [analysis]. Previously, stillness was taken as primary; therein, stillness is movement and movement is stillness. Now, movement is taken as primary;
therein, movement is stillness and stillness is movement. This serves to reveal that two words converge upon a single meaning. Part Two:

Revealing Similarities and Differences by Reference to External Teachings. This section has two parts. First, citing the Confucian and Daoist traditions of this land to explain movement in order to reveal stillness.
Thus, this restates the thesis that motion and stillness are non-dual—
the reason why Zhuangzi chose to hide his mountain.
The "Inner Chapters" of the *Zhuangzi*, in the chapter titled "The Great Ancestor," state: "To hide a boat in a ravine or to hide a mountain in a marsh is considered secure;
yet at midnight, a powerful man may carry it off on his back while the oblivious do not know."
Guo’s commentary states: "There is no power greater than transformation than the power of the powerless. Now, taking his meaning:

if a mountain possesses lush growth and one wishes for it not to wither, yet one conceals it within marshes or lakes, its transformations will be obscured and altered; how then could it be made to remain stable?
It is only those who are ignorant who do not understand this.
Regarding Zhongni’s [Confucius] contemplation by the river, the *Analects* states:
"When the Master was by a stream, he said: 'That which passes away is like this; it never ceases day or night. I now borrow this sentiment.
Zhongni used the rapid transformation of human affairs to exhort [others] toward study and the cultivation of virtue. These two sages—"
While Buddhism likewise teaches impermanence to refute permanence, its underlying intent is necessarily to cause one to abandon the one and adopt the other;
how could it possibly require that one realize impermanence through immediate identity?
All of these reflect the difficulty of retaining what has passed; how could it be said that one can "push away" the present and thereby proceed?

"Pushing away" (*pai*) means to set aside; "can" (*ke*) means to determine. Both the teachings of Zhuangzi and Confucius lament the fact that things pass on and are difficult to retain, thus perceiving only movement in a single direction.
What the Master of the Treatise perceives—could he possibly mean that one pushes away and sets aside present things to determine [the future]?
"Is there any transition? This means that within movement, one perceives stillness; it thus clarifies the meaning of "going above" without any actual shifting.
△ Second, citing the account of a neighbor in the Western Land to demonstrate permanence in order to clarify impermanence. The text has four parts. First, stating the primary intent.
Therefore, one who observes the mind of the Sage does not seek to grasp it through the perspectives of ordinary people.
By means of the principle that movement and stillness are non-dual, one must observe the mind with which the Buddha and Sages established their teachings;
if this is necessarily the case, then one cannot apprehend their intent through the perceptions of human sentiment. △ Second, the Inference.
Constant attachment.
What is this? It is explained below by inferring from what people commonly perceive.
Ordinary people say that youth and adulthood constitute a single body.
"Youth" refers to early childhood; "adulthood" refers to those in their thirties. As for "a single body," commoners mean that youth and adulthood are one and the same person.
"A hundred years, one substance.
"Years" refers to age. To dwell in the world for a hundred years is likewise but a single physical form.
One merely knows that the years pass, yet remains unaware that the body follows along with them.

This is merely empty talk. One vainly perceives that there is a "self" which exists in youth and persists through middle age, yet fails to realize that the physical form changes with the years, its states of decline and vigor differing as it transforms.
Because one does not perceive this, one clings to the notion of a single, identical substance; this is a sentiment mired in the attachment to permanence.
△ Third, citing their own texts:
For this reason, the *brahman* leaves the household life.
"Brahman" is fully called *brahmā*; here it means "purity and tranquility," which is to say, "cleansing.

In the Western Land (India), the *brāhmaṇa* who serves the gods is called a "Pure-Vowed One" (*jingzhi*) or also a "Pure-Practitioner" (*xingxing*). Those who leave the household life are precisely these individuals who serve the gods.
He practiced the method of transformation. At fifteen, he entered the mountains, subsisting on grasses and fruits for food and clothing.
At thirty, he returned home, took a wife, and fathered sons to ensure the continuity of his lineage through successive generations. At fifty, he entered the mountains again and never returned;
therefore, it is called "leaving home" (chujia).
He returned with white hair.
There was a certain brahmin who had not returned by the age of thirty; everyone said he was dead.
When he returned at the age of white hair, a neighbor saw him and said, "Is that man still alive?"
This refers to neighbors. Five households constitute a neighborhood; those who know the people living there are called "neighbors.
When a Brahmin has not returned home by the age of thirty, it is said that he is dead. That he still survives now is merely the neighbor's adherence to conventional expectations.
The brahmin said: "I am still the person of old, yet I am not the person of old.
"Still" (*yōu*) means "as before. In the first phrase, he cites his neighbor and points out that he is still the person of old;
in the second phrase, he tells him: "The person of old has passed away. I am now old, therefore I am not the person of old. This is the brahmin's lingering attachment.
"It is impermanent.
The neighbors were all stunned; they did not believe his words.
"Stunned" means to be struck with alarm. The neighbors remained obstinate; hearing that he was no longer the person of former times, they were shocked and refused to believe him.

Therefore, it is said that these are not his words. Although the Brahmin cited above maintains impermanence while the neighbor maintains permanence, it is solely by means of the neighbor’s view of permanence that impermanence is revealed. Thus, the conclusion below states: △ Fourth, revealing impermanence.
This refers to the passage from the *Zhuangzi*: "A strong man carries it on his back and runs away, while the deluded do not perceive it.

This concludes the refutation by borrowing from that text. Although the neighbor clings to the notion that the person of former times still exists, he does not realize what Zhuangzi meant by impermanence:
that a powerful force carries one away and flees, such that there is no abiding in renewal from moment to moment.

It does not cease. This is because the ignorant neighbor is unaware of this principle of impermanence. Thus, the neighbor clings to permanence and perceives only the past, while the brahmin clings to impermanence and perceives only the present.
If the present and the past were each to abide independently, then permanence would itself be impermanent;

it is only by synthesizing these two views that one arrives at the correct principle. For now, I have merely used the neighbor’s clinging to permanence as a point of reference to conclude [the argument].
This reveals impermanence; it is precisely what was previously stated as "being still yet not remaining.
Is this not what that refers to? "Qi" (其) means "that"; "si" (斯) means "this"; "wei" (謂) is a term used for "to say. Zhuangzi said: "The ignorant do not know. Now, [it is] neighboring...
"People do not know that within the permanent there is the impermanent"—this is precisely what those words mean. The particle "乎" (hu) is merely a grammatical particle.

II. Revealing the Provisional Intent and the Reality. Although it was previously clarified that while the teachings differ, their intent is the same, one might still not understand the principles of their agreement and difference;
therefore, they are now demonstrated so that one may penetrate the provisional and the real. This section has five parts. First, the dual presentation of the teachings and their intent.
Therefore, the Tathāgata— the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata—
teaches the doctrines of permanence and impermanence according to conventional truth, in accordance with the dispositions of sentient beings.
The "multitude" is not uniform, for they are obstructed by the two attachments to annihilationism and eternalism.
They are stuck in the two realms of existence and non-existence; these aforementioned ailments to be remedied serve as the cause for the arising of the teaching.
Thus, local dialects are used to distinguish and dispel delusions.
The Sage establishes conventional teachings on permanence and impermanence as skillful means to analyze and dissect deluded sentiments; these are precisely the medicines capable of treating them.
One rides upon the true mind of non-duality.

That which accords with the principle of the non-duality of the constant and the impermanent is called the "true mind. Because the teachings are established by riding upon and employing this mind, it emits the diverse teachings of manifoldness.
This means to expound. It refers to the teaching of two doctrines in response to the two types of grasping.

That which appears divergent (the difference in teachings) yet is not actually different (the oneness of principle)—is this not uniquely the sacred word? (This restates the preceding points regarding identity and difference.)
Only in Buddhism do these words differ while their meaning remains the same. △ Second, the simultaneous clarification of the provisional and the real:
thus, when discussing the True, it is called "discussing the True" because one speaks of stillness amidst movement.
There are those who claim there is no transmigration;
they are those who destroy the adherence to impermanence and repudiate the principle of cause and effect,
leading the common people astray.
Because worldly views are largely conservative and prone to creating complications, he spoke of movement within stillness to guide and engage them. There is the teaching of flux:

that all things are impermanent and do not remain for even a single kṣaṇa; that the past and present succeed one another. Above, this reveals the provisional nature of the teachings; below, it clarifies the ultimate reality of the intent.
Although there are a thousand divergent paths and differing expositions, they ultimately converge upon the same destination.

"A thousand" is used to denote a great number; "paths" refers to ways. Although the teachings established according to various attachments may have many different paths, if one accords with the principle to which they all return, one must perceive stillness within movement and perceive movement within stillness; therefore, it is said that they are the same.
Thus, one knows that while the teaching is provisional, the underlying intent is real. △ Third, regarding the reproach of those who cling to the literal teaching and demand textual evidence:
"demanding" refers to demanding adherence to the text.
This follows the previous section where those who clung to the literal words were interrogated and refuted.
Hearing that there is no transition, one says that past things do not arrive in the present.
Because the former object is seen by all to be different from its state in the middle [of the process], and because it does not arrive from the past, the Master says: "It is quiescent, not moving.
Upon hearing this, the objector concludes: "Then it must be something static."
To "listen to the moving" means to say that present things can reach the past;
it refers to hearing. Hearing the movement of the superior person’s life passing swiftly, one says that present things can depart—this is called "movement."
This, too, does not depart from the sentiment expressed in the preceding passage—that movement is not stillness.

Since the objector has not yet attained an understanding of the principle of non-duality, they perceive stillness in the fact that past things do not arrive in the present, and they regard the fact that present things can reach the past as movement.
Both of these are merely calculations based on emotional conceptualization; therefore, the previous critique asked: "Since past things do not come, what is there for present things to go to?"

[The Master] went on: "Since your attachments have not yet been severed, you still harbor difficulties arising from clinging to the two teachings of movement and stillness. Below, he rebukes the view that clings to movement, saying:
'If it is already called "past and present," why do you wish to shift it?'"

Since it is said that "the ancient abides in the ancient" and "the present abides in the present," what is the intention of those who, out of deluded attachment, wish to transfer the present into the ancient?
△ Fourth, the refutation of the view of impermanence: This refers to the previous objection, which used the teachings, principles, practices, and fruits of impermanence to pose a challenge.
Since it has already been demonstrated above that the two [traditions] are identical in their teachings and principles, this section now refutes that partiality.
This is attachment.

Therefore, when it is said that "the past [teaching of impermanence] does not necessarily go," this is intended to dispel such attachment. That which exists eternally across antiquity and the present does so because it is immovable.
Because past and present each exist within their own time without moving, how could one hear of impermanence and immediately conclude that [the self] must definitely depart?
Or perhaps you have explained it as referring to the past, intending thereby to dispel those who cling to the teaching of permanence;
however, we are currently refuting those who posit objections based on the notion of movement, and therefore we do not accept your interpretation.

To say "it departs" (which also cites the teaching on impermanence) does not necessarily mean it departs; rather, it is used to dispel attachment. This means that it does not proceed from the present to the past, because it does not come.

The previous elimination of attachments was intended to make known that the ancient and the modern each exist [separately]. This present elimination of attachments is intended to lead to the realization that the modern does not depart from the ancient, nor does the ancient come to the modern;

both are explained as this principle of permanence within the teaching of impermanence. This is because, as in the former case of "seeking stillness within movement," the teaching and the principle illuminate one another.
Because they do not come, they do not gallop through past and present;
for "galloping" refers to the incessant cycle of going and coming.
Because they are unmoving, each nature abides within its own single world.

The ancient abiding and the present abiding each constitute a single world, for the ancient abides in the ancient and the present abides in the present. △ Fifth, the conclusion establishing non-duality:
Thus, while the provisional teachings cited above differ in their intent, their reality is identical.
The texts of various schools differ in their phrasing;
the various sutras speak of both permanence and impermanence;
and the hundred schools present divergent doctrines.
Various treatises speak of "going" and "staying";
if one truly grasps their underlying convergence, how could divergent phrasing be capable of causing confusion?
If one accords with the principle that the permanent and the impermanent are non-dual, then how could divergent phrasing ever be a source of delusion? △
The meaning of the three religions is further revealed as being non-transmigratory. This section has four parts. First, the religious teachings reveal the underlying meaning:
"Therefore," [it is said], which restates that while the Buddhist teachings differ according to the capacities of sentient beings, their fundamental principle remains the same.
What others call "abiding," I speak of as "departing.
Now, people cling to the doctrine of permanence, whereas the Master speaks of it; for this school holds that all is impermanent and establishes its teaching upon impermanence.
What people call "departing from me" refers to its abiding;

this is spoken by the proponents of the doctrine of impermanence. Since this school establishes its teaching based on permanence, although departing and abiding differ (differing according to the capacity of the audience and the specific teaching), their ultimate intent is one and the same.
The former phrase speaks of impermanence within permanence; the latter phrase speaks of permanence within impermanence.
Thus we know that seeing stillness within total movement and seeing movement within total stillness leads to the same realization. It is not only the latter school that is thus;
the original intent of seeking stillness within prior movement is likewise so. △ Second, citing evidence of profound depth.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Right words appear to be contrary; who would believe them?

This means that when words of correct principle speak of permanence and impermanence as if they were contradictory, those who have not yet realized the principle of non-duality will doubt and fail to believe.
The character "zi" (字) here serves to cite the Sūtra. The ancient commentary states: "This passage appears in the *Lalitavistara* (Puyao jing)."
These words have their basis.
These words are words that are not easily believed. Because the principle is non-dual while the words express duality, those who do not penetrate this truth often fail to believe.
△ Third, an analysis and explanation of movement and stillness.
What is the meaning of "the subtle ascending toward oneness"? People seek the past; yet regarding the present, they say it does not abide.
Ordinary people do not see the past within the present; they grasp at the past as something that has shifted and no longer abides.
I, however, seek [the truth] in the present. From the past, I know that [the essence] does not depart;
the Master of Treatises was not seen in ancient times, yet we know that present things exist in the present and do not depart.
If the present were to reach the past, the past should possess the present. If the past were to come to the present, the present should possess the past.
By reversing this explanation, we see that while the present exists, the past does not; thus, one knows that [the past] does not come.
The ancient abides in antiquity and does not come;
being ancient, there is no present, and thus one knows it does not go.
The present abides in the present and does not go—this is the exegesis in accordance with the preceding [verse].

If the past does not come to the present, and the present likewise does not go to the past, then each phenomenon abides in its own nature. Within a single world-age, what thing could possibly come or go?
As for phenomena, a present phenomenon resides in the present, and a past phenomenon resides in the past. △ Fourth, the conclusion demonstrating non-transmigration.
Thus, the movement and stillness mentioned above are non-dual;
the four signs race like the wind.
Spring, summer, autumn, and winter are called the four images (*sìxiàng*). The transition and change of the four seasons rush as swiftly as the wind;

the celestial sphere (*xuánjī*) rolls like a flash of lightning. The *Shūjìng* says: "By means of the *xuánjī* and *yùhéng*, one aligns the seven administrative powers. *Xuán* is the name of a jade; both *jī* and *héng* are [astronomical instruments]. *Jī*...
The Sovereign possesses the instruments for rectifying the celestial patterns: the *heng* (transverse tube) is positioned horizontally above, while the *ji* (revolving ring) moves below;
both are adorned with jade. Thus it is called the "Jade Tube of the Revolving Ring of the Seven Luminaries," referring to the sun, moon, and five planets.

As the revolving ring turns below, the Sovereign gazes directly at the inch-long aperture of the Jade Tube; thus he knows the movements and changes of the celestial patterns, thereby examining them with precision.
Regarding administrative affairs, I shall now borrow that meaning for my purpose, taking only the sense of the *xuánjī* (celestial sphere) revolving as swiftly as a flash of lightning;
hence it is called "swiftly unrolling like lightning. As for the common ancient claim that *xuánjī* is one of the two names for the Big Dipper (*běidǒu*), I fear that this explanation is incorrect.
The *muhūrta* (moment) is swift, yet it does not move.

A *muhūrta* refers to the smallest unit of time, as subtle as the tip of a hair. If, regarding a single hair-tip, one realizes that its nature and characteristics abide each in their own original position, then all things may be said to be non-transient.
Although the four celestial signs and the *xuánjī* (celestial sphere) appear to move with the speed of the wind, they remain as they are.
Although electricity does not cease, it abides at each stage; thus, it is movement that is itself stillness.

Previously, because outsiders did not understand that movement is discussed within the midst of stillness, they clung to the teachings of impermanence regarding doctrine, practice, and fruition, thereby giving rise to difficulties.

Having already clarified the identity and differences between the provisional and the real, and having harmonized the principle of non-duality so that it is no different from the Buddha's teaching, we now manifest stillness through movement.

This establishes that the practitioner should once again reflect upon the principle of non-transmigration previously mentioned, thereby defining it as the tenet of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Someone might ask:
"If this is so, which of the two vehicles' paths and fruits is correct and which is incorrect? The answer is: conventionally they are correct, but ultimately they are incorrect.
Since this treatise is a teaching that discards the provisional and establishes the ultimate, the paths and fruits of the two vehicles are precisely what is to be refuted.

This is because they are biasedly attached to the teaching of impermanence. If one realizes the principle that movement and stillness are non-dual, then emptiness and existence will naturally be illuminated simultaneously;

by relinquishing the provisional to return to the ultimate, one accords with the Middle Way. Therefore, it should be known that the previous citation of the practices and fruits of the Two Vehicles as a challenge is not logically established.
The above concludes the explanation of the intended meaning of the teachings. △ Third Section: Causes.

Regarding the benefit of establishing the fruit and its connection: when sages establish their teachings, they must necessarily provide some benefit. Since movement is used here to manifest stillness, one already knows that the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is in reality the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Thus, by now citing cause and fruit, it is intended to lead to the realization that one dwells in the ancient fruit by means of the cause.
Furthermore, because one abides in the present, the Buddha’s teaching states that when a cause has produced its fruit, it is fixed and difficult to escape for ten thousand kalpas.
How could this be called the impermanence of all phenomena? The benefit of being able to escape the non-transience of cause and effect lies precisely here. The text is divided into two parts.
First, inferring the cause from the fruit. This section contains six parts; first, the direct explanation.

For this reason, the Tathāgata is cited as the fruit of Buddhahood. Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses two bodies: when complete wisdom returns to principle, it is called the True Body (dharmakāya);

when complete principle gives rise to wisdom, it is called the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya). According to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school, they say that the Buddha has two bodies, namely the Dharma-body and the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya).

Among these, there are the self-retribution and the other-retribution bodies. Now, the other-retribution body corresponds to the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), while the self-retribution body corresponds to the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).

The dharma body is quiescent and fundamentally not brought about by causes; even if it is manifested through a provisional "revealing cause" (*vyañjanahetu*), it is certainly not produced by a "generating cause" (*janakahetu*).
This meaning has not been clarified within the gate of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*); now, we shall specifically address it with respect to the Tathāgata as the transformation body.

The fruit is inferred from the cause. The various characteristics of the resultant body (phala-kāya) as perceived prior to and upon the stages (*bhūmi*) are manifold, as extensively analyzed in the various teachings.

Furthermore, this specific inference of the non-transmigration of the cause based on the Tathāgata’s fruition is intended to manifest that the central tenet (*siddhānta*) of this treatise lies in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which is neither dual nor triple.
"Merit" (gōng) refers to karmic action. To clarify the correspondence between present fruits and past causes, we speak of "merit.

Beginning from the initial mind of the ten stages of faith and extending through the forty-one intermediate positions, the causes cultivated—the ten *pāramitās* and myriad practices—are all termed "meritorious karma" (*gōngyè*).

It flows through ten thousand generations. "Flow" refers to the movement of water. To say "ten thousand generations" is to employ a large number; "generations" (*śe*) refers to divisions of time. In Sanskrit, this is called *kalpa*, which here means "division of time.

Even according to the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith), which clarifies the mind of faith, it still requires ten thousand *kalpas*; how much more so for one who has entered [the Way]?
Having already dwelt therein for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the meritorious deeds cultivated during that time are here referred to as "ten thousand ages.
This is because the remote causes have undergone a continuous flow until they reached their fruition after many kalpas had passed.
And it exists eternally.
Because one realizes on the level of the fruit that the past cause existed in the past, it is said to exist eternally.
This is the Way.
The *Shuowen* states: "That which is traversed is called the Way (dào), as well as a road. Both take the sense of being something that can be stepped upon.
When a person proceeds toward the principle through wisdom, such that all their actions are authentic, this is called "cultivating the Way" (xiūdào).
This, then, defines the Way as the cultivation of correct practice; the Way is thus the cause.
It remains firm throughout a hundred kalpas;

"mí" (彌) means "for a long time. In the past, when practicing the Way, it flowed through until the fruit was attained. Although many kalpas have passed, one knows with certainty that it existed in the past;
hence it is said to be "firm throughout" (mígù). △ Second, citing a metaphor.
The completion of a mountain depends upon beginning with the first basket of earth.

The *Lunyu* says: "It is like building a mountain; though one has only covered it with a single basket of earth, if I am advancing, I shall go on. Here, "jiǎ" (假) means "to rely upon" or "to take as a basis."
A *kui* is an earthen basket, a tool for taking up soil. Having already relied upon the soil from the initial baskets, one stacks them to form a mountain;
thus, the baskets of soil remain. This is used as a metaphor for how the meritorious achievements of the past endure forever without perishing.
The long journey relies upon the first step. The *Daodejing* says:
"A journey of a thousand li begins with the first step. Now, "long journey" (*xiutu*) refers to a distant road; "rely upon" (*tuo*) means to depend on.
One who wishes to travel a road of a thousand li first depends upon the first step; once the thousand li have been reached, [the journey is accomplished].

Knowing that the first step lies at the beginning yet is not extinguished serves as a metaphor; it shows that while the path traveled in the past becomes ever more solid, this is like a mountain formed by accumulated earth.

This uses the metaphor of the completed mountain and the long journey to manifest the fruit, and the first step to clarify the cause. Since the fruit depends upon the cause for its invitation, the cause must persist.
Thus, it is certain that the cause exists within the fruit. △ Third, the conclusion:
The fruit is so called because its meritorious deeds are indestructible;
the fruit is definitive. To illustrate this with a metaphor, one can certainly know that the Tathāgata’s meritorious deeds from former days reside therein.
In the past, that which is imperishable does so because it does not undergo transition.
Since one’s meritorious achievements cannot perish, they remain untransformed even though they belong to the past.
To be untransformed means to be imperishable and non-extinguished.
Because there is no transformation, there is no transition.
That which does not transition does not come to the present time of fruition.
Because there is no transition, it is profoundly still and luminous.
Master Shuicheng said: "The term 'tranquil' (zhàn) now reveals that the causal stage is unmoving; therefore, it is said, 'Tranquilly clear,' which means the meaning has already manifested.
△ Fourth, citing scriptural evidence:
Thus the Sūtra says, "While the three calamities pervade all things, one's karmic actions remain tranquil."
The three calamities are fire, water, and wind. "Pervasive" means to fill and extend everywhere.

At the time of the kalpa's destruction, fire reaches the First Dhyāna, water reaches the Second Dhyāna, and wind reaches the Third Dhyāna; everything below the Third Dhyāna is destroyed and dispersed without exception.
Only the practitioner’s path and the fruits of their meritorious deeds remain serene and unmoving.
One should believe his words, for the Buddha’s speech is trustworthy. △ Fifth, the inquiry and explanation: Why is this so?
This is a rhetorical inquiry. If the effect is not seen upon the cause, how do we know that it does not transform or migrate? The following provides the explanation:
"The effect does not coexist with the cause.
"Co" (俱) means "together. Since the effect exists in the present while the cause existed in the past, they are not simultaneous.
From cause comes cause, and from cause comes fruit.

The superior cause is dependent upon the inferior cause; thus, although these causal practices were causes in the past and fruits in the present, the fruit is nonetheless established by depending upon the cause.
Because there is a cause, there is a fruit; the cause does not perish in the past.
Since the fruit is accomplished by depending upon the cause, one knows with certainty that at the time of the fruit, the cause cannot have perished. Therefore, it was said above:
"Although it exists in the past, it does not undergo transformation."
The effect does not coexist with the cause, and the cause does not come into the present.
Since cause and effect are not simultaneous, it is certain that the cause abides in the past and does not come into the time of the present effect.
The Emperor said: "Because there is no transformation, there is no transition.
Since there is no extinction and no coming, the principle of non-transition is clearly evident.
If one seeks the cause through the fruit, one already knows that the meritorious deeds and the practice of the Path within the cause do not perish; they do not depart, nor do they come. Thus,"
The principle of the past is clear. △ Sixth, the conclusion and reprimand:
Why, then, are you deluded regarding departure and remaining, hesitating between movement and stillness?
"Departure and remaining" are precisely movement and stillness. "Hesitating" is a term for being unable to advance or retreat; the principle of things (physics) lies herein.
Within the non-duality of movement and stillness, why do you harbor doubts and fail to advance? Therefore, I now reprove you. △ Second, citing an event to conclude and manifest this;
this conclusion applies to both. First, concluding the present [text]; the passage has two parts. First, concluding the single treatise.
Thus, based on the preceding analysis of the causes and effects of past and present events, since movement and stillness are non-dual,
even when heaven and earth are overturned, there is no state that is not still.
The *I Ching* says: "Heaven is honored and Earth is humble; thus Qian and Kun are established. Heaven covers above while Earth supports below.

As for the present mention of "inverted," if it were the case that Heaven supported from above and Earth covered from below, then the relative dignity of Qian and Kun would not be lost, nor would the fundamental positions of Yin and Yang be altered;
therefore, all would remain quiescent.
The great flood reaches the heavens; do not say it moves.
"Great flood" refers to vast waters. "Reaching the heavens" means they overflow everywhere. The *Shangshu* says, "The surging floodwaters are now causing havoc.
Because each of the waves abides in its own position, there is no movement.
If one can harmonize with the spirit through the very objects before them, then [the truth] is not far away and can be known.
If one can achieve mental harmony and spiritual understanding by meeting principle through things, then the principle of non-duality is not distant from those of middling capacity;
they may know the existence or non-existence [of this truth] through this.

△ Second, the *Treatise on the Non-Emptiness of That Which Is Identical to Reality* (*Ji-zhen-bu-zhen-kong-lun*) is presented. "Identical to reality" (*ji-zhen*) refers to what was previously clarified as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Now, by discerning that which is identical to reality, ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is revealed; thus, this treatise has come forth.
