However, in the teaching of ultimate reality, when discussing the real, one must first establish the conventional, and in speaking of the conventional, one must rely upon the real. Thus, while emptiness and existence are presented as two, in principle, the real and the conventional are a single, integrated whole.

The three truths are either combined or analyzed; while the teachings have many approaches, their underlying principle does not differ. The former [section] was the conventional that is identical with the real;

now, it clarifies the real that is identical with the conventional. The non-duality of the real and the conventional reveals the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is the object of the illumination and realization of *prajñā*.
Therefore, compared to the preceding [section], this treatise shows that the real and the conventional are mutually integrated.
Correct. In relation to what follows, "correspondence" (*pratigha*) refers to the relationship between object and cognition as subject and object; therefore, it appears next.

Furthermore, ordinary people merely know that the myriad phenomena arise through conditions and, having arisen, perish again. They do not understand that arising is not true arising and perishing is not fixed perishing;

rather, arising and perishing proceed from conditions, and those conditions arise from the Truth (*tattva*). Indeed, because all things arise from conditions, there is not a single dharma among them that does not [participate in this].
Those who do not understand this "true emptiness" (zhēnkōng) stubbornly cling to existence and non-existence; therefore, in order to refute this attachment, this treatise was established.

Among the five preceding names, this is the Gate of True Truth (zhēndì mén). By using the emptiness of intrinsic nature (xìngkōng) to infer that conditions meet [to form phenomena], one reveals the true principle of the dharma-nature (fǎxìng zhēnlǐ) within conventional reality itself, thereby returning to original non-being.
Thus, one knows that the two treatises are simultaneous and that the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual.

It is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); hence it is called "one meaning" (*ekārtha*). However, because subject and object still persist, it has not yet reached the single meaning of the perfect quiescence of *nirvāṇa*.
This section is divided into two parts; first, the title.
**Discourse on the Non-Reality of Emptiness, Part Two** "Non-real" means not truly real.

Because things arise through conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the nature of things is not substantially existent; because they arise through conditions, the nature of things is not substantially non-existent.

By means of this, one infers that their nature is neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, it is called "non-real. As for the term "emptiness": [...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.*
It is quiescent (*śānta*). Because phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not real, it reveals that the nature (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally empty and quiescent.

Here, the character "not" (*a-*) is the wisdom that performs the refutation, and the character "real" (*bhūta*) is the attachment to be refuted; thus, by means of the conventional, both existence and non-existence are simultaneously refuted.

The character "empty" (*śūnya*) is the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) that is revealed. Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* says: "The phenomena produced through dependent origination..."
What I call emptiness means that things do not exist as substantial realities. It is also called "provisional designation," meaning they are not non-existent either.

It is further termed the "Middle Way," signifying emptiness and quiescence. Moreover, those who fail to understand dependent origination cling to existence or non-existence, giving rise to divergent views and becoming deluded regarding the ultimate principle.
Now, by means of the non-true, both extremes are simultaneously refuted, so that one may accord with the principle through phenomena themselves.

Principle is fundamentally quiescent; therefore, it is called "not truly empty. Furthermore, the previous *Wu buqian lun* (Treatise on the Non-transmigration of Things) established the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) by showing that dependent phenomena are indeterminate and non-existent.

Now, the present [treatise] clarifies the ultimate (*paramārtha*) to reveal that all phenomena do not exist as substantial realities. These two treatises function simultaneously to manifest the Middle Way.
Because principle is fundamentally quiescent and both the true and the conventional are equally absent, it is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*). Moreover, the *Wu buqian lun* [demonstrates] both...

Because it illuminates that the positions of existence and non-existence each abide [in their own nature], the two characters "not-true" (*buzhen*) simultaneously negate both existence and non-existence.

Because the single character "emptiness" (*kong*) accords with the Middle Way by negating both [existence and non-existence] together, and because this "emptiness of the not-true" (*buzhenkong*) can manifest that which is manifested,
while the "treatise on the emptiness of the not-true" (*buzhenzhen lun*) can express that which is expressed, all [terms] are explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.

△ Second, the Treatise. This section has two parts. First, the exposition of the intended meaning, which has three sub-sections. First, clarifying that the principle is profound and difficult to realize, which is divided into four parts.
First, stating the fundamental tenet to manifest its wondrousness.

Now, "ultimate emptiness" (*zhìxū*) refers to the ultimate state of emptiness and stillness. Since the fundamental principle is originally empty and still, it is the emptiness of the true ultimate; therefore, it is called "ultimate emptiness.
This is precisely the principle of the Middle Way, the First Noble Truth. Furthermore, the single term "emptiness" generally extends to the Great Emptiness (*tài xū*) and—
It is the emptiness that transcends all dependence. Because the ultimate truth is free from dependence and devoid of annihilation, it is called "ultimate emptiness" (*zhìxū*).
Furthermore, "ultimate" (*zhì*) means "to reach. By investigating the nature of phenomena until one reaches the limit of quiescent extinction, it is called "ultimate emptiness.
Thus, various teachings point to this as the "Reality Limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*), the "Actual Limit," the "Original Source," and so forth; all of these names derive from having reached the ultimate point.
It is non-arising.
It does not arise from the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), nor does it cease toward the posterior limit (*aparānta*); furthermore, there is no abiding in between. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"Fundamentally unborn, now also unceasing"—this is the meaning of *nirvāṇa* (quiescence). Moreover, it does not arise from existence, nor does it...
Is there no non-arising? Indeed, there is non-arising; yet this non-arising does not exist apart from arising. It transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
Since the principle is fundamentally thus, it is called "non-arising."
This refers to the principle established above as the fundamental tenet; it is,
in essence, the wondrous import of the profound discernment of Prajñā.
This "ge" (蓋) is a term used for pointing out or supporting [an argument]. "Prajñā" is translated here as "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*). It means "to reflect" and "to incline toward.
Reaching the void and non-arising is the locus toward which *prajñā* reflects and inclines. *Prajñā* is that which is capable of reflecting and inclining;
it reaches the void and non-arising as that which is reflected upon and inclined toward. *Prajñā* is capable of reflecting, yet it reflects without...
It is for this reason that it is called "mysterious" (xuán). To discern the principle is the destination; because one reaches it yet there is no reaching, it is called the "wondrous destination.
This indicates that the present treatise, *Not Truly Empty*, is contrasted with the subsequent treatise, *The Principle and the Intellect*.
It is that which is the ultimate source of all things.

All phenomena (*sarvabhāva*) act as the honoring subjects (*pūjaka*), while the supreme voidness and non-arising (*parama-śūnyatā-anutpāda*) serve as the honored object (*pūjya*). This is the ultimate pinnacle of such honoring.

Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all things exist in accordance with conditions (*pratyaya*). Thus, this designation indicates the truth within the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); the truth is not separate from the conventional. This is what is revealed here.

This treatise stands in contrast to the previous treatises on principle and phenomena. Herein, the three wisdoms of superior principle, superior wisdom, and superior phenomena act as the illuminators;
that is, the phenomena that accord with principle serve as the illuminated. The general purport of this single treatise does not exceed this. II.
Praising the Profundity in Terms of Wisdom (divided into two parts): 1. First, a retrospective description of the capacity of wisdom.
Were it not for one who is sagely and brilliant, and uniquely penetrating, how could one possibly bring the spirit into accord between existence and non-existence?
Phrases such as "were it not for whom" are all inverted expressions. "Sagely and brilliant" and "uniquely penetrating" refer to *prajñā*.

This is because the spiritual brilliance of the sage possesses an exceptionally outstanding and penetrating function of illumination. "Spirit" (*shen*) means that which is unfathomable. To "bring into accord" (*qie*)—
This unfathomable and wondrous principle exists within the midst of the existence and non-existence of all phenomena; were it not for *prajñā*, how could such capacity exist?
This reveals that the ultimate void is realized solely by wisdom and is not accessible to the ordinary mind. To accord with principle through phenomena, one must rely upon wisdom.
II. Explaining the Function of Wisdom in Accordance with Principle. This section has two parts: first, explaining the essence of wisdom’s illumination and function.
Therefore, because they have attained awakening through wisdom based on the reasons mentioned above, the Perfected Persons (zhiren) [are as described].
To realize the ultimate is called the stage of the perfected fruit; to manifest traces within human society is a title reserved solely for the Buddha.

Now, because we speak of wisdom by way of one who has attained the fruit, the term "perfected person" (zhiren) is used. However, as long as one can accord with the truth through mundane events, all may attain the wisdom and function of a perfected person.
One must not loftily attribute this to the sages alone while harboring self-conceit regarding one's own spiritual nature.
The divine mind penetrates the infinite; that which is finite cannot obstruct it.

To "penetrate" means there is no obstruction. "Divine mind" refers to the mind of immediate spiritual illumination within the threefold liberation. "Finite" refers to the process of inferential investigation.

Because it illuminates yet is without illumination, it is called "infinite. As the *Xia lun* (Treatise on the Lower) states: "Wisdom possesses the mirror-like discernment that penetrates the profound mysteries."
Yet there is no knowing. Furthermore, the sage of the ultimate person does not fathom a mind of spiritual illumination; his thorough penetration lies in non-illumination.

When he illuminates, he does not stagnate in that illumination; therefore it is said, "He exhausts all that cannot be stagnated. This describes how the superior wisdom embodies the essence and the inferior manifestation reveals the function of illumination.
"To exhaust the ears and eyes in hearing sounds and seeing forms" means that what cannot be restrained is exhausted by the ear in hearing sound and by the eye in seeing form.
Why is it that among these sounds and forms, not a single one can obstruct or hinder the ears and eyes? The following commentary explains:
Is it not because all things are inherently empty that no thing can obstruct their spiritual intelligence? "Obstruction" means being bound.
Since all things are fundamentally empty, numinous wisdom clearly perceives that there is not a single thing capable of binding or obstructing its cognitive function;
therefore, sounds and forms cannot constrain or hinder it. This is precisely the function inherent within the essence.
"Shine" (zhào) refers to the principle within phenomena; hence it is called "not non-true emptiness. △ Second, explaining the capacity for the function of shining:
"Therefore, the Sage" reiterates that the aforementioned sagely wisdom accords with principle through phenomena.
When one rides upon the true mind, one accords with principle; thus, there is nothing that is obstructed or does not pass through.
To "ride upon the true mind" means to employ the true wisdom of non-illumination and to harmonize with the truth-principle of non-arising.

Because wisdom and principle correspond to one another, it is called "accordance with principle. Since there is no phenomenon outside of principle, wisdom has no place of delusion, obstruction, or non-penetration. This...
This explains how the divine mind of the Superior penetrates the meaning of the infinite;
by examining the single vital energy (*yiqi*) to observe transformation, one encounters all things with spontaneous adaptability.
"Examining" (*shen*) means to scrutinize with clarity. "Single vital energy" refers to the terminology of the *Daoshu* (Books of the Dao), which designates the Way of Non-being (*xuwu*) as "the One."

"Qi. Here, the term is borrowed to refer to the "One Qi" within the ultimate void and the Middle Way. One who contemplates transformation perceives that all things suddenly come into being through conditions.
"Adaptation" refers to reaching a profound realization; through sage-like wisdom, one comprehends the ultimate void while observing phenomena.
Thus, all matters encountered accord with principle. Releasing the extremes of the ears and eyes from sight and hearing, one realizes that the myriad things are inherently empty;
nothing remains obstructed or blocked. Therefore, one can blend the chaotic to achieve purity.
Regarding the explanation that the meanings of "wisdom" (*jñāna*) and "principle" (*tattva*) are blended into a single pure unity: this is established because they share the same essential meaning.

Since wisdom and principle accord with one another, when wisdom is empty and non-existent, it illuminates; when principle is empty and non-existent, it gives rise [to wisdom]. Thus, they can blend together within the same emptiness to establish the principle of non-dual, pure harmony.
This explanation serves to demonstrate that the substance of wisdom and principle is identical as revealed through their mutual correspondence.
Whatever is encountered is harmonious and appropriate; therefore, all things are one upon contact.

This further explains the meaning of the preceding "principle and phenomena" (li-shi) as being in mutual correspondence. Since all phenomena accord with principle, whatever objects are encountered are all identical to that single principle.
This establishes that the manifestation of principle and phenomena is non-dual. △ Third, concluding that phenomena are not real.
In this way, the principle that phenomena and reality are non-dual is restated:
although the myriad phenomena are distinct, they cannot be differentiated by themselves.

This means that phenomena manifest the principle. Although phenomena are myriad and diverse, they all arise from the diversity of the principle; apart from the principle, phenomena cannot be diverse of themselves.
It is like waves: there are no waves outside of water, and waves cannot be diverse of themselves.
They cannot be distinguished from one another; thus we know that the elephant is not a true elephant.
All phenomena lack reality because they arise through the total principle following conditions.
Since the elephant is not a true elephant, it is an elephant yet not an elephant.

Because although phenomena are not real, their underlying principle is fully manifest. Although they appear as images, they are not images; observing them as being like the appearance of waves, their emptiness is revealed, thereby exposing the essence of the water.
Therefore, the title is "Not Truly Empty" (*buzhenkong*), signifying the non-duality of principle and phenomena (*lishi wuer*). This is the fundamental meaning of this treatise.
△ Fourth, describing the preceding subject and following with the subsequent.
Thus, things and the self share the same root.

"Things" refers to principle (*li*), and "the self" refers to wisdom (*zhi*). Since the substance of principle and wisdom is identical, they are said to have the same root; this concludes the preceding discussion by pairing principle and wisdom.
Right and wrong are not two distinct breaths.
"Right and wrong" refers to the phenomena of existence and non-existence. Since all phenomena ultimately return to the underlying principle, they are called "the single qi.

These two preceding lines describe what has gone before. They reveal that ultimate emptiness and non-arising constitute the profound discernment of prajñā, and furthermore, serve as the supreme source of all existing things.
The following clarifies what arises thereafter.
Profoundly subtle and obscurely hidden, these are likely beyond the full comprehension of the common mind.
"Profound" (*qian*) means that the principle resides within phenomena; "subtle" (*wei*) means it is inconceivable; "obscure" (*you*) means it is without form or appearance;

and "hidden" (*yin*) means it is beyond the reach of intellectual understanding. "Largely" (*dai*) is a particle used here to indicate that while the true principle is profound and subtle, it is nonetheless present. And...

The emotional views of sentient beings cannot be exhausted. △ Second, the narration of divergent views that delude the fundamental tenet. This section has two parts. First, the statement of the cause for its arising:
"Therefore, for a moment, we have engaged in discussion."
This is because, according to principle, there is no exhaustion of sentient beings. "A short while ago" (*kǐng'ěr*) refers to the recent past.
"Those who engage in discussion" (*tánlùn zhě*) refers to those who establish the arguments of various schools. As for the school of Emptiness (*xūzōng*), there are always differences between them.
Within this school of emptiness, there are various differing doctrines.
Since they seek to reach accord through their differences, what thing could possibly be identical?
This is a general refutation of all schools; for by means of differing views, they all desire to arrive at a state of accord.
As for principle (*li*), since principle is fundamentally without difference, how could it be made identical? Therefore, one need only eliminate divergent views rather than seek uniformity.
As it is said in the critique below: "Thus, various treatises compete to be composed, yet their fundamental natures do not coincide."
Because various treatises were composed in competition, the meaning of *svabhāva* (nature) has come to have many paths, none of which can be reconciled. This is what is meant by the saying:
"When there are many diverging paths, one loses the sheep. Part Two: Extending the Refutation and Establishment. Sub-part One: The Deduction.

Why is this? If one investigates what is meant by "various treatises competing to establish [theories of] nature," why would they not be identical? △ Second, the explanation. This section has three parts. First, the refutation of the meaning of "mindlessness" (citta-nāstitva).
This section has two parts. First, the presentation of the [opponent's] calculation.
Regarding "the absence of mind" (*wuxin*):

Kang’s Commentary states that this was first set forth because he intended to refute the doctrine of the absence of mind (*xinwu*) by the Jin dynasty monk Zhi Mindu. Thus, it is presented here first for the purpose of refutation.
To have no mind directed toward the myriad things does not mean that the myriad things have ever been non-existent.
What is meant is simply that one has no mind that clings to the myriad things; therefore, it is called "conforming to principle through phenomena.
This does not mean that the myriad things themselves are non-existent. II. The Actual Refutation.
This attainment lies in the stillness of the spirit; this failure lies in the emptiness of things.

Furthermore, while one may attain a clarity and stillness of mind, if one has not yet realized that the myriad things are fundamentally empty, yet persists in maintaining an objective realm where the mind exists, how can the mind be truly clear and still?
This is a divergent view within our school. The commentary states: "This refutes the doctrine of Vasubandhu regarding the non-existence of the mind. Part Two.
The third section: Refuting the Meaning of "Form is Identical to Emptiness. First, the presentation of the [opponent's] position.

Regarding "form is identical to emptiness," the sub-commentary notes: "This refutes the meaning of 'form is identical to emptiness' established by Zhi Daolin. Kang’s commentary states: "Zhi Daolin arose during the Jin dynasty."
"Roaming the profound meaning within form" (*jise youxuan yi*) is the initial heading.
It clarifies that form does not exist as form by itself; therefore, although it is form, it is not [merely] form.
This statement originates from Master Lin’s *Jimi guan zhang* (Chapter on the Sublime Contemplation), which says: "The clarification refers to that which is clarified therein."
"Form is not form by itself" means that the dharma of form must depend on conditions to be established; it is not a form that exists inherently.
Although there is form established through conditions, because this form is not substantially real, it is empty. Therefore, it is said: "Though it is form, it is not form.
This intends to clarify that the Buddha’s teaching of form is such that form is itself emptiness, and that phenomena manifest the principle. △ Second, clarifying the difference in understanding.
Now, as for the phrase "speaking of form," this refers back to that which was spoken of as form;
it simply means that when there is form, it is just form.
The causal form and the resultant form are both form.
How could they wait for [the presence of] form after form before being considered form?
How could they wait until the causal form has combined and produced the resultant form before they are finally considered form? △ Third, the formal conclusion.
Refutation:
This merely states that form is not itself form; it does not yet grasp that form is non-form.
It is simply a negation. This master merely asserts that resultant form is not itself form, thereby reaching the emptiness of resultant form, but he has not yet attained full realization.
"Form as a condition is also empty. The commentary states: This refutes Sengdao’s theory that "form is itself emptiness. △ Third, the refutation of the doctrine of "original non-existence" (benwu).
Part one: An exposition of their conceptual calculations.
Regarding "original non-existence":
The sub-commentary notes that the "Treatise on Original Non-being" by Zhu Fatai was also a work from the Jin dynasty;
he was one who first set forth [this doctrine], being personally inclined toward non-being and frequently employing words to guest at non-being.
"Still attached" means "submissively compliant. This master’s views were biased toward emptiness and non-existence, frequently engaging in discussions on the profound mysteries of Buddhism.
He merely submitted to and returned to non-existence, taking "non-action" (wuwei) as the standard for this; this is the author of the treatise describing that master's views.
Below, he sets forth what was seen [of those views], saying:
Therefore, it is not that existence itself is non-existence, nor is it that non-existence itself is non-existence.
Because their views and understandings are biased and erroneous, when they hear the teaching "not existent," they take this to mean the negation of existence;
hence it is said "not existent. When they hear the teaching "not non-existent," they take this to mean the negation of non-existence; hence it is said "not [non-existent]."
There is none. This, then, is a definitive return to non-existence. △ Second, showing the correct meaning:

To investigate the fundamental intent behind the establishment of this text, the Master [Vasubandhu] thoroughly examined all teachings to establish the text’s fundamental intent as being "neither existent nor non-existent. The current interpretation does not accord with this.
The character "zhě" (者) cites the fundamental purport of the text. What follows expresses the underlying meaning to demonstrate it:
"Directly, it is neither existent nor truly existent.
This means that when we say it is "not existent," it is because all phenomena arise through conditions and are therefore not substantially real.
It is not that they do not exist; it is simply that they are not truly existent.
To say "not non-existent" means that the characteristics of conditions are not destroyed, for they are not actually non-existent. △ Third, refuting divergent views:
Why must there be no existence here? If there were no existence, there would be no such non-existence.
"What must it be? is a word of inquiry. "This" and "that" are merely words used for reference; they do not mean that "this" and "that" are fixed or determined.

"What must it be" refers to hearing [of] what is not existent as being non-existent; it means there is nothing at all. Hearing [of] what is not non-existent as being non-existent means there is nothing at all.
△ Fourth, the refutation of erroneous conceptions.
This is merely a discourse that favors non-existence; how could it be said to accord with and penetrate the facts of reality?
This master’s teaching is simply a discourse that prizes returning to non-existence;

how could it be a verbal instruction that accords with and penetrates that which is neither existent nor non-existent, thereby aligning with the Middle Way and the true principle? The following passage rebukes this:
This is indeed the true nature of things.

To abandon existence and cling to non-existence are both merely attachments to the nature of manifold phenomena. The commentary states: "This refutes Zhu Fatai’s [claim] that 'fundamentally there is no self.
This above briefly clarifies the divergent views of the three schools; because each clings to one extreme, the ultimate principle remains unmanifested.
Within identity and difference, they are intensely established as distinct. Now, because people are deluded regarding difference by means of correct principle (*yukti*), this treatise has arisen.

Furthermore, it is precisely because of difference that identity is established. Since in principle there is neither identity nor difference, where would words have any place? Therefore, it was said above: "What entity could possibly be identical?
△ Third, the humble presentation of the intent, which has three parts. First, describing that names and things do not reach one another.
Now, when one takes an object to objectify another object, that which is thus objectified is indeed an objectifiable thing.
This is because it is used [as an object]. "Objectifying objects" is the name of the object; "taking [it] as an object" is the characteristic of the object in relation to other objects.
Since there is an object that possesses both a name and its corresponding characteristic, that object must necessarily be nameable.
Because things are not things, although they are things, they are not things.
Because the names of things point toward non-things, although there are names for things, they definitely lack the substance of things; as it is said:
"The horns of a rabbit have a name but no substance. The following clarifies that [things] do not reach one another.
Therefore, things do not coincide with their names but rather proceed toward the reality.
This means that when one sets aside the aforementioned "thing" (the object) that can be named, the manifestation of the essence does not reach the name; this is what is meant by "coinciding.

To "proceed toward the reality" is to attain the name that corresponds to reality. Since the thing is not the name, the name cannot be applied to the thing. As the *Shi* (Classic of Poetry) says: "To see..."
The understanding of the emptiness of persons laughs at the play of objects whose names are not known;
for objects have no names, just as an infant receives an object but cannot know its name. This demonstrates that the object does not reach the name.
The name does not coincide with the object, yet it treads upon the truth.
To tread upon the truth means to reach the actual substance of the object. Because the name is not the object, the name cannot reach the true essence of the object.
It is like a person saying "fire" without the fire being hot in the mouth; this is because there is no substance within the name itself. This clarifies the nature of the name.
It does not reach objects. △ Second, revealing that the ultimate principle transcends words and thought:
Thus, the True Truth (satyadharma) is uniquely quiescent, beyond the realm of names and teachings.
Even the worldly objects of name and form, which can be spoken of and seen, do not reach it; how much more so the True Truth, which is beyond words and thought?
Furthermore, since [the truth] stands alone beyond the realm of conventional teachings (*mingjiao*), how could it be subject to verbal debate? Thus, the text below states:
"How can it be said that literary discourse is capable of discerning it?
These two sections constitute the Master’s refutation of the divergent doctrines of various schools; yet, as for the correct principle, its alignment remains unknown.

How so? Therefore, even the worldly names and characteristics currently being discussed in this general account do not reach [the ultimate reality], let alone the profound supramundane principle that is signless, nameless, and beyond the reach of speech.
To resort to verbal explanations is merely intended to enable people to understand what is correct and know what is erroneous;
it is by no means meant to suggest that the essence of the Dharma can be reached through words and intellectual understanding. △ Third, a humble statement of the intention to compose the work.
Nevertheless, one cannot remain silent.

"Nevertheless" refers to the reasoning set forth above; although it is not something that can be fully expressed, because there is much confusion and divergence in the world, one cannot remain silent and cut off all discourse.
I shall briefly set forth my words to propose a comparison. Let me attempt to discuss this, saying:
"Fu" (復) means to restate a previously established argument; thus, it signifies "to present. "Ni" (擬) is a term indicating that a decision has not yet been reached;

it is a humble expression meaning "to briefly present these words for deliberation and trial," and so I shall now discuss them. △ Second, the formal establishment of the argument, divided into six sections according to the ancient classification.
This is now divided into three sections: first, a general discourse on all phenomena directly revealing their ultimate identity with reality;
second, a specific analysis and explanation of the causes and conditions of form and mind; and third, an investigation into names and realities to refute deluded attachments.

Now, while the ultimate truth manifests as all phenomenal dharmas through its adaptation to conditions, ordinary beings fail to understand this and instead cling to phenomena, thereby losing sight of the truth. Because they may give rise to erroneous views, we shall first clarify [the first section].

Since this is a true comprehensive treatise on all phenomena, it is not yet known by what means they accord with principle; therefore, next, one specifically points to form and mind based on causes and conditions to investigate and explain them.
Since form and mind collectively comprise all phenomena, and all phenomena do not transcend causes and conditions, and because causes and conditions are empty, they are thus real.
If one asks: "If causes and conditions are fundamentally empty, how can they be called that which summons the essence? Upon that essence..."

Because names are established, one subsequently investigates the substance of those names. Through grasping, emotional attachment arises; yet since the substance of names is fundamentally non-existent, how could such attachment exist?

These three categories [of investigation] lead, respectively, to the abandonment of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), the realization of the dependent nature (*paratantra*), and the realization of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).

Although the meaning proceeds from the profound to the shallow, it is explained by means of the latter [to clarify the former], precisely because one has not yet attained understanding of the substance of names.
This is the causal condition. To thoroughly understand the reality of all phenomena, there are now three parts. First, citing the teachings to establish the fundamental tenet.
In the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*, "Mahā" means "Great" and "Yāna" means "Vehicle."
Regarding "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*):
they are called "all" because conventional, factual phenomena are not uniform.
Furthermore, they possess neither marks nor are they markless.

The term "also" (*yi*) is a word used for emphasis; it indicates that not only is the principle of ultimate emptiness neither existent nor non-existent, but the various phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are likewise neither existent nor non-existent.
Furthermore, as stated above, all phenomena are phenomena of both existence and non-existence. Because they exist yet are not [ultimately] existent, it is said they are "neither existent";
because they are non-existent yet are not [ultimately] non-existent, it is said they are "also not non-existent. However, the Truth (*tattva*) is not...

Regarding "existence and non-existence," there are two senses. First, because it is without form or name, it is not existent; yet because its essence and function are truly eternal, it is not non-existent.
Second, it cannot be grasped through the view of permanence, thus it is not existent; nor can it be sought through the view of annihilation, thus it is not non-existent.
Now, as for the various phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are likewise neither existent nor non-existent, for they arise in dependence upon conditions.

Therefore, it is not truly existent, because the characteristic of conditions is indestructible; nor is it truly non-existent, for if one realizes that what arises from conditions is not truly existent, one immediately knows that the true reality is fundamentally without name or form. Thus, it cannot be sought through the view of eternalism.

If one penetrates that the characteristics of conditions are not truly non-existent, one then sees that the true essence possesses wondrous function. Thus, it cannot be grasped through the view of nihilism. Now, this is precisely...

It clarifies that, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), existence and non-existence are not real. Next, it cites the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* to reveal that this is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*) states: "All phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent."
To state that all phenomena of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) are neither existent nor non-existent is precisely the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
this is the primary ultimate truth.

This clarifies the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional, manifesting the wondrous principle of the Middle Way, which transcends all oppositions and does not fall into numerical categories.
Therefore, it is called "the foremost. The *Dharmadruma Sūtra* states: "Even 'one' is not made one," because it shatters all numerical categories.

However, in the Dharma-character school (*lakṣaṇavāda*), conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is mostly explained as being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), thus not exceeding the realm of existence, non-existence, arising, and ceasing;

whereas ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) belongs to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), thus being neither existent nor non-existent and neither arising nor ceasing. This has not yet been fully understood. [In reality,] the conventional itself is the ultimate, transcending all relativity—this is the foremost.

Now, the primary purpose of this treatise is to harmonize the provisional with the ultimate. For this reason, it first investigates conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and subsequently reveals the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional.

Furthermore, because it is ultimate, it does not exist; because it is conventional, it is not non-existent. Thus, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the simultaneous negation of both existence and non-existence.
Moreover, all phenomena of conventional truth possess three propositions: first, existence; second, non-existence; and third, both existence and non-existence. The ultimate...
The fourth phrase, "neither existence nor non-existence," refers to the characteristics of the ultimate and the conventional. This implies that the four phrases are simultaneous;

for how could the ultimate that corresponds to the conventional transcend numerical categories? If one realizes non-duality, one forever transcends all oppositions; therefore, it is called "the foremost.
What this treatise elucidates does not exceed this, and thus it is designated as the fundamental tenet (*arthasiddhānta*). Next, the tenet is further analyzed and explained.

The meaning has two parts. The first clarifies the truth that is identical to the conventional; this section has three parts. The first is the repeated analysis and explanation of the text, which has three parts. The first restates what preceded:
"Now, if we investigate... (尋夫).

The above constitutes an extended discourse taking the verbal teachings as the authoritative measure. By investigating and exhausting the principles of causes and conditions regarding all phenomena, it is said:
"Seeking into the matter," [one finds that things are] "neither existent nor non-existent."
This directly cites the Mahāyāna treatise. △ Second, the counter-inference:
"How could it be said that one washes away all things?
The phrase "how could it be said" is a term of reproof. "Washing away all things" refers to the dissolution of the objective realm of defiled and pure names and marks.
Furthermore,
"to block sight and hearing" means to sever the mind that reflects and discerns through the ears and eyes.
Is it that only after becoming silent and desolate, empty and vast, does one arrive at the ultimate truth?

"Silent" means there is no sound; "desolate" means there is no form—this is the dissolution of objects upon the page. "The Great Void is vast and open, without cognition or utility"—this is the dissolution of the mind upon the page.
Does this not mean that one subsequently dissolves and cuts off all phenomena of the mind and objects, whether defiled or pure?
It is neither existent nor non-existent; the meaning of the True Truth (*satyārtha*) is not like this. △ Third, the sequential explanation:
Truly, because one accords with and penetrates through things as they are, no thing can oppose it.

This is the meaning of sincerity. The true intent of this discourse is that all phenomena proceed in accordance with [the truth]. It is the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that things are neither existent nor non-existent.
No phenomenon can contravene this principle. This deduces that, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), things are neither existent nor non-existent.
The false is immediately the true; therefore, the nature [of things] cannot be altered.

"False" refers to the provisional, while "true" refers to the real. Because conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) arises through causes and conditions, it is provisional; ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), however, is inherently real by its very nature. Thus, one realizes it.

Dependent origination is neither existent nor non-existent, because true nature itself is neither existent nor non-existent. It does not require the transformation of the conventional into the ultimate;
rather, by investigating the ultimate within the conventional, one finds that the ultimate truth is neither existent nor non-existent.
The nature cannot be altered; therefore, although it is non-existent, it exists.
Although it is empty and eternally quiescent, illusory existence is perfectly manifest.
No thing can oppose it; therefore, although it exists, it is non-existent.
Although illusory phenomena appear in profusion, true emptiness remains unhidden;
though they exist, they are non-existent—what is called "non-existence.
Illusory existence is itself true emptiness, and the true nature is profoundly still and quiescent; therefore, they are one and the same in their non-existence.
Although it is non-existent, it exists; that is to say, it is not non-existent.
True emptiness does not obstruct existence, for the true nature is eternally abiding. Thus, they are identical in being "not non-existent.

This concludes the clarification of the truth within the conventional—that which is neither existent nor non-existent—whose meaning has already been revealed. II. Concluding the Manifestation from the Perspective of the Conventional.
In this way, [as inferred above], it is not that there is no thing;
because the characteristics of conditions (*pratyaya*) are not destroyed, it was stated above that it is "also not non-existent.
Yet, this thing is not a truly real thing.
Because that which arises through conditions is not real, it was stated above that it is also "not existent.
Since things are not real things, how could they be considered things?

It is merely because conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is not ultimate reality that we perceive the myriad phenomena; yet, as things, how could they possibly exist? Therefore, the preceding Mahāyāna treatise states: [and so forth].
All phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent; this reveals the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). △ Third, citation of scriptures to establish the proof.
Thus, a sutra says: "The nature of form is empty; it is not that form is destroyed for it to be empty."
The Qin translation of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said: 'Form and emptiness constitute a duality. The nature of form is empty;

In explaining the intent of the sutra, he says:
This clarifies how the Sage, regarding all things, acts for their practical utility;

This is the wisdom regarding all phenomena. As for how this was explained previously, it says:
"All phenomena are inherently empty.
