although this refers generally to people, the intent behind contemporary discourse is to hold the questioner accountable;
for the most part, they seek to establish the definitive meaning through their words.
"Many" refers to the majority; it does not necessarily mean that all are exactly so. This expresses a definitive conclusion, like pointing to the moon with one's finger.
Seeking the great direction while examining the corners, and harboring prior knowledge to indicate the profound mystery.
The *Daofang* (Great Square) says: "The Great Square has no corners. To "investigate" (*zheng*) means to infer or deduce. "Corners" (*yu*) refers to angles.
One who seeks the Great Square must first understand that it has no corners; yet if one infers and searches for corners and angles, how could such a person understand the Great Square?

"To harbor in the mind" (*huai xin*) means to possess it within the heart. Regarding "prior knowledge" (*qian shi*), the *Daodejing* also states: "Prior knowledge is the flower of the Dao. Thus, prior knowledge is merely the superficial manifestation of the Dao.
It is not the profound Way. "To point out" means to indicate. To take prior consciousness as the profound Way—how can this be called attaining the Way?

This is a case of borrowing from external texts to refute scholars who cling to words and teachings, thereby remaining deluded regarding the ultimate principle and obstructed by the dualities of existence and non-existence.
What Master Liu said—“one desires to seek the difference within the Sage’s mind”—is precisely this.
To “preserve what is to be preserved” is necessarily correct;

to “discard” is also correct. “Preserving” refers to grasping. The mind is that which is capable of preserving; the principle (dao-li) is that which is to be preserved. When the mind preserves, there is difference.

[The opponent] explains: "Since this must surely be the correct principle, one clings to its existence and harbors no doubt regarding the wisdom of the Sage. △ Second, clarifying the clinging to the teachings:

Thus, upon hearing that the Sage possesses knowledge, one says he has a mind; upon hearing that the Sage lacks knowledge, one says he is equal to the great void. This concerns existence and non-existence.
The persistence of extreme views within the realm [of such a path]—how could this be the Middle Way free from duality?

As for "extreme views," they refer to the grasping views of the two extremes of existence and non-existence. Here, "view" is the subject that persists, while the "two extremes" are the objects that persist.
If one hears it said that the sacred mind exists, one clings to existence as if it were a delusive thought;
if one hears it said that the sacred mind does not exist, one clings to non-existence as if it were the great void. Thus, by means of extreme views, one becomes stuck in existence and non-existence.

How could one attain the profound path of Prajñā within the non-duality of existence and non-existence? △ Second, the investigation and explanation of the profound principle, in two parts. First, the investigation.
What is this? Why is it called the "Middle Way"? It is because there is no duality therein. △ Second, the explanation has three parts. First, the indication of the true realm:
Although the myriad things are diverse (their *lakṣaṇa*), their nature is fundamentally and eternally one.
This is its nature. Thus, one speaks of the ultimate reality (dharmatā) without destroying conventional designations; therefore, it is called the "Sublime Path of the Middle Way.
△ Second, showing delusion and awakening:
It cannot be reduced to a thing, yet it is not that it is not a thing.
The preceding phrase means that one must not cling to characteristics as being real; the following phrase means that one must not destroy characteristics in order to perceive the principle.
When it says "it is not non-thing," it means it is not the case that there is no thing.
If a thing can be treated as a thing, then name and characteristic are presented as distinct.
To cling to existence is delusion. Because the single nature is equal, it is said that names and appearances differ;
yet, by not treating things as mere objects, one finds that objects are themselves the truth.
Since one perceives the nature without being obstructed by appearances, one accords with the truth through the very objects themselves. This is called abiding in the Middle Way, which is non-dual.
△ The three types of clear knowledge (vidyā) illuminate through wisdom.
Therefore, the sage does not treat things as objects, nor does he treat things as non-objects.

Not treating them as non-objects means not destroying the characteristics of things. Not remaining stuck in the characteristics of things as being real means not destroying the characteristics of things.
Seeking the truth: one does not take things to be things; thus, things are not existent. One does not take things to be non-things; thus, things are not non-existent.
Conditioned appearances are not truly existent; conditioned arising is not truly non-existent.
It is not because things exist that one does not grasp them; it is not because things do not exist that one does not relinquish them.
One does not grasp at the characteristics of objects because those characteristics are illusory; yet one does not relinquish the characteristics of objects because those characteristics are manifest.
Because there is no abandonment, the wondrous existence is itself the truth.

Without abandoning the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one contemplates these very characteristics as being without characteristics (*animitta*). This is called "wondrous existence"; therefore, phenomena themselves are the truth.
This reveals that because one contemplates the unchanging in accordance with conditions, one does not abandon them;
yet because one does not grasp them, names and marks have no cause.
Although the myriad things are numerous, they are not [independent of] names; although they are not without marks, they are [not independent of] causes. All myriad things are the true nature.

It arises by grasping conditions; because there is no separate cause external [to it], it is said to be "without cause. This is because apart from ultimate truth (tattva), not even a fragment of a thing can be found.
This clarifies that while remaining unchanging, one realizes the capacity to follow conditions, and thus does not grasp at them.
Names and marks have no cause; they do not exist as objects of cognition.
To realize that the ultimate is devoid of the conventional is for wisdom to be free from the existence of grasped marks.
This wondrous presence is precisely the ultimate; it is not a state of non-cognition.
Thus, the reality of phenomena accords with true wisdom; it is not the voidness of wood or stone. △ Third, citation of scriptures to establish this proof:

Therefore, a sutra says: "Regarding all dharmas, Prajñā (marks both object and wisdom) neither grasps (it does not grasp because they are not existent), nor does it abandon (it does not abandon because they are not non-existent), neither knows (it is not a cognition of existence), nor does it not know (it is not a lack of cognition)."
This establishes the aforementioned meaning. △ Fourth, the conclusion and reprimand regarding emotional attachments:
This realm beyond objective grasping is the domain where the mind is severed.
Objective grasping is itself deluded thought (*vikalpa*). "Severing the mind" means severing the deluded mind; the deluded mind is precisely objective grasping, and objective grasping is...
Existence and non-existence are established [as extremes]. Since noble wisdom transcends the external, it cuts them off.
To conclude this by holding the preceding and following sections accountable, and then to seek to interrogate with existence and non-existence—is this not far removed from the truth?
This is a reductio ad absurdum. To seek whether the Holy Mind exists or not and thereby pose a question is to be profoundly remote from the truth.

Nevertheless, because the emotional mind cannot reach the realm of wisdom, one becomes increasingly distant from it. △ Fourth, the response consisting of a counter-reductio on the profound principle; this has two parts. First, the statement of the intent.
Second, the refutation of existence and non-existence. First, the statement of the intent.
Please examine this. "Chen" (陳) means to present; it means to request or to interrogate.
"Fu" (夫) is a particle used for discourse; it means to explain. Master Liu previously explained the differences regarding the existence and non-existence of the essence and function of *prajñā*.
Now, by investigating and interrogating [his position], one finds that such a principle must not exist. This is the restatement (*niedie*).
This is the conclusion. △ Second, the refutation through inquiry. Part three: First, the demonstration that existence cannot be established.
Now, as for the arising of cognition: it is limited to within the realm of appearances.
Because deluded cognition arises dependent upon objects, it is limited to within the realm of appearances; thus, it is said to "possess knowing."

The Dharma is fundamentally without marks. What does noble wisdom know? Noble wisdom illuminates the true Dharma; the true Dharma is fundamentally without marks. What knowing can there be in true wisdom? Thus, seeking it as existent is not established.
2. Inferring that it is not non-existent.
The world refers to those who are "without knowledge" as being like wood, stone, or the great void—beings devoid of sentience (*nir-cetana*).

"Devoid of sentience" means lacking spiritual awareness (*vijñāna*). "Beings" (*jāti*) means categories. Thus, worldly people describe wood, stone, the great void, and all such categories that lack spiritual awareness as being without knowledge.
The numinous mirror illuminates the profound even before forms have manifested. The Way possesses no hidden mechanisms; how could it be said to be without knowledge?

"Numinous mirror" refers to the function of wisdom. "Profound" (*you*) means deep; "illuminating" (*zhù*) means shining. The first phrase clarifies that wisdom penetrates the source of principle. "Forms" (*xing*) means manifestation;
"before they have manifested" (*wei zhào*) means that traces and signs have not yet arisen. The second phrase clarifies that illumination exhausts the very beginning of things.
The Way is the principle of non-duality. "Mechanism" (jī) refers to the movement of a mechanical device; it serves as a metaphor for the functioning of wisdom (*jñāna*).

When the Way of non-duality resides within wisdom, it cannot remain hidden or latent. The subsequent phrase clarifies the simultaneous illumination of both principle and phenomena (*dharmatā* and *dharma*), thereby revealing the functioning of wisdom by contrast:
how could it be like wood or stone, devoid of cognition? The final phrase concludes this clarification. This demonstrates that there is nothing that is not [manifested] through non-being.
△ Third, revealing that it is neither existent nor non-existent.
First, ignorance arises from ignorance; there is no such thing as ignorance [without a basis].
"First" (qie) serves to cite the preceding argument: although the world has the designation "ignorance," it originates from the ignorance of wood and stone.
As for its essence: because Prajñā is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, it lacks even the name of "non-knowledge. Its essence can be described as being without knowledge.
This text reflects upon the preceding passage which stated that "knowledge arises from knowledge" and that there is the name of "having knowledge" in the world.

Arising from deluded conceptualization, there is the substance of knowing; yet when illuminated by *prajñā*, it is fundamentally quiescent. Therefore, there is no name or substance of "knowing" that can be described.
It is not that there is no knowing; rather, because it is not existent, it is called non-existent, and because it is not non-existent, it is called non-non-existent.

The term "so-called" (*yì*) refers to critical evaluation. Since *prajñā* possesses neither the name "existence" nor "non-existence" that could be interrogated, one must necessarily employ the dialectical analysis of "neither existence nor non-existence" to investigate and evaluate it.
Therefore, it was stated previously that the essence of *prajñā* is neither existent nor non-existent, and so forth.

Therefore, it is empty yet does not lose its illumination (it is not non-existence); it illuminates yet does not lose its emptiness (it is not existence). It is profound stillness and eternal quiescence. "Stillness" (*pa*) refers to the tranquility of the mind;
"profound stillness" (*pa-ran*) is thus quiescence. The essence of wisdom is fundamentally quiescent; hence it is called "eternal quiescence."
"Neither grasping nor constraining.

"Mí" (靡) means "not to have. Grasping and constraining both involve the mind being attached to something. Since the function of wisdom is non-action (*wuwei*), how could there be grasping or constraint?
Who then could move it to cause existence, or bring it to rest to cause non-existence?
One must not grasp at it as being existent, nor grasp at its essence as being non-existent, and thus describe it in terms of existence and non-existence.
△ Second, revealing the profound purport, in three parts: First, citing a sutra to indicate the profundity.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "True Prajñā" (the term "true" distinguishes it from the false and illusory)—it is not existent (for its essence and function are empty and quiescent), nor is it non-existent (in terms of its essence and function);
it has no arising (its essence and function are not newly produced), and it has no cessation (its essence and function do not subsequently perish).
Within Prajñā there are six "nots. Now, "neither existent nor non-existent" means neither increasing nor decreasing, and neither arising nor ceasing;
thus, how could defilement or purity exist? Therefore, these are combined. Furthermore, existence, non-existence, arising, and ceasing each possess four propositions:
first, not existent; second, not non-existent; third, not both existent and non-existent; and simultaneously, fourth, neither existent nor non-existent—wherein all arise in mutual extinction.
The same applies to cessation (*nirodha*). That is to say, it cannot be grasped from any of the four directions;
it cannot be shown or explained to others.

Apart from these four positions, what could one possibly say to show it to others? It can only be attained through internal realization (*pratyātma-vedya*); it is not an object of [discursive] vision.
What is heard is that which is known through learning. △ Second, an exposition to infer the profound purport: Why is this so?
Since it is said that "that which is neither existent nor non-existent and so forth is true prajñā," for what reason is it further said that it "cannot be explained or shown"?
Regarding the statement "it is not existent" (the citation of the sutra): this means it is not [inherently] existent;
it expresses the intent of the sutra. It is to clarify that Prajñā is not a substantial existence; because it is knowing and illuminating, it is said to be non-existent.
This does not mean that it is non-existent.
To dispel the attachment [to existence], one cannot hear it said that it is non-existent; otherwise, one would claim that Prajñāpāramitā belongs to the realm of nothingness.
To say "it is not non-existent" (citing the sūtra) means to state that it is not the case that it is non-existent.
This is the intended meaning of the sūtra. Since Prajñā is not something dull or blind, it is not for this reason that one says it is "not non-existent.
"Not" does not mean it is simply non-existent;

rather, it also dispels the attachment [to existence]. If one hears it said that it is "not non-existent," one might then claim it belongs to the category of existence. Thus, we know the sūtra speaks of it as "not existent."
It is not non-existent, and so forth; it merely dispels attachment. Ultimately, one cannot speak of prajñā; therefore, know that prajñā is ineffable.
It is not existent, not non-existent, not non-existent, and not not non-existent.

This further serves as a double negation. Regarding the previous statement that there is fear concerning the traces [of the teaching], some say that because one departs from the two extremes by means of *prajñā*, the Sūtra speaks of "neither existence nor non-existence.
Although it cannot be described in terms of existence or non-existence, does not the phrase "neither existence nor non-existence" itself constitute a description of *prajñā*?
Therefore, this is now negated; the first two characters [“非有”] are cited from the preceding [text], and the character “非” (non-) from the middle of the Sūtra [“非有非無”] is taken as the subject.
The two characters "able to sweep away" (*neng fu*) serve as that which sweeps away. This is truly because the emotional attachments of the two types of grasping have perished.
Prajñā is fundamentally without names such as "neither existent nor non-existent. This is like the principle of the medicine being discarded once the illness is exhausted.
To transcend the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) and sever the hundred negations is called true *prajñā*. △ Third, the conclusion and exhortation to seek the profound mystery.
For this reason, Subhūti concludes his discourse on the *prajñāpāramitā* by stating that there is nothing to be taught.
How can this path beyond words be transmitted?
The meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: When the sons of the gods heard Subhūti’s exposition of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the sons of the gods said: "O Night..."
The speech of Vimalakīrti can still be understood; the speech of Subhūti cannot be understood. Subhūti said:
"The sons of the gods do not understand or know me, for I have said nothing at all. This is because true wisdom transcends words; words cannot reach it."
It is unknown by what means [the teaching] was transmitted. An ancient poem says: "The withered mulberry tree knows the wind of heaven; the sea water knows the cold of heaven.
Now it is likewise said, "Knowing how it was transmitted," which is essentially a way of saying that it is not known.
"I hope" means "I look forward to. "The gentlemen who have penetrated the mystery" refers to Master Liu. It expresses the hope for a realization of the profound principle beyond words.
△ Second, answering that illumination and function, emptiness and existence, are simultaneous; this has two parts. First, briefly restating the previous question.

Furthermore, it is said that one should first settle the Sage’s mind. Regarding the Way to which one ought to accord: does it consist solely in illuminating the signless, or does it consist in beholding all its transformations?
The preceding [text] may be seen [in the source]. △ Second, the direct answer to the doubts raised has two parts. First, directly stating the nature of the doubt to answer it has three parts.
First, stating that the question deviates from the truth:

The speaker seems to suggest that "non-appearance" (*amūrti*) and "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) are not of one intent; upon observing transformation, it appears different from non-appearance. To illuminate—
If there were no characteristic (animitta), one would lose the capacity for harmonious integration.

This implies that regarding the previous question, you do not permit the simultaneous operation of illumination and function, or of emptiness and existence; this greatly contradicts the true principle of the Mahāyāna.
Since I do not wish to refute you directly here, I say "it appears as if. Its essential meaning refers to the purport of Prajñā. As for "not being one":
Because it does not permit emptiness and existence to be illuminated simultaneously.
That being so, the meaning of "identical with reality" (ji-jin) would be hindered by delusion.

Since existence and non-existence are illuminated together and principle and phenomenon are fused as a pair, it is called "identical with reality. This is the meaning of the True Teaching (Shōkyō). Thus it is asked.
This indicates that [the person] has not yet understood the profound purport; they are deluded and hindered. △ Second, showing the correct meaning, in four parts.
First, citing the sutra to establish the meaning.

The Sutra says (from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter on Practice and Response): "Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form."

"Form. This is established based on the simultaneous operation of wisdom and its function, as understood through the objects of cognition. "Above" refers to the meaning of the True. However, regarding form, emptiness, existence, and non-existence, these are mostly distinguished according to the deluded mind (*qing*) in terms of phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*).
Regarding nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*), these are mostly discussed in terms of wisdom. Now, based on what Master Liu asked, [this is not so].

It is permitted that mutual illumination may stagnate in the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism; therefore, the first phrase excludes substantial form (*rūpa*), and the next excludes nihilistic emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

The final two phrases exclude both simultaneously within a single thought-moment. For one who attains the function of wisdom, phenomena do not differ from principle, and principle does not differ from phenomena;

thus, phenomenon and principle are mutually fused, and emptiness and existence are illuminated together. Although this fourfold formulation also exists in the *Heart Sūtra*, it did not exist during the Qin period.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is cited to establish this point. △ Second, the awakening to delusion is explained in two parts: first, describing the state of deluded sentiment;
second, revealing the correct principle. Now, for the first:

"If it were according to the Tathāgata’s intent (referring to the intent of your question hereafter), when contemplating the emptiness of form (when illuminating the emptiness of form), one should perceive form with a single mind."
The mind perceives emptiness;
emptiness and form are illuminated distinctly. Therefore, each has its own single mind.
If a single mind perceives form, then there is only form and no emptiness. If a single mind perceives emptiness, then there is only emptiness and no form.
As stated above: "To perceive transformation is to differ from the signless; to illuminate the signless is to lose the grasp of their convergence.
Thus, emptiness and form are presented as two, with neither able to establish a fixed foundation.
This is the reality; this is the true exposition. True emptiness and illusory form are fundamentally non-dual.
Since they are now spoken of separately, the fundamental state of non-duality is lost. △ Second, showing the correct principle.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "That which is not form.
This refers back to the preceding section of the Sūtra to clarify the meaning that emptiness is manifest within form itself;
for indeed, "not-form" is [discussed] in relation to form.
Because the Sūtras state that true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is itself illusory form;
thus, one does not negate form within non-form.
The "non-form" mentioned above is true emptiness, while the "non-form" mentioned below is nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*). It is not said that true emptiness is separate from form.
Because it is the cessation of form.
If that which is not form were [the emptiness] within non-form—[meaning] being separated from form and the cessation of form—then the great void would be non-form.
This explains why the aforementioned position is irrational. If emptiness were separate from form, it would be nothing more than the great void being separate from form.
What does that which is not form clarify? It is transcendence.
This emptiness of annihilation is without cognition and without utility; it is neither cultivation nor realization. Why, then, must it be distinguished and clarified?
If one takes "non-form" (to be true) in relation to "form" (to be illusory), then non-form is not different from form. Since non-form is not different from form, form [is non-form].
This is precisely what it means for form to be non-form;
that form and emptiness are non-dual. Thus, the true meaning of the sutra is clearly revealed. △ Third, the conclusion which clarifies the reason:

Therefore, one should know that transformation is itself signlessness, and signlessness is itself transformation. It is only because the dispositions of sentient beings differ that the traces of the teachings vary.

As for "the sentiments of the multitude," this refers to the fact that their minds do not hold a single view. For those who cling to form as being real, it is taught that it is not different from emptiness;
for those who cling to emptiness as nihilism, it is taught that it is not different from form. Therefore, there are differences in the establishment of the teachings and the manifestation of traces.

Examining the profound scriptures and tracing back to the intent of the Sage, how could there again be a distinction between the minds of truth and falsehood, or a difference in illumination between the empty and the existent?
"Examining the source" means to investigate and collate. "Profound scriptures" refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Dapin*). "Falsehood" means emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

That which is conventionally real and illusory existence is called "false. This means that when one investigates the textual meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, how could it be said that the mind possesses a distinction between the ultimate and the conventional, while the objective realm [is otherwise]?
There is a distinction between existence and emptiness; this also refutes what was previously grasped. △ Fourth, reconciling the preceding meanings:
Therefore, illuminating formlessness does not lose the merit of harmonious engagement, and observing change and movement does not deviate from the principle of formlessness.

The creation of existence is not different from non-existence (just as the illumination of form is not different from the contemplation of emptiness); the creation of non-existence is not different from existence (just as the contemplation of emptiness is not different from the illumination of form). It has never been otherwise than existence.
There has never been a time when it was not so.

"Sang" (甞) means "formerly" or "ever. Principle and phenomena are illumined simultaneously; emptiness and existence are viewed as one. Therefore, if there is no illumination, that is that; but if there is illumination, there has never been any difference.
Therefore it is said: "Without moving from equal enlightenment, one establishes all dharmas.
This is from the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*. Since this was previously cited as the opening of the inquiry, it is now again quoted for corroboration and to provide further clarification.
△ Third, a reprimand regarding the question posed:
By this reasoning, what hindrance is there to the identity of quiescence and function?

It is because of function. By investigating the correct meaning of the sutras through their application, one knows that the quiescence and function of *prajñā* are simultaneous; what hindrance could there be?
It is an obstruction.
How can that which is called "knowledge perceiving change" differ from the illumination of the signless?
This is a reprimand. △ Second, the refutation through analysis based on understanding, in three parts. First, the description of erroneous understanding.
I fear that the speaker might mistakenly claim that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhāva*) possess two distinct minds, and that stillness and agitation have different functions.
"I fear" (*kǒng*) is a term of uncertainty; "mistakenly" (*tuō*) means erroneously; "agitation" (*zào*) means movement. What Master Liu perceives may not necessarily be so.
It is perhaps due to this error or omission that he claims the Sage’s mind illuminates both emptiness and existence separately, with movement and stillness having distinct functions.
Because of this erroneous interpretation, the following section reiterates what was said there;
thus it says: "The cognition that perceives transformation cannot be said not to exist.
△ Second, the exhortation to investigate the profound.

If one can relinquish one's own mind within the realm of worldly attachments and seek the profound mechanism beyond mundane affairs, then how could wisdom such as *prajñā* reside solely in the minds of sages and not in the minds of ordinary beings?
Since the state of absolute truth gives rise to delusion, [wisdom must likewise be present in both].
One should simply abandon delusion to seek the truth. Therefore, I now exhort you to relinquish internal attachments. Since Prajñā is not obtained from without, "attachments" refers to clinging.
One clings internally to existence and non-existence; I exhort you to let go of these. Profound mechanisms and wondrous wisdom transcend the affairs of existence and non-existence;
I exhort you to seek them. Those who grasp the meaning by seeking through words can forget the words; having forgotten the words, they attain [the meaning].
The mind. When the mind finds nothing to grasp, who can say it has not realized [the truth]?
To unify the myriad existents within the single void and to understand that this ultimate void is not non-existence—this is to encourage the attainment of realization and its subsequent application.
"To unify" means to level. The "single void" is the ultimate principle. The profound mechanism is activated.
When one illuminates [reality], then every encountered phenomenon is the principle; the principle does not depart from phenomena. Therefore, the principle of ultimate emptiness is not non-existent.
This refers back to the person: one who can act in this manner is as described below.

It should be said: The Perfected One (zhiren) responds to all things throughout the day; he moves in accordance with phenomena and rides upon the flow of fortune to soothe and transform beings, yet from the beginning he has never acted as if they truly existed.
This further encourages the preaching of transformation and its transmission. At such a time, these words may be spoken. The above three [points].
The preceding phrase refers to "bowing down and looking up in accordance with transformation," and so forth; the final phrase means that there is no merit in the act of illuminating.
△ Third, the refutation of what is clung to: If the Sage’s mind is thus, how could there be anything to be grasped? Yet you say, "You have not yet explained the principle of non-grasping."
Master Liu said: "Originally, there was no delusion regarding the knowledge of non-appropriation (*anupādāna*), yet you have not yet explained the principle of why one does not appropriate.

Therefore, I now question you. Since the Sage’s mind is fundamentally without appropriation, he speaks of 'non-appropriation. As for the principle of non-appropriation, what further explanation could it require?
**3. The Dual Negation as the Appropriate Awakening to Delusion (Answer Four)** **A. Restating the Previous Point and Acknowledging the Question**
It is further said: "That which is without 'is' is precisely what constitutes true being; that which is without 'appropriateness' is precisely what constitutes ultimate appropriateness.
This may indeed be the word of the Tathāgata.
First, he restates the preceding [point]; second, he acknowledges the question. If it were as the questioner asks, it could also be like this. However, Master Liu already knew this.
True wisdom knows through non-knowing; the true realm is without marks, yet it is precisely the marks themselves.

However, because [the interlocutor] has not yet realized that knowing is itself non-knowing and that marks are themselves marklessness, he previously established what is "ultimately appropriate" versus "not ultimately appropriate," and what is "truly real" versus "not truly real," and thus asked his question.
Therefore, I first acknowledge what he has awakened to, and subsequently refute what he clings to; hence, I say, "It may also be so. △ Second, the method of concession and refutation.
The response consists of two parts. First, it accords with what has been realized:

if one can be "without mind" (if there is no internal mind of attachment or differentiation, only then is one truly capable)—establishing what is true as being "true," yet being "true" within the state of non-truth.

"Reality" (*tattva*) is established in opposition to "non-reality. Although it is known that the wisdom of reality is non-knowing, this is posited as "reality" by virtue of its dependence [upon its opposite];
thus, "non-reality" exists in relation to it. The delusion of viewing things as real or unreal resides in the grasping mind.
Only when there is no grasping mind can one truly understand; the following passages have the same meaning.
One should be "appropriate" (dang) by having no intention to act (wuxin yu wei dang), yet be appropriate within the state of non-appropriateness (dang yu wudang).
Even when one stands in the state of "as-it-is" (yathābhūta) in opposition to "not-as-it-is," although one has realized that the true realm is without marks yet possesses marks,
it is not permissible if the mind of attachment does not cease when confronted with what is as-it-is and what is not-as-it-is.
This refers back to what was stated above. One who is able to sever the attachment to "is" and "is not" will, though all day long asserting "is," not deviate from the state of "no-is";
though all day long asserting "it is so," not deviate from the state of "no-it-is-so."
Once one has realized that knowing is non-knowing, then one understands that throughout the entire day one knows yet there is no knowing.
Furthermore, once one has realized that form is formlessness, then one knows that throughout the entire day there is form yet there is no form. This merely removes their attachment;
the preceding meaning then becomes manifest of itself. II. Refuting What They Cling To. This section has two parts. First, the direct clarification.
I only fear that there may be "being right" where there is no being right, and "appropriateness" where there is no appropriateness;

this is what constitutes the affliction. "Being right" refers to having true correctness; "no being right" refers to the absence of cognitive knowledge. The principle of "appropriateness" should be understood accordingly.

I only fear that Master Liu might establish "true correctness" within the state of non-cognition and establish "ultimate appropriateness" within the state of signlessness; thus, he would become attached to his own mind.
It is not removed, for the affliction of delusion arises. △ Second, the inquiry and explanation.
What is it? (This is the inquiry: what affliction is there? If it were truly real, it would be acceptable; if it were ultimately appropriate, it would be fitting.
However, that which responds truly possesses authentic wisdom and an authentic realm. The following passage provides the critique:
"Thus names and forms take shape, and beauty and ugliness (pronounced *wū*) arise. Life after life, beings rush in competition; who can bring them to rest?"
"Form" (*rūpa*) means manifestation; it means being beautiful. When manifestations of names and forms appear that are ultimate and truly real, a mind of delight arises.
When manifestations of names and forms appear that are not so, nor ultimate, a mind of aversion arises. As long as delight and aversion do not cease, one will rush about in the cycle of saṃsāra;
who then could stop this? This is precisely to be in the deep pit of ignorance. How could the illumination of Prajñā-wisdom possibly be present here?
Can this be attained? Furthermore, as beautiful and foul thoughts proliferate and compete with one another, how could they ever be stilled?
Therefore, it is not through such [limited] wisdom that there is tranquil illumination. △ Third, revealing the correct principle.
For this reason, the sage makes his breast (his inner being) hollow and vacant;

he has no discernment and no cognition. "Inner breast" refers to the heart-mind (*citta*). "Hollow" means empty. The substance of the mind is quiescent extinction; it is empty and yet further empty, hence it is called "hollow and vacant.

To differentiate is called discernment (*vijñāna*); to engage with objects through thought is called cognition (*jñāna*). Since the substance of the mind is fundamentally transcendent of these, both are said to be non-existent.
This reveals that the essence of wisdom is the realm of quiescence, where object and cognition are identical to suchness (*tathatā*).
Thus, while abiding within the domain of dynamic function, it rests in the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); though situated within the sphere of names, it dwells in the land beyond words.
These two phrases each clarify the essence of immediate function. While abiding in the sphere of dynamic activity, they may be so named;
yet in both cases, the mind and its objects are seen with vivid clarity. Thus, the mind being no-mind, the objects are no-objects. Therefore, cessation is the dwelling of non-action, beyond words.

This reveals the meaning of the aforementioned "being while having no being" and "appropriateness while having no appropriateness. Furthermore, the preceding phrase clarifies the mutual identity of mind and objects.
It is without marks (*animitta*). The latter phrase reveals that names are themselves nameless. When there are no names and no marks, there is profound stillness;

when there are marks and names, there is manifold activity. Therefore, it was said above: "When speaking of function, they are different while being the same; when speaking of stillness, they are the same while being different."
It is tranquil, vast, and empty; it cannot be grasped through form or name. It is simply like this.
If one realizes the essence of total function—an essence that transcends mind, object, form, and name—then with such an understanding, one may respond to the question as it was asked.
△ Fourth, the conclusion and reprimand for improper questioning.
He then said: "Truly so, indeed so; most appropriate, truly appropriate. This does not yet convey your elegant meaning.
"Yù" (喻) means to explain or clarify. This above is a concluding reprimand:
I fear that what you call "so" (rán) refers to things being produced by conditions; yet those things themselves are not "so. How, then, can they be deemed "so"?
This is not what was asked. "Fear" (*kō*) is a term denoting uncertainty; it refers to arising. "Things" (*motsu*) refers to the myriad phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"However" (*naru*) means "in this way. "That" (*haku*) refers to the true mind (*shinjitsu-shin*), which is beyond all characteristics.

Mind and objects are that which arise; they are not fixed forms in opposition. While one may say of the myriad phenomena of conventional truth that they are "in this way," that true mind is fundamentally...
Having severed the distinct characteristics of subject and object, what is the need to insistently seek them through the sentiments of right and wrong?
△ Third, the conclusion and exhortation to explore the profound mystery. Now, the previous conclusion to the questions arose because [the seekers] clung to words and were hindered by traces;

as their lineages of transmission differed, even though they aimed for the Sage’s mind, they inevitably fell into biased attachments. Therefore, the present conclusion summarizes the previous answers, erasing traces and brushing away words so as to...

Directly penetrating the profound and subtle, one is precisely "mind itself is wisdom. This section has three parts. The first discusses the traces of delusion and awakening, which in turn has two parts.
The first clarifies that delusion gives rise to attachment.
Now, the emergence of verbal traces is the source from which diverse paths arise.
These "verbal traces" refer to the teachings and their meanings; that is to say, as previously stated, while the established stages have a common foundation, their underlying principles differ.

To establish the teachings is to provide the words, and to set forth the meanings is to provide the traces. Furthermore, the sages established these teachings and expounded these meanings for the sake of those who do not yet understand.
The finger points to the moon; yet, as subjective perceptions are manifold, the expressions arising from them also differ.

If each were to establish their own doctrinal teachings, then views and understandings would follow many paths. Thus it is said that "diverse paths arise therefrom. △ Second, when one realizes the ultimate truth, one enters the profound mystery.
Yet there are things that words do not express, and traces that footprints do not record.
Since words and traces cannot fully elucidate or discern the ultimate principle—it being, in fact, beyond the reach of mind and speech—it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
△ Second, citing those who have attained mastery.
Therefore, one who is skilled in speaking seeks that which words cannot express;
one who is skilled in understanding speech and listening to it is alone able to seek the words within the wordless.
The "trace of the traces" is that which cannot be traced by following after traces.
One who skillfully masters the meaning and contemplates the meaning is only then able to seek the meaning within the traceless. Once the traces of speech have vanished, [the truth is revealed].
How could this be a matter of sectarian division? △ Third, the conclusion reveals the profound mystery:

The ultimate truth is void and transcendent; to direct the mind toward it is already to err (for it is not something reachable through intellectual understanding). How much more so when words are employed—fearing that what is shown will only become further removed (for it is not something that can be reached by speech).
It is hoped that gentlemen of penetrating mind may find something to expect beyond the written text.

This is my humble hope. As for those gentlemen who have attained a thorough understanding of the mind, I hope that Master Liu will provide internal illumination; that we may share the same realization beyond words and traces is what I expect of you.

△ Third, the *Nirvāṇa-wuming-lun* (Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvāṇa): It clarifies that principle and wisdom are non-dual, manifesting proof of their unity. The preceding treatise addressed the objective realm; [this one addresses the subject].

The ultimate and the conventional are mutually integrated; in terms of wisdom, they are the root, and subsequently their substance is one. Now, because object and wisdom are non-dual, the single suchness is no different from the suchness of non-duality.
This alone is the one dharma, which from the beginning is unconditioned, truly constant, and quiescently extinguished.
It is free from all marks yet is identical with all dharmas; this is the pinnacle of realization. To manifest this meaning, the following section is presented.
In terms of the provisional teachings and principles, the former is shallow and the latter is deep; thus, the single path extends vertically to this ultimate point.

In terms of practice and fruition, however, cultivation and realization occur simultaneously. When arising, it must be entirely true. It is simply that when mind and object are non-dual yet appear dual, this is cultivation;

when they are dual yet non-dual, this is realization. Therefore, in the previous treatise, subject and object were not yet extinguished; in this treatise, they are obliterated and find no locus. Great!
In the Real Teaching (*shijiao*), from cause to fruit, the application of the mind remains consistent from beginning to end.

Therefore, it is permitted that even at the initial stage (*chuzhu*) of generating the bodhicitta, there is the principle of partial realization of Buddhahood. Thus, we know that cause and fruit, practice and realization, are simultaneous.
As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "The initial mind and the ultimate mind are not two; yet between these two minds, the former is more difficult. This refers to...
The former refers to suddenness in terms of phenomena; this refers to suddenness in terms of principle. Thus, one knows that the fulfillment of the fruit does not await three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Furthermore, although this treatise follows the previous one in terms of its principles, its initiation also lies with the Qin Emperor.

Since the Qin Emperor first proclaimed this doctrine, the Master [of the Treatise] then welcomed and expounded its profound purport. For these reasons, the arrival of this treatise carries two intentions: first, to establish [the doctrine]; second, [to propagate it].

Because it establishes the fundamental tenet and because it perfects the scriptural principles—due to these two intentions, there is first a prefatory statement (*pratijñā*), followed by the formal treatise (*śāstra*).

Based on this, the text is divided into two parts: first, the prefatory statement; second, the formal treatise. Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, the title of the prefatory statement.

The original title of the *Shang niepan lun biao* (Memorial on the Treatise on the Ultimate Nirvāṇa) included the word “with memorial” (*bing biao*). I now follow the recent edition; this title was also established by later generations. To address a superior is called “upward” (*shang*);

“memorial” (*biao*) refers to that which is external. The intent of the original meaning has already been set forth in the text of the memorial itself. Since this treatise was composed at the request of the Prince of Qin, [it is titled accordingly].
Because the treatise has been completed, this preface is presented to advance it.
△ Second, the text of the preface has three parts. First, a general praise of the King’s virtue. Sengzhao says:
"Zhao has heard that Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the Sovereign attains the One and [becomes... "

"Govern the world" is what is heard in the external texts, namely the *Daodejing*. The current text is abbreviated; those [external texts] say, "The feudal lords and kings obtain the One and thereby govern the world.
Because the First Emperor tabooed the character for "govern" (*zhèng*), it is here said "govern the world" (*zhì tiānxià*).
I humbly observe that Your Majesty’s sagacity and wisdom are reverent and enlightened.

These four qualities are terms derived from the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents), specifically from the two canons concerning Yao and Shun. Here, they are used to extol the supreme virtue of the King of Qin.
The Way and the Spirit meet.

That which is non-action is called the Way; that which is unfathomable is called the Spirit. When the spiritual understanding accords with the nature of the Way, it is called "meeting. This clarifies the possession of royal virtue.
Wondrously in accord with the center of the ring, there is no principle that it does not encompass.
The "center of the ring" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If the center were not empty, it would not be a ring.
Because one penetrates the principle of emptiness, one is able to universally encompass all phenomena. This praises the knowledge of the Buddha’s principle.
He wielded his skill over the myriad affairs of state and propagated the Way throughout the day.
The first phrase praises his sovereign achievements; the second lauds his external protection.
His majesty extended to all living beings, and he bequeathed written records to serve as a model for posterity.

"Blue-Clad Beings" (Cāngshēng) refers to the living spirits born by Heaven, whom its majestic virtue covers and protects. Furthermore, it bestows instruction through the patterns of ritual and music to serve as a standard;
thus, among the four great things within the realm, the King occupies one.
Laozi said: "The Way is great, Heaven is great, Earth is great, and the King is also great. [△] Second, the exposition of the school’s origins has four parts.
First, praising the profound and mysterious ultimate truth:
the Way of Nirvāṇa (marking the fruit-dharma of the One Vehicle). This is indeed that to which the Three Vehicles return; it is the deep reservoir of the Vaipulya teachings.
The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the Mahāyāna is called "square and equal" (*vaipulya*). "Deep" refers to a profound depth; "repository" (*fu*) means a gathering place.

This signifies that the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is the ultimate destination to which the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) return, and furthermore, it is the locus where the teachings of definitive meaning are gathered.
Vast and boundless, remote and ineffable—this is a realm beyond the reach of sight and hearing.
"Vast and boundless" (*miaomang*) refers to water that has no limits. Laozi said: "That which one hears but does not perceive is called *xi*; that which one sees but does not behold is called *yi*.
These terms all describe the wondrous Way’s profound mystery.
Its profound and mysterious essence is such that it can hardly be fathomed by the common mind; "hardly" (dài) here implies a sense of difficulty.
△ Second, the narration of profound gratitude and humble emotion. This section has two parts. First, the narration of the emotional response to the encountered grace.
Zhaò considers himself a man of humble station who has, by a great stroke of imperial favor, been granted the leisure to dwell in seclusion and study at the academy.
"Mí" (微) means weak or inferior; "wěi" (猥) means base or lowly—both are terms of humility. Because he has received this grace, he has left secular life to dwell in seclusion and study at the academy.
He remained in the school of Master Kumārajīva for more than ten years;
"in the school" (*xué sì*) refers to his period of study. Here, "years" (*zǎi*) means "anniversaries.
Since the Master of the Treatise was nineteen when he studied under Kumārajīva and passed away at thirty-one, it is evident that he entered nirvana not long after the treatise was completed.
Although the various scriptures have diverse purports and their superior goals are not uniform, the single meaning of *nirvāṇa* always takes listening and study as its priority.
Listening and studying the meaning of *nirvāṇa* is the most excellent among the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*); therefore, it is said to be "prior. △ Second, the power of humility.
I am humble and insignificant.

My talent and understanding are dim and obscure; although I have repeatedly received your instructions and exhortations, I still harbor doubts in a state of mental haziness. I have exhausted my foolishness without ceasing, and it seems as though I have attained some comprehension.
However, having not yet heard the preliminary teachings of a sublime and superior master, I do not dare to reach a definitive conclusion on my own. Unfortunately, Master Kumārajīva...
The Master has passed away; there is no one left to consult or seek counsel from, which causes me eternal regret.

Although I have repeatedly received the instructions and exhortations of Kumārajīva, my doubts remain shrouded in darkness, hence I say "vast and desolate. Yet, having exhausted my own foolishness without ceasing, it seems as though there is some understanding.
However, because I have not yet undergone the seal of approval from a master of clear realization, I do not dare to decide for myself. This is what I respectfully [submit].
These were the words of the Master. Furthermore, because Kumārajīva had passed away, the Master had no one to question; thus, he sighed with deep regret over this long-standing loss.
△ Third, praising the King’s clear understanding.

Yet Your Majesty’s sagely virtue is not solitary; you alone share a spiritual resonance with Master Shi. To witness the Way directly is to realize its presence; you have thoroughly exhausted the depths of his inner mind.

As the *Analects* says: "Virtue is never solitary; it must have neighbors. "Spiritual resonance" means that their spiritual understandings are in perfect accord. "Directly witnessing" (mùjī) refers to the eyes—[the direct perception of reality].
"Striking at the Way so that it exists" is from the *Zhuangzi*. Zhongni said: "As for the benevolent person, the Way exists within the mere glance of the eye;
it cannot even admit a sound. To "swiftly exhaust what is within one's own square inch" means that by looking with a piercing gaze, one suddenly grasps the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, he was able to rouse that profound wind (*xuanfeng*) to enlighten the customs of the final age.

"Rouse" means to lift up. The "profound wind" refers to the true path of *nirvāṇa*. Because the profound wind was about to fall, he exerted himself with vigor to lift it up and rouse it, thereby opening the way for those of inferior capacity;
hence the term "customs of the final age. Kang’s Commentary states: After Dharma Master Kumārajīva passed away, the King of Qin...
This penetrates the meanings of four categories: first, it penetrates the meaning that the Sage does not abide in dharmas but abides in *prajñā*;

second, it penetrates the meaning of the Sage emitting great radiance; third, it penetrates the meaning of the three periods of time; fourth, it penetrates the meaning of the emptiness of all dharmas.
The fourth is precisely the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. Emperor Qin Tong said: "Now, the Way takes non-action (*wuwei*) as its essence. If it were non-existent..."
What else could there possibly be? These words are spoken now because he is praising this matter. △ Fourth, the sequence of the response;
the profound meaning is deep. This section has two parts. First, the direct elucidation.
One day, he encountered Mengda, who answered a letter from Yao Song, the Marquis of Ancheng, inquiring about the ultimate principle of non-action (*wuwei*).

"Marquis of Ancheng" refers to his enfeoffed title. Yao Song was the younger paternal uncle of the Prince of Qin. Regarding the "letter of inquiry," Yao Song had written a letter to the Prince of Qin questioning three principles;
it did not inquire about the principle of the Three Periods of Time, but rather questioned the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
The commentary states: "I do not yet clearly understand that the Way is non-action (*wuwei*); what, then, should be taken as its essence? and so forth. The King of Qin replied:
"My intention is to take non-action as the Way; the Way rests solely in non-action. I have not yet fully grasped its fundamental principle," and so forth.
Having encountered this response which clarified his purpose, the Master of the Treatise resolved his doubts and consequently composed this treatise. Below...
I shall now cite the reply given by the King of Qin.
What was it? (What is the meaning of "unconditioned" [wuwei]? It is because sentient beings cling to desire that they have long wandered through birth and death.
"Desire" refers to the mind of longing. As long as one has not realized that the myriad phenomena are entirely true, seeking principles and affairs externally is all desire.
Therefore, one perceives birth and death as truly existent, cycling through them without end.
If one wishes to bring [the mind] to rest within the mind, there will then be no further birth and death.
Since reality is identical with phenomena, there are no phenomena outside of principle that can be grasped, and no principle outside of phenomena that can be sought;
this is precisely what it means to bring [the mind] to rest. Since birth and death are themselves reality, there is then no further birth and death.
Since there is neither birth nor death, the spirit is hidden in profound stillness, merging its virtue with empty space;
this is called *nirvāṇa*. Because the mind is itself the truth, it is called "the spirit is hidden"; because the objective realm is itself the truth, it is called "profound stillness.

The Way of non-duality runs vertically through the three periods of time and extends horizontally throughout the ten directions; thus, its virtue merges with the Great Void. This is precisely the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state of *nirvāṇa*.
Since it is called "nirvāṇa," how could there be any name remaining within it?
When the hundred rivers enter the sea, each loses its original name; when the myriad dharmas return to the Truth, they all lack distinct appellations.
Therefore, it is said that nirvāṇa is nameless. This critique addresses the differing views regarding the essence of what the Marquis of Ancheng asked. The above [points] are all...
The words of King Qin. △ Second, the praise of excellence.
This is indeed the perfection of subtle discourse and the ultimate of talk beyond the realm of forms.
The following praises the Master of the Treatise. The *I Ching* says: "One attains the meaning and forgets the images; one attains the images and forgets the words. Now...
The Prince of Qin has reached the ultimate depth of the subtle and wondrous meaning of non-action (*wuwei*). Thus, his words transcend the realm of mere symbols.
Were it not for one whose Way rivals that of Mañjuśrī and whose virtue equals that of Maitreya, who could proclaim this profound path and serve as a defensive rampart for the Dharma?
"Can" (參) means "to attend" (廁). "Mou" (侔) means "to be equal to" (並). Both share the same meaning. "Mañjuśrī" is an incomplete transliteration of a Sanskrit term;
in full, it is "Mañjuśrī," which here means "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (妙吉祥), also called "Wondrous Head" (妙首) or "Wondrous Virtue" (妙德).
He is the son of the Dharma King. "Maitreya" is his clan name; in Sanskrit, it is "Maitreya," and his personal name is "Ajita," which here means "Unconquerable" (無勝).
Because his supreme virtues surpass those of men, he is a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood.

That you now instead praise the moral virtue of the Qin ruler is not comparable to these two Great Beings; how else could he proclaim the profound purport of the mysterious Way and serve as a rampart for the Buddha-dharma?
It causes the Great Teaching, which had been rolled up, to unfold once more; the profound purport, which had sunk into obscurity, to become manifest again.
The "Great Teaching" refers to Buddhism; the "profound purport" refers to the deep principle of non-action (*wuwei*). Both of these have been far removed from the Sage since ancient times;
that they are now being revived is why it is said they are "unfolding once more" and "becoming manifest again."

I have studied and contemplated this with such earnest devotion that I could not bear to set it aside for even a moment. Joy and awakening mingle within my heart; I am so overcome with delight that I find no leisure to stop my hands from dancing.
This is not merely a supreme path for its own time, but serves as a bridge and raft across many kalpas.
I have searched the text and contemplated its meaning; it never left my mind and eyes. Joy and awakening alternated, converging within my breast.
Thus, I could not help but move my hands in dance. "At that time" (*zhí dān*) refers to the present moment. "Ferry and bridge" (*jīnliáng*):
a ferry (*jīn*) is where one may cross by boat for transport; a bridge (*liáng*) is where one may traverse on foot along a path. Now, the King of Qin...
He established the supreme track of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), so that from this day forward there might be the true path for transcending the mundane dust.

△ Third, the petition for audience and the mental application (*manasikāra*) has two parts. First, clarifying the mental application; the text has two sections. First, praising the profound depth of the preceding meaning.
However, the Sage’s intent is profound and mysterious; its principles are subtle and its words concise. It is capable of guiding those who are already advanced and uplifting those of lofty character.
Yet, I fear that those of superficial expression may not have fully grasped the Supreme One’s meaning.
First, the meaning of the preceding text is precise and appropriate; hence it is said, "So it is. Regarding "the Sage’s intent is profound and mysterious":
the King of Qin’s underlying purpose is lofty and deep, while the principle of non-action (*wuwei*) is subtle. The King’s words are concise and serve as a master craftsman.

"To rescue and assist" means that those of advanced faculties who may have doubts can take this as a teacher’s instruction for rescue and assistance in their progress. [The text ends with] "fearing the words..."
Regarding those of inferior capacity: since the titles are so concise, those who do not understand them may be apprehensive.
Fearing that such individuals of middling or lower capacity might fail to fully grasp the superior intent, I have now composed this treatise to provide for them.

I hope to emulate the composition of the Ten Wings of the *Kongyi* (the Ten Wings of the *Yijing*). How could I covet elaborate prose? My intention is to illustrate and manifest the profound and hidden meanings.
"Shu" (庶) means "to hope for. "Ni" (擬) means "to emulate" or "to compare. Regarding the "Ten Wings of the *Kongyi*": Confucius composed the Ten Wings to extol the Way of the *Yi*.

The Ten Wings are: 1. the *Tuan* (Commentary on the Hexagrams) of the Upper Canon; 2. the *Tuan* of the Lower Canon; 3. the *Xiaxi* (The Great Appendix) of the Upper Part; 4. the *Xiaxi* of the Lower Part; and 5. the *Da*... [text truncated]

The *Xiang* (Images) is fifth; the *Xiaoxiang* (Small Images) is sixth; the *Wenyan* (Words on the Lines) is seventh; the *Xugua* (Sequence of the Hexagrams) is eighth; the *Shuogua* (Explanation of the Hexagrams) is ninth; and the *Zagua* (Miscellaneous Hexagrams) is tenth.
Now, comparing these to what was composed by Zhongni (Confucius), how could he have been intent upon ornate diagrams? He sought rather to reveal the profound depths of the *Yi*'s purport.
Herein, I likewise do not seek for many words, but merely wish to clarify the profound intent of King Qin.
I have composed the "Treatise on Nameless Nirvāṇa. This treatise consists of nine sections and ten expositions, which set forth the framework of what follows; these shall all be explained below.
Drawing extensively from various scriptures and employing them as evidence and analogies, I humbly expound upon Your Majesty’s realization of the nameless.
Extensively collecting and excerpting from the Buddhist scriptures, he relies upon the sacred words as authoritative testimony to establish his expositions and analogies;
by means of these, he praises and describes the meaning of the King’s non-action (*wuwei*).
How could it be said that this concerns penetrating the divine mind or exhausting the investigation of distant and ultimate principles?
It does not mean that it involves penetrating the King’s mind of spiritual liberation, nor does it mean exhausting the investigation of the King’s profound and ultimate intent. As it says below:
This is merely intended to provide a tentative appraisal of the Mysterious Gate (the Way) and to offer a general explanation for the sake of my students.
It is simply a desire to attempt to fathom the Mysterious Gate of Non-action and to spread a broad exposition for the benefit of later disciples.
△ Second, the concluding chapter on assisting [the teaching] with a lofty judgment. This section has two parts. First, the introduction of the meaning of the judgment and its critique.
The final chapter of the treatise states:
"King Qin [Wenxuan] understands the fourth meaning. This final chapter says:
"The various schools understand the first noble truth (paramārtha-satya), all claiming that it is vast, empty, and quiescent, such that no sage exists."

The various schools of the Xiaoyao Garden discuss the meaning of the emptiness of all dharmas; by annihilating all phenomena and returning to emptiness, they are entirely identical to the view of nihilism.
I have always considered this to be far too extreme and remote, lacking any affinity with human nature.
“I” (Wú) is the self-designation used by the King of Qin. “Too extreme” (tài shèn) and “beyond the bounds of reason” (jìng tíng) are from the *Zhuangzi*.

Li Yī’s commentary states: “Beyond the bounds of reason means to exceed the limit. This [critique] is overly extreme in its negation of emptiness and does not accord with human sentiment or understanding. The following objection says:
If there were no sages, who would know non-existence?

To "know" is to realize. Since there are no sages, who could realize the principle of non-existence? This refutes those who fail to understand, being unable to accord with non-existence by means of existence itself.

"Truly as your illustrious decree says! Truly as your illustrious decree says!"—thus the Master of the Treatise praises it. The King’s words are called "decree" (*zhào*) because the purport of the decree is clear and manifest.
Now, the Dao is vague and obscure; within it there is a subtle essence. If there were no sage, who would roam with the Dao?
Laozi said: "Vague and indistinct, yet within it there is something," and so forth. I shall now borrow that text:
"Vague and indistinct" means it seems to exist yet is as if non-existent, for it cannot be seen. "Profound and dark" means it is deep and far-reaching, beyond measurement.
"The Way of Non-action" resides in the cessation of all thought and deliberation; though it exists, it is subtle and refined. "To roam" means to tread upon it.
Although their flavor is equal and their Way is unified in its subtlety, is this not the prerogative of the Sage alone?
Were there no Sage, who would testify to the Way?

Lately, among the various disciples, there are none who do not hesitate at the gateway of the Way; they remain dissatisfied with this profound principle, harboring doubts throughout the day and finding no resolution.
This is correct. It is fortunate that we have encountered your lofty judgment; the followers of our school are filled with clarity.
Those who had been knocking at the gate now flourish as they ascend to the profound chamber. Previously, those who "hesitated" were those who wavered and did not advance;

those who were "discontented" harbored doubts and resentment. This principle is the principle of the vast void; your "lofty judgment" refers to the Emperor’s decisive repudiation; "filled with clarity" means their hearts are delighted.

"Decisively resolved" means it is clear and distinct. "Chou" (儔) implies a state of being settled. "Wei" (蔚) describes the flourishing appearance of grasses and trees; here, we take the sense of flourishing.
Once the doubting mind is resolved, the one who advances upon the Path flourishes.
Truly, it can be said that the Wheel of the Dharma has turned once more in Jambudvīpa, and the light of the Way has shone again for a thousand years.

This also serves as a lament for the past: since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the sages and worthies have already vanished; the Wheel of the Dharma has not turned for a long time, and the radiance of the Way has been obscured for ages.
Now, through the proclamation of King Qin, it is made to turn again and shine once more. △ Second, the detailed exposition.
