△ Second, the Treatise on the Text in Two Parts. First, the Title.
○ *Nirvāṇa-anāmaka-śāstra*, Chapter Four.
*Ni*, *niyuan*, and *niepan*—these three names appear differently according to their chronological order. They are likely merely variations between the dialects of Chu and Xia.
It is said that *niepan* is the correct pronunciation. The commentary states: *Niepan* is the Sanskrit sound as used in China.

To the west, there are the five regions of India; however, only the Chinese pronunciation is correct. This is because, just as in this land, the Xia dialect is correct while the Chu dialect is corrupt, so it is with *ni*.
It is said that "Nirvana" (泥洹) is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound. In the language of Qin, it is called "Non-action" (無為), and is also termed "Extinction and Deliverance" (滅度).
Although the myriad dharmas are numerous, they do not exceed the realm of mind and objects. Mind and objects are precisely the conditioned phenomena of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
Phenomena are fundamentally without intrinsic substance; their arising is necessarily the perfection of reality (*bhūtatathatā*). This true essence is limpid, equal, and of a single characteristic.

Therefore, although they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they are without birth, without abiding, without change, and without cessation. Since the mind is suchness and objects are suchness, they are called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Birth and death are fundamentally without arising or ceasing; afflictions are fundamentally without bondage or liberation. Therefore, it is called "nirvāṇa" (extinction and crossing over).
In this regard, the first three treatises merely involve the non-extinction of object and wisdom; now, object and wisdom are non-dual.

Thus we know that among the four treatises, the teaching is shallow in the former and deep in the latter, yet in principle they are simultaneous and of one accord. This is truly because the object is empty and without marks, while wisdom is...
Quiescent and devoid of cognition, where object and wisdom are of one suchness—this is the meaning of present unconditioned *nirvāṇa*. Yet, there are four kinds of *nirvāṇa*:
first, *svabhāva-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity), which refers to the fact that the principle of nature is fundamentally pure and does not depend upon cultivation.
Second is *nirvāṇa with remainder*, which refers to the permanent cessation of afflictions while the basis for subtle suffering has not yet been extinguished.
Third is *nirvāṇa without remainder*, which refers to the exhaustion of afflictions such that the remaining basis is also extinguished.

Fourth is *non-abiding nirvāṇa*, which refers to true thusness (*tathatā*) emerging from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), being constantly supported by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). This is explained in terms of cultivation.

Because it is manifest, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "All sentient beings possess the first [body]. Those of the two vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning may possess the first three.
This is based on those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*). Only our World-Honored One can be said to possess all four.

However, when this treatise discusses these four within the context of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) teaching, the middle two are categorized as the transformational and emanational bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya* and *saṃbhoga-kāya*), while the first and last are categorized as the true body (*dharmakāya*). This is because the emanational body must necessarily...
Ultimate Reality (*zhen*) does not depart from phenomenal response (*ying*); all phenomena encompass principle (*li*), for there are no phenomena outside of principle.
Thus, reality and response are non-dual, and all four [aspects] are fully present. However, to cling to response as being external to reality is precisely what is refuted here.
If response is identical to reality, this accords with the meaning of unconditioned *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, among these four, the latter three pertain to cultivation, while the first does not.

It awaits cultivation; yet if there is cultivation, there is no cultivation, and if there is realization, there is no realization. Thus, the causes and fruits of the Three Vehicles all simultaneously attain the fruit of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) of the One Vehicle.

The subsequent refutations and establishments may be understood by analogy with this. As for what is called "nameless": when the myriad dharmas return to their source, each loses its own characteristic (svalakṣaṇa);
they are equal and of a single flavor, allowing no room for divergent names. It is not only that the characteristics themselves are non-existent...
The marks are likewise identical to being nameless; thus it is said, "Because there is nothing to be attained, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

How much more so for Nirvāṇa! Furthermore, previously the True and the Conventional were shown to be identical; next, Quiescence and Illumination were shown to be identical; now, Mind and Objects are shown to be identical.
Since no dualistic marks are perceived, how could different names be tolerated? The treatise is explained as before. Fourth.
This refers to the aforementioned three preceding [categories]. The discourse on the namelessness of *nirvāṇa* follows the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound analysis.

Among the five aforementioned names, when conditions assemble, all phenomena fundamentally lack any distinction between principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*). Since that which assembles through conditions is itself fundamentally non-existent, it is called "one meaning" (*ekārtha*).
△ Second, within the main text there are two parts. First, the presentation of the headings.
Regarding the phrase "ninefold unfolding and tenfold exposition":
"unfolding" (*zhe*) means to bend or contract; it refers to the difficult terminology of the names found in the nine subsequent chapters. "Exposition" (*yan*) means the long flow of water.
This takes up the meaning of uninterrupted continuity; that is, the principle of the namelessness of the ten subsequent chapters.
Although they may be constrained by having names, the purport of namelessness remains ever-pervasive. Thus it is said: "Nine turns and ten unfoldings.
The single character "one" (者) serves to reference what precedes and indicate what follows.

△ Second, the main treatise consists of nineteen chapters, divided into three sections. The first section, comprising one chapter, establishes the fundamental tenets and defines the subject matter. This section has two parts.
First, the title of the chapter: "The First Chapter: Establishing the Fundamental Tenets."
It opens up the meaning of Nirvana as nameless, true, and eternal, serving as the fundamental principle for the eighteen subsequent chapters.
It is like Confucius’s discourse on filial piety, which first contains a chapter that establishes the school and clarifies its essential meaning.
△ Second, within the main text, there are two parts. First, the presentation of the thesis and the sequence of its intent. This section has two parts. First, the presentation of the thesis.
Within this, first, the scripture is cited to provide a general heading. Anonymously it says:
This is the primary tenet of the masters; therefore, I shall set forth what they designate.

When the sūtras speak of "nirvāṇa with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa) and "nirvāṇa without remainder" (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa), these two types of nirvāṇa are explained in all the sūtras as referring to that which remains. Although the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted, the body and wisdom have not yet [ceased].

"Extinction with remainder" refers to [the state where] there is still a physical existence. Reaching the point where the body is reduced to ashes and wisdom is extinguished is called "extinction without remainder.

Those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) with fixed natures enter from existence into non-existence and thus possess these two types of extinction. Those of the two vehicles who have turned their minds toward enlightenment, as well as all bodhisattvas, do not enter extinction without remainder, as they differ from the two vehicles.
That the Buddha’s response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) manifest as possessing both is precisely what the sūtra states. △
Second, the explanation of the meaning based on the sūtras has three parts. First, the translation of the name *nirvāṇa*.
In the language of Qin, it means "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*). It is also called "extinction and transcendence" (*mie-du*).
Regarding the former term *nirvāṇa*, there are these two translations from the Qin dynasty. Below, he explains it himself as follows:
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) refers to that which is empty, void, and tranquil, which is wondrously transcendent of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This "emptiness, voidness, and tranquility" means that ultimate truth is devoid of sound and form. "Wondrous transcendence" means being non-existent while yet existing.
The conditioned refers to all phenomena within the three periods of time, characterized by the four marks, and comprising the objects and states of mind.
Now, as for the reality of the absolute truth (*dharmatā*), although its phenomenal aspects appear distinct and clear, the truth inherent in these very phenomena is eternally quiescent and void.

Therefore, all conditioned things—past, present, and future, including birth, abiding, change, and cessation—are fundamentally unborn from the beginning and are likewise without cessation now. Being without birth and without cessation, they are... [non-existent].
Because it is devoid of going and coming, and lacks both form and sound, this meaning is revealed; thus, it is translated as "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).

Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "That which arises is immediately subject to cessation; this is not taught for the sake of the ignorant. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* states: "Arising, ceasing, going, and coming are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha."
"Extinction" (*nirvāṇa*) means that the great affliction has been eternally extinguished and one has transcended the four currents.
The "great affliction" refers to birth and death. As Laozi said: "I have a great affliction, which is that I have a body.
The "four currents" are desire, existence, views, and ignorance. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* also speaks of these four; they constantly cause sentient beings to drift and drown.
Therefore, it is called "flowing" (*āsrava*). Birth and death are the false effects; the four flows are the false causes.

If one knows that birth and death are fundamentally true and the four flows are eternally quiescent, then one can extinguish great suffering and cross over the four flows, attaining wondrous enlightenment without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
The preceding was a general translation, meaning that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are themselves unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this is according to the specific [meaning].

To overturn birth-and-death and afflictions is itself extinction (nirvāṇa). As for the ordinary and the sage, defilement and purity, the environment and its inhabitants, and so forth—each and every one can be seen as immediately equal. Thus, the meaning of nirvāṇa is manifest everywhere.

Therefore, the Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang translated it as "perfect stillness" (yuánjì), meaning that there are no virtues not fully possessed and no obstacles not completely exhausted. △ Second, [the section] regarding...
In principle, it is beyond naming;
this is surely the destination of reflected images, the profound abode where all designations cease.
"This" refers to *nirvāṇa*. "Reflected images" means that while images appear within a mirror as if they were real, they are actually non-existent. This is the profound abode.

This is the profound principle in which the sages and worthies abide. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and the four torrents (*catasra oghāḥ*) are as unreal as reflections in a mirror.
When one investigates them and finds them to be unreal, they all return to the single nature (*ekadhātu*). Since this nature is fundamentally equal, it transcends all designations of differentiation;
thus it is called *nirvāṇa*, the nameless. It is like the hundred rivers returning to the sea, each losing its original identity.
[This is the] name. △ Third, regarding the manifestation of provisional names through their application:

to speak of "with remainder" and "without remainder" is truly nothing more than different designations for [the states of] emergence and cessation, and merely provisional names applied according to the capacities of sentient beings.
"Good faith" (*liangxin*) refers to abiding. Arising transformation from the True, one abides among humans and devas;

therefore, the *Xianchu* (Appearance) says that "existence" refers to remaining life, while "transformation" refers to non-remaining [life]. To believe this is not in vain is entirely the activity of the True. △ Second, the Preface to the Meaning.

"Previously" (嘗) means "formerly"; "attempted" (試) means "provisionally. I have not yet dared to definitively state its principle; rather, it shall be deliberated upon. △ Second, establishing the doctrine and inferring the school.

Now, as for the Way of Nirvana—this phrase indicates that which is taken as the primary tenet; thus we know that the subject under discussion is the supreme Way of non-action (*asamskrta*). Furthermore, "the Way" is that which is practiced.
Although sentient beings do not lose it, they constantly turn their backs upon it; although the Sages do not grasp it, they constantly [realize it].

"Practice this. Since the current discussion concerns the place where the Noble One acts and realizes, this phrase serves as the general heading, while the many subsequent phrases constitute the particulars.
By using the particulars to explain the general, this phrase is present at the beginning of each sentence.
It is still and desolate, vast and empty; it cannot be grasped through form or name. It is profound and deep, unfathomable.
It is silent and without sound; it is desolate and without color. Because it is full yet empty, it is profound;
because it is expansive and great, it is vast. Therefore, it cannot be sought through form or name.
Subtle and wondrous, it is signless; it cannot be known by a mind possessed of conceptual thought.
This subtlety and wonder is unknowable by such a mind. As for those who seek to know it with a conceptualizing mind, their deluded intellects and false wisdom are unable to reach it.
To transcend all existing beings and ascend through the profound is not "existence.
As for "all existing beings," they refer to the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms:

namely, the four continents, the four evil destinies, the six heavens of the desire realm together with the Brahma heavens, the Heaven of No-Thought, the five Pure Abodes, the four dhyānas, and the four formless abodes. These are the twenty-five locations.
All belong to the realm inhabited by sentient beings; Nirvāṇa is not a "being. Therefore, it is called "sublime ascent.
Its magnitude is equal to the great void and it endures forever;
it is not non-existent. "Magnitude" here refers to comparison. The great void is eternally abiding, its essence being without birth or extinction; the Way is likewise. Therefore...
It is said: "Eternal. Following it, one finds no trace; welcoming it, one beholds no head. "Fu" (弗) means "not"; "wang" (罔) means "none";
"chao" (眺) means "to see. For those who follow in accordance with it, no traces can be found; as for looking back to welcome it—
This has no beginning or end that can be perceived. The preceding phrase finds attainment in non-attainment; the subsequent phrase perceives presence in non-perception.
Only one who is without attainment can accord with this; only one who is without perception is said to gaze upon and welcome it. The mystery lies herein.
The six destinies cannot encompass one’s birth;
this is precisely non-birth. These six—the heavens, humans, hells, hungry ghosts, asuras, and animals—are the destinations of birth for those wandering in delusion.
Since they cannot encompass it, non-birth is called the Way.
The power of transformation cannot alter its essence;
it is not subject to extinction. As for this "power of transformation," it is the force of change that abandons the old and hastens toward the new.
Therefore, there is no power greater than impermanence, for it cannot transform the wondrous essence of true permanence.
Vast and boundless, indistinct and elusive, as if present and yet as if departed.

"Huang" refers to accumulated water; "mang" refers to a great expanse of water. Here, these terms merely describe its depth and breadth. It is "huhuang" (indistinct and elusive) because it is not fixed.
Regarding the substance of this depth and breadth: if one wishes to say it exists, both mind and form are absent; if one wishes to say it does not exist, its profound spirit remains.
Because it is eternally present, it may seem to exist or to pass away; this reveals its inconceivability.
The five eyes do not behold its form, and the two types of hearing do not hear its sound.
The fleshly eye, the heavenly eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye are called the five eyes. The two ears on the left and right are called the two hearings.
Since principle transcends seeing and hearing, it cannot be seen or heard.
Profoundly obscure (meaning deep) and far-reaching (meaning distant): who sees it? Who understands it?
"Who" means what; by what does one see? By what does one comprehend and realize it?
It encompasses all things such that there is nowhere it does not reach, yet it alone is drawn out beyond the realm of existence and non-existence.

"Encompassing" (*mi-lun*) carries the meaning of pervasiveness; "nowhere" (*mi*) means "not"; and "drawn out" (*ye*) means "to emerge. Thus, while it is everywhere and not absent anywhere, it alone emerges outside of both existence and non-existence.
The former phrase refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), while the latter phrase is free from all marks (*sarvanimitta*). However...
The preceding phrases all discuss the wondrous path to *nirvāṇa*. Its essence is fundamentally thus; although the phrasing may seem repetitive, each meaning possesses its own logic.
Specifically, among these: the first phrase is because it is free from names and signs; the second is because it transcends cognition and understanding;

the third is because it is detached from common sentiments; the fourth is because it surpasses the view of annihilationism; the fifth is because the Buddha has not newly attained [this]; and the sixth is because Bodhisattvas [cannot...].

Because they are elusive; because their arising and ceasing during the seventh and eighth stages are difficult to discern; because their existence and non-existence during the ninth and tenth stages are unfathomable;

because they are beyond the reach of seeing and hearing during the eleventh and twelfth stages; because they are profound and remote, difficult to exhaustively fathom during the thirteenth and fourteenth stages;

and because they universally pervade according to conditions during the fifteenth stage, while their essence remains eternally unchanging during the sixteenth stage—all such meanings refer to *nirvāṇa*. All [these]...
Since the Buddha has taken each of the eighty-four thousand afflictions as a gateway, one knows that there are sands-of-the-Ganges worth of subtle meanings;

for now, I shall briefly discuss sixteen phrases. II. Explaining that inferential cognition (*anumāna*) is difficult to attain. Now, the Dharma-character school (*Faxiang zong*) speaks of three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):

first, the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); second, the path of seeing through images (*nimittadarśanamārga*) is called inferential cognition (*anumāna*).
Because inference is not true, it is called "non-valid cognition" (*aprāmāṇya*). Now, since inference is difficult to apply here, employing it leads to error;
error constitutes invalidity. Therefore, all profound meanings are said to be "cut off from the path of language and extinguished where the movements of the mind reach";
they can only be realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That being so (it follows from what precedes): those who speak lose the truth;
language is not this Way. To employ words is to deviate from the truth;
those who know it return to a state of simplicity.

The fool is ignorant. The essence of the Way is eternally quiescent; if one understands it through the intellect of a fool, this is not the presence of the Way. Such knowing loses the state of cessation.
To have [such a view] is to deviate from its nature; to lack [this understanding] is to harm one's person.
Existence and non-existence are not the correct path; to cling to them is to stagnate in the two extremes. Thus, one harms their physical form and deviates from their true nature.
Since the essence of *nirvāṇa* is free from these four, all four are in error. How could they be compared to or measured by views and intellectual speculation?
This does not mean there is some other mysterious path that cannot be sought through these four. △ Third, showing the reason for direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*).
This is because [the principle] cannot be attained through comparison. Śākyamuni “concealed his chamber” in Magadha.
When Śākyamuni first attained enlightenment, while in the Bodhimaṇḍa of the Aṭavī-dharma at Rājagṛha in the kingdom of Magadha, for seven days he did not preach the Dharma;
this is identical to “concealing the chamber. This was because he personally experienced the bliss of the Dharma, or as it is said, he was practicing the cause through contemplation.

This is due to the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Now, adopting the former interpretation: when practice is perfected and realization is complete, one attains direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) through personal witness; thus, there is nothing further to be said.

Regarding the number of seven days—whether it be seven days, fourteen days, or even twenty-one days, or half a year or a full year—these variations in the various sūtras exist merely because they were taught according to the capacities of those who heard and saw them.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that five weeks passed from the time the Buddha first attained enlightenment.
The Buddha did not preach the Dharma. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also says: "During the twenty-one days, he contemplated such matters as these.
Vimalakīrti remained silent in Vaiśālī.
In Sanskrit he is called Vimalakīrti; here it means "Pure Fame. He was one who maintained a profound silence. In Sanskrit, the place is called Vaiśālī;

here it means "Extensive Splendor," which is the name of a city. Formerly, Vimalakīrti, together with five thousand bodhisattvas, was within a room in the city of Vaiśālī, where they discussed the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.
Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word. Mañjuśrī praised him, saying: "This is the true [Dharma]."
Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality:
Subhūti proclaims "no teaching" to manifest the Way; Śakra and Brahmā cease their listening and rain down flowers.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: While Subhūti sat in serene meditation within a mountain cave, Śakra and Brahmā rained down flowers as an offering. Sājī (Subhūti).
[Subhūti] asked: "Why do flowers rain down from the sky? The deva said: "I see that the Venerable One has skillfully expounded the Prajñāpāramitā.
[Subhūti] said: "In the Prajñā, I have never spoken a single word. The deva said: "Where the Venerable One has nothing to say, I have nothing to hear.
This state of no-speech and no-hearing is the true exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā. Then, once again, flowers rained down from above.
Regarding that which is revealed: first, the Buddha of the fruit has no teaching; second, the bodhisattvas have no teaching; third, those of the two vehicles have no teaching;
and fourth, devas and humans have no teaching. Thus we know that in realization, both the holy and the ordinary are thus;
in turning away from it, all forms of inference are incorrect. Therefore, four matters are cited as proof, as found extensively in various sutras.

All of these are governed by the spiritual principle (*li*). Therefore, the mouth remains silent because of it; how could one say there is no discernment? It is simply that there is that which discernment cannot express.
The "spiritual" (*shen*) refers to unfathomable wisdom. "Governance" (*yu*) means control and direction. Since the principle ought to be governed by wisdom, the mouth remains silent.
How could it be that there is no discernment? Discernment (*pratibhāna*) cannot reach this. This is established as being accessible only through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
it cannot be understood through inference (*anumāna*). Part Two: Citing Teachings to Investigate Thoroughly. 1. Citing Teachings to Clarify Profundity.
The Sūtra states: "True liberation.
Liberation (*vimukti*) is one of the virtues of *nirvāṇa*. In the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, all possess the meaning of liberation as the release from bonds.
Now, the three virtues of the One Vehicle are distinguished from those; therefore, it is called "true. Since raising one [virtue] implies the three, it is simply so.
It is called liberation because it is free from words and numbers, being quiescent and eternally peaceful.
Since verbal explanations and numerical measures cannot reach it, it is said to be "beyond words and numbers. Because birth and cessation have been extinguished, it is called "quiescence."
Because it is truly eternal and immovable, it is called "eternal peace. The first part provides a general summary; the second part offers a specific explanation.
"Without beginning and without end" explains the meaning of the aforementioned "quiescence," which is the quality of bliss, for quiescence is bliss.
It is neither dark nor bright, neither cold nor hot.
Because its substance is not subject to darkness, brightness, cold, or heat, and because numerical quantities cannot reach it, this explains the aforementioned meaning of being beyond number;
it is the virtue of the Self (*ātman*), for it is sovereign.
It is as profound and still as empty space.

"Profound" (*zhan*) refers to water that is clear and still; thus, it is unmoving like empty space. It is pervasive and eternally abiding. This explains the meaning of "eternal peace" mentioned above;
it is precisely the quality of permanence (*nityatā*).
It is nameless and ineffable.

Because its essence is fundamentally nameless, it is ineffable. This explains the meaning of being beyond words mentioned above; it refers to pure virtue (*viśuddha-guṇa*), for it is free from the faults of partiality and excess.
Although I have not yet seen the text of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the principle must necessarily be thus.
The Treatise says: Nirvana is not existent (for existence would contradict its nature), nor is it non-existent (for non-existence would harm its essence).
It is where the path of language is cut off (for speech would distort the truth), and where the sphere of mental activity ceases (for cognition would lead back to folly).
The texts can all be seen [in the sources]. △ Second, investigating to reveal the profound mystery, in two parts. First, the general explanation:
To seek the origins of the composition of the sūtras and śāstras—how could they be mere fabrications?

"Composition" (zuò) means establishing; it means constructing. When one investigates the sūtras and śāstras, one finds that they all establish their texts based on meaning; how could they be established in vain?
Yet there is nothing that can be expressed by words.
There is a reason why it does not exist, yet it cannot be apprehended as existing; there is a reason why it is not non-existent, yet it cannot be apprehended as non-existent.
"Result" (*phala*) means the sense of certainty. When one investigates the wondrous essence of *nirvāṇa*, it is certainly neither existent nor non-existent;

therefore, it cannot be apprehended through the categories of existence or non-existence. The reason why it is neither existent nor non-existent is explained below through inference. △ Second, the inferential explanation.
What is this? For what reason? The following provides the explanation:
when one returns to the realm of existence, the five aggregates are eternally extinguished.

"Root" (mūla) means to investigate. The "five aggregates" (pañca-skandha) are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Because these five obscure the true principle of the Dharma-body, they are called the five aggregates;
that is, the two matters of conditioned form and mind. Since the five aggregates are themselves quiescent extinction, [they are not to be abandoned].
If one says it is *nirvāṇa*, then *nirvāṇa* cannot be taken as being existent.
When one traces it back to the direction of non-existence, the profound spirit (*yōurei*) is inexhaustible.
That the profound spirit is inexhaustible means that the essence of tranquil yet alert awareness is infinite; therefore, it cannot be said to be non-existent.
When the numinous spirit is inexhaustible, one embraces the One in profound stillness. When the five aggregates are eternally extinguished, all myriad entanglements are utterly cast off.
Regarding "embracing the One in profound stillness": the joining of both hands is called "embracing. To embrace them is to be unified. "Profound stillness" means unchanging.
This is the essence of the inexhaustible numinous spirit; because principle and wisdom are non-dual, it remains unchanged from beginning to end.
"Those who have cast off all myriad entanglements": all gates of worldly toil and affliction are collectively termed "myriad entanglements. "Cast off" means to abandon.
Because reality is realized within phenomena themselves, the myriad entanglements are extinguished in their very substance.
Because all myriad entanglements have been cast off, one penetrates and merges with the Dao.
"Penetration" (dòng) means thorough understanding. When phenomena and principle coincide, it is said that one "penetrates and merges with the Dao.
Because one embraces the One (yī) in profound stillness, the spirit acts without merit.
Because the unfathomable essence transcends the two marks [of subject and object], there is no merit of cultivation or realization as subject and object.
This is because that which cultivates and realizes is itself that which is cultivated and realized; thus, it is equivalent to cultivating without cultivation and realizing without realization.
Because it is divine yet without deliberate effort, its ultimate efficacy ever abides.

Since there is no cultivation and no realization, no cause and no fruit, it is identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); therefore, it is said that its ultimate efficacy ever abides.
Because it penetrates and comprehends the Way, it remains profound and unchanging.
"Profound" means emptiness. Since it is profoundly empty and constantly unchanging, the essence of the Way is thoroughly realized even within the midst of worldly afflictions.
Therefore, the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) said: "When a bodhisattva practices on what is not the Way, this is called penetrating the Buddha-way.
It is profound yet unchanging; it cannot be said to exist.
The essence of the Way does not change and is profoundly empty; how then can it be said to exist?
The ultimate merit ever abides; it cannot be said to be non-existent.
This ultimate merit of equality penetrates vertically through the three periods of time and extends horizontally throughout the ten directions—how could it be called non-existent?

For this reason, the sūtras and śāstras all state that the wondrous essence of nirvāṇa is not something that can be grasped through the mind or expressed as existence or non-existence. Therefore, it is not [non-existent].
This is a conceptual construction. △ Third, the conclusion that demonstrates its profound mystery. This section has three parts. First, the conclusion that it is unfathomable:
"Thus, existence and non-existence are cut off within" (meaning it is free from essence and characteristics); "designation and speech are submerged without" (meaning it is free from names and words);
it is beyond the reach of sight and hearing.
"Ji" means "to reach. Its essence transcends names and forms; it is neither sound nor color, and therefore it is beyond the reach of sight and hearing.
It is obscured even by the four *ākāśas* (the four formless attainments).

As for the four *ākāśa-samādhis* cultivated by non-Buddhists—namely, the infinite space, the infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception—[it is even more obscure than these].
[They] conceptualize and falsely reckon [this state] to be ultimate. Being deluded regarding this wondrous Way and failing to know it, they are called "obscured and ignorant.
△ Second, the conclusion on equality:
It is tranquil and level; it is serene and expansive.
"Serene and fearless" (*tiánpò*) refers to the stillness and tranquility of the mind; it denotes evenness and impartiality, as well as expansive penetration.
Because the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* is equal, pervasive, and reaches everywhere, there is nowhere it does not abide.
Thus, the nine streams converge and return [to one source]. As for the nine streams:
the single stage of the desire realm constitutes one stream, and the eight stages of the two upper realms constitute eight streams.

Although these nine categories differ, their principle is but one; therefore, they are said to "converge and return. Thus, form is gathered and returned to emptiness; this "returning" is precisely [the realization of suchness].
Regarding the meaning:
herein the various sages meet in profound harmony.
"Various sages" refers to those of the three vehicles. "Meeting in profound harmony" means to be in accord. The three vehicles all return to the single Buddha.
"Vehicle. Since those who ride the Single Buddha Vehicle attain unconditioned extinction (*nirvāṇa*), it is said that they "converge in mystery herein.

By contrasting the nine schools with the various sages, one sees that the holy and the ordinary share the same essence; thus, it is called "equality. △ Third, the conclusion transcending conceptual thought.
This is the realm of the rarefied and silent (*xīyí*), the domain of the Great Mysterious (*tài xuán*).
Laozi’s meaning of "rarefied and silent" refers precisely to the absence of sound and form. Yangzi’s meaning of "Great Mysterious" takes *xuán* to mean black;
being black, it is without differentiated perception, and thus it is unfathomable. How much more so when "the mysterious within the mysterious" is called "Great."
How profound! Now, I regret my words. Since the wondrous Way of Nirvāṇa cannot be attained through thought or deliberation, it is called the realm of the Utmost Profundity (*tai-xuan*).
To wish to label its domain with the categories of existence and non-existence, and thereby speak of its divine Way—is this not far too remote?
Ah! "Title" (tí bǎng) refers to writing a title for display; all such terms explain names. "Miao" means distant. This [passage] refutes the divergent views of the Three Vehicles.
Since they cannot accord with reality through phenomena, they claim that there truly exist the names "with remainder" and "without remainder."
Those who take the marks [of phenomena] to be *nirvāṇa* all use written titles and placards to point toward the realms of arising and ceasing, while discussing the wondrous Way;
they are utterly deluded and far astray. Since the Master of the Treatise intends to turn back from the provisional and accord with the ultimate, it is only logical that he should act in this manner.

△ The final eighteen chapters consist of questions and answers that investigate and exhaustively analyze the subject matter, which are combined into nine layers to reveal the sequence of faith, practice, and realization.

These are divided into three major sections. The first three [chapters] clarify equal understanding by means of the True and the Responsive; the next four contrast the Bodhisattva with the Three Vehicles to manifest equal practice;

and the final two address persons and dharmas to demonstrate equal realization. Within the first section, there are three layers. The first concerns the distinction between the True and the Responsive.
The same discussion. The text has two parts. The first narrates the response to the doubts regarding the true question. This part has two sections.
The first is the chapter title;

the second is the critical examination (*nirūpaṇa*). Since it was previously stated that "existence and non-existence are transcended within, while designations sink away without," this section now proceeds to demonstrate [the truth] by means of grasping.
Manifesting the characteristics of arising and ceasing, one investigates and scrutinizes why the true essence of *nirvāṇa* transcends the names and marks of existence and non-existence.

This is based on the perceptions of humans, devas, and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), who take the manifested transformation body to be real; therefore, they doubt how the true body can be free from names and beyond all marks.
△ Second, within the section on the formal inquiry, there are two parts. First is the introductory inquiry.
It is said that the objector [claims]:
"That which is called *nirvāṇa* must necessarily have a name and a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that can be apprehended. Therefore, he cites the existence of a name as the basis for his objection.
These words mean that names do not arise in vain;
names exist because of characteristics.
"Designation" (chēng, level tone) means not arising of itself;
"discursive designation" (shēngchēng) refers to speech that necessarily arises from names, and is therefore not spontaneous. The above is a general exposition.

The sutra refers to "nirvana with remainder" and "nirvana without remainder" (referring to the aforementioned scripture); these are truly the names for returning to the source and the sublime designations for the Way of the Spirit.
"Returning" (*fan*) means "to go back. It refers to the Sage returning to the source to realize the wondrous and unfathomable Way.
This is precisely these two types of *nirvāṇa*—existence and non-existence; therefore, the scriptural text establishes this nomenclature.

However, as for the one currently bearing a name, Chenxiang poses a question based on the perspective of the Two Vehicles, taking the manifested transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) to be the true [body], yet failing to reach the ultimate quiescence of the True Body (*dharmakāya*).
Extinction. Because the retributive body (*vipākakāya*) continues for a long duration, one clings to the manifested body of birth and extinction;

once this has returned to the fundamental reality, one knows that what is explained below merely recognizes the *nirmāṇakāya* manifesting as perfect enlightenment and takes this to be the complete *dharmakāya* of the Great Awakened One.
Thus, the explanation of the characteristics of cause and effect precisely accords with the Hīnayāna teachings, even though it employs the terms *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*.
The names are designated and their meanings explained; the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* describes the characteristics of transformation.

This intention is intended to refute the attachment of the two vehicles and ordinary beings who hold transformations to be real, so that they may realize the principle that the real and the transformed are neither identical nor different.
Please attempt to explain this. This phrase is the question posed by the Nameless One: "Please attempt to explain it for now. What are its characteristics?

△ Second, within the establishment of the question, there are three parts. First, the presentation of the remaining characteristics. This section has two parts. First, the citation of the name and description of the characteristics, which has three sub-parts. First:
Listing the names.
Regarding "there are others":
△ Second, the description of the characteristics has five parts. First, the characteristic of the perfection of the fruits and virtues.
This refers to the Tathāgata as the Response-body (saṃbhogakāya) Tathāgata; that is, one who comes from the path of suchness to respond to sentient beings,
the Greatly Awakened One.
Because the awakening of oneself and others is fulfilled, one begins;
through thirty-four moments of mind, the afflictions of the nine stages within the three realms are completely severed at the seat of diamond beneath the Bodhi tree.
Beneath the tree, at the moment he first attained perfect enlightenment, the Dharma-body was first established;
this was the initial fulfillment of the fivefold Dharma-body consisting of precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. This is the eighth [chapter].
He manifested a body sixteen feet tall, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Since those of the Two Vehicles took this to be the true Buddha, it is now pointed out and identified.
One bathes in the clear currents of the eight liberations and rests in the lush grove of the seven factors of enlightenment.

As for the "eight liberations," they are the eight *vimokṣas*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: first, possessing internal signs, one perceives external forms; second, being without internal signs, one perceives external forms;

third, the liberation of purity; fourth, the concentration of the sphere of infinite space; fifth, the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness; sixth, the [sphere of nothingness]... [text truncated]

The eight [attainments] consist of: (1) all the *samāpattis* of the form realm; (2–7) the seven *samāpattis* of the non-percipient sphere (*asaṃjñi-āyatana*); and (8) the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Because these eight possess the capacity to sever delusions, they are like a clear stream that has the function of washing and cleansing. Since the Buddha has already washed himself therein, he attains the initial establishment of the supreme Dharma-body.

"Resting" means to take repose. The "seven awakenings" refers to the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*): first, the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*); second, ... [and so forth].
Vigor, right mindfulness, concentration, joy, equanimity, and relinquishment—each is said to possess the term "limb of awakening" (*bodhyaṅga*), or alternatively, "factor of awakening.
These are the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), so called because they collectively constitute the path to awakening, much like a lush and flourishing grove.
The Buddha has already rested therein; thus, he attained the Great Enlightenment and first gave rise to it. Regarding these two meanings, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* is frequently employed.
It says: "The bathing pool of the eight liberations is filled with the tranquil waters of meditative concentration, strewn with the flowers of the seven purities."
Bathing this stainless person. △ Second, the marks of having fulfilled causal practice:

Having accumulated ten thousand virtues over vast eons—this is also taught in the Hīnayāna—it is certain that a Bodhisattva fulfills three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before attaining Buddhahood, cultivating the four out-flowing *pāramitās*.
The honey, as well as the cultivation of the marks and signs over a hundred kalpas, all represent the accumulation of goodness throughout vast eons.

Sweeping away the residual dust of beginningless time, one proceeds directly to the foot of the Bodhi tree; there, the three thousand four hundred mental states simultaneously sever the afflictions, casting them aside. "Dust" refers to—
"Dust" (pèn) signifies defilement; it clarifies that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of both the paths of seeing and cultivation are dust and grime that have been discarded since beginningless time.

Because these are now exhausted, they are called "cleansed" (*dàng*). This indicates that what is taught in the Lesser Vehicle—that during the first three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* one merely suppresses the afflictions—is understood here as being surpassed.

Only beneath the Bodhi tree does the meaning of severance truly exist. If one refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Initial Teaching (Śāstra), it is merely the meaning of severing the seeds at the stage of the Vajra-mind.
Within, the three types of clear mirrors reflect; without, the divine light shines forth.
The divine eye knows the present; knowledge of past lives knows the past; and the exhaustion of outflows knows the future—these are called the three insights (*vidyā*).
Because one internally realizes the fundamental [nature] and externally manifests the subsequently attained [wisdom], there is the divine light of the three insights that shines forth externally.
This constitutes the fulfillment of wisdom and conduct.
One binds the *saṃnāha* (armour) at the initial mind and, concluding with great compassion, rushes to the rescue of those in distress.
*Saṃnāha* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as the "Four Great Vows. These are:

the vow to sever afflictions, the vow to study the Dharma-gates, the vow to realize the Buddha-way, and the vow to deliver all sentient beings. The first three constitute wisdom, while the last one is compassion. Thus, [it is] compassion and wisdom.

The three vows are the very essence of bodhi. One first binds the four minds and practices the two types of conduct together. Once one's own practice is perfected, the benefit of others becomes inexhaustible;
thus, the final mind of great compassion responds to hardships for a long duration to fulfill the vow to deliver sentient beings.
This, then, constitutes the perfection of vows and conduct.
Looking upward, he grasps the profound root; looking downward, he uplifts those who have lost their way.

The upper phrase refers to his wisdom exhausting the deepest principles, hence it is called the "profound root. The lower phrase refers to his compassion rescuing all sentient beings, hence he "uplifts those who have lost their way.
"Weak" refers to those of inferior capacity, namely those who delight in minor teachings. "Lost" refers to those who have fallen away, namely the sentient beings within the three realms.
This explains the aforementioned four minds; they do not exceed these two categories.
"Transcending the three realms" means emerging from the three worlds (*tridhātu*).
"Traversing alone the Great Way" means having already perfected the path of Buddhahood. It does not... [text continues].

Because he shares [the path] with those of the Two Vehicles, it is said that he "walks alone. The first phrase indicates that his retribution transcends the three realms; the second phrase indicates that his fruition differs from that of the Two Vehicles.
△ Third, the aspect of benefiting others and aiding sentient beings.
It opens the level road of the Eightfold Right Path and provides the easy way for the multitudes.
"Opens" means to reveal. The "Eightfold Right" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: right view, right intention, and right speech.
Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration—these constitute the Noble Path for liberation in the Three Vehicles;
hence they are called the "level road," meaning it is smooth and even. "The multitudes" is a term for those who are not uniform. "The level path" refers to severing the two extremes of false views:
eternalism and nihilism. Now, by means of the Eightfold Noble Path, one takes this as the path of equality and brings all sentient beings to equanimity.
Because these various divergent views all ultimately converge upon the Right Path, one gallops upon the divine steed of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

"Gallops" (*chěng*) carries the sense of rapid movement or galloping. Regarding the six supernormal powers: in addition to the three types of clear knowledge (*trividyā*), two more are added—divine hearing and [divine sight].

The five supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) include the knowledge of others' minds. The latter three are called the "three clear knowledges" (*vidyā*) when attained through one's own realization; they are called the "six supernormal powers" when applied to others.

This is because the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) perceives sounds, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) cognizes the mental activities of others, and the power of transformation (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*) proceeds with such swiftness.

As for the "divine steed," it refers to a vigorous horse capable of traveling a thousand *li*; likewise, the six supernormal powers of the Sage proceed with rapidity according to circumstances, just like that divine steed.
"Rushing and galloping. This clarifies that the power of the Great Compassionate Vow benefits others such that there is nowhere it does not reach.
"Mounting the secure chariot of the five *yānas*":
"mounting" refers to the movement [of the vehicle]. "*Yāna*" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "vehicle," meaning the five vehicles constitute the five *yānas*. [The three vehicles...]
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "adding the vehicles of humans and devas" and "placing them in the chariot": it means to settle them securely within the vehicle.

By employing the divine steeds of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), one drives the secure chariots of the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*), thereby causing all beings to transcend the three miserable realms (*apāya*) and the triple world (*triloka*).
As for entering birth and exiting death, and shifting along with all things, the Way is nowhere not pervasive and virtue is nowhere not bestowed.
"Pervasive" means to moisten and soak. Entering and exiting within the realms of birth and death, one accords with the five destinies and manifests the taking on of bodies;
the unconditioned Way and its virtues are entirely bestowed upon sentient beings, like the spring rains that nourish everywhere. This concludes the matters concerning benefiting others. △ Four.
The aspect of the constant activity of the two wisdoms exhausts the origins of things through the "Mother of Transformation" and reaches the ultimate wondrous function of the "Mysterious Pivot.

This clarifies that subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) penetrates the conventional. The "Mother of Transformation" refers to causes and conditions; all phenomena (*dharma*) arise from them.

Causes and conditions arise from non-existence to existence; therefore, causes and conditions constitute the beginning of things. "Mysterious Pivot" (*xuánshū*) refers to conventional wisdom (*sāṃvṛti-jñāna*). The *Erya* states:

"The device used to attach a door to its frame is called a pivot (*shū*)," which carries the meaning of movement and operation. This serves as a metaphor for wisdom possessing the function of illumination.
To distinguish it from deviant wisdom, it is called the "Pivot of Sublime Function. The ultimate function of wisdom is used to exhaustively investigate [reality].
This is the matter.
It expands the empty universe across the boundless and illuminates the *sattvadhātu* with a lamp in the darkness.

This clarifies that fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) penetrates principle; it is a vast and penetrating clarity. As for "the empty universe," it refers to the true reality (*tattva*), which is empty, quiescent, and devoid of limits.
"Jiang" (疆) means "boundary" or "extent. "Sāyún" (薩雲) is a Sanskrit term; in its full form, it is *samyak-saṃbodhi*, which here is translated as "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajñatā*).

This refers to true wisdom. "Yào" (耀) and "zhù" (燭) both carry the meaning of "illuminating. It signifies using fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to illuminate profound and subtle principles. △ Fifth, regarding the signs preceding his entry into parinirvāṇa:
He is about to sever the traces of manifestation within the nine realms of cessation and shall forever sink into the Great Void.

Because he wishes to sever them but has not yet severed them, it is said that he "is about to sever. "Traces" (*zhèn*) refers to the vestiges of transformation; the "nine cessations" refer to the aforementioned nine classes, which are the dwelling places of sentient beings.
The Sage manifests these appearances with the intent to bring them to rest; this state of rest is identical to the Great Void.
Yet there remain residual conditions that have not been exhausted, and remaining traces that have not vanished; the retribution of karma still persists as a soul, and sacred wisdom still endures.
Because the conditions are not yet exhausted, the remaining mechanisms of response are unfinished; because the traces have not vanished, the transformation bodies have not ceased.

This is what is summoned by untainted karmic retribution, wherein a soul and sacred wisdom still persist; this is for the purpose of responding to and manifesting in accordance with [the needs of beings]. △ Three.
This is the name of the fetters; it refers to *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
The characteristics of the fetters correspond to their names. △ Second, citing scriptures to provide proof.
The Sūtra says: "To refine away dust and dross is like smelting genuine gold; when all myriad burdens are exhausted, spiritual awakening alone remains.

First there is the analogy, then the application to the Dharma. As for the method of smelting gold: through refining, purifying, dissolving, and smelting, once the dross and ore are entirely removed, the genuine gold appears.

The cultivation and realization of the principle of nature is likewise so. When both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are cultivated together and the two hindrances are exhausted, spiritual awakening manifests.

This body of spiritual awakening and wisdom is precisely the "body with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*). △ Second, the description of the characteristics of the "body without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), which has two parts.
First, citing the name and describing the characteristics, which has three sections. First, citing the name:
"Without remainder" (nirupadhiśeṣa).
△ Second, the description of its characteristics has two parts. First, the general presentation:

When the conditions for the teaching of the Perfected One have been entirely exhausted and spiritual illumination is eternally extinguished, there is a vast openness without a trace; hence it is called "without remainder."

"Transformation" (*hua*) refers to the completion [of the work]. "Spiritual illumination" (*lingzhao*) refers to wisdom (*jñāna*). "Vast emptiness" (*kuokong*) refers to the void. When the manifestation of transformation has finished according with conditions, the illuminating wisdom also ceases.
Because both body and wisdom have dissolved, this vast emptiness without trace is called "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

This is the phase of entering *nirvāṇa* among the eight phases [of a Buddha]. II. A detailed exposition of the four [aspects] within [the state of no-remainder]: 1. First, the inquiry and explanation regarding the cause.

Why is this? (How does it come to be that the Perfect Man extinguishes the body and its cognition? Now, there is no greater affliction than having a body; therefore, one extinguishes the body to return to non-being.
Laozi said: "I have a great affliction, because I have a body. Borrowing those words for the moment:

the "great affliction" exists because of the two kinds of birth and death—those of the segmented and the transformative—and these exist because of the body. Therefore, by extinguishing the body now, the great affliction is forever ended.
Detachment.
There is nothing that precedes wisdom in the matter of diligent effort; therefore, by severing [conceptual] wisdom, one merges into the void.
As for diligent effort: it consists of severing delusions to realize principle, abandoning the false to seek true practice, and applying oneself with vigor to all pure conduct.

Exertion exists because of wisdom; therefore, if wisdom is now severed, exertion will forever cease. Because the followers of the Two Vehicles weary of the human and celestial realms, they perceive that the arising of practice is truly existent;
thus, they extinguish their bodies and wisdom in order to seek quiescent extinction.
Thus, wisdom exhausts the form, and the form tires the wisdom. They revolve upon the long road, wearying without end.
Because wisdom depends on the form, there is the exhaustion of birth and death; because the form depends on wisdom, there is the toil of loss and gain.
This "long road" refers to the winding journey through the three realms and six paths, which has no beginning and arises entirely from the mutual entanglement of body and wisdom as they revolve.
And it does not cease. △ Second, citing scriptural evidence for the arising of causes.
The Sūtra says: "Wisdom is like mixed poison; the body is like shackles.
Just as toxic medicine can damage the body, so too is wisdom compared to it; thus the body is exhausted by wisdom, and the shackles are like the mountains and seas."
The Sūtra says, "To shackle the feet and cuff the hands" refers to being bound by fetters. If one takes this as a metaphor for the physical form, then wisdom becomes weary because of the body;
profound silence is thereby obstructed, and suffering and difficulty arise because of it.
Profound stillness is precisely *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Because there is still the body and cognition, one remains distant from *nirupadhiśeṻṣa*, and afflictions arise therefrom.
△ Third, the explicit clarification of the characteristic of cessation.
Therefore, the Perfected One (Tathāgata) reduces the body to ashes and extinguishes wisdom, casting off the physical form and severing discursive thought.

Because those of the Two Vehicles do not understand that these are manifested through transformative appearances (*nirmāṇa*) and instead cling to them as being real, they claim that the Buddha-body truly undergoes birth and extinction.
To refute this clinging, this specific question was posed. "Reducing the body to ashes" means that the transformed fire burns it until it becomes ash; thus, the physical form is cast off.
As for the wisdom of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*): because both ultimate and conventional wisdom have ceased, deliberation is cut off.
Internally, there is no exertion of the "triggering" illumination;
this refers to triggering-wisdom (*jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom of cessation, there is no laborious effort.
Externally, one halts the root of great suffering;
by casting off the physical form, the great suffering becomes rootless.
Thus, one transcends and is forever separated from all existing beings, while becoming harmoniously one in essence with the Great Void.

"Transcending all existences": because the body and mind of the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms have ceased, one transcends all existences and becomes identical with the great void.
This clarifies the cessation of form and mind.
It is silent and without sound; it is still and without sign. In profound obscurity it departs forever, and none know where it has gone.
That which is without sound is called "silence" (*jì*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "To be silent and without sound is precisely to enter parinirvāṇa.
As for "it is still and without sign," this is because sounds and forms have been extinguished; one perceives only profound stillness, and its destination cannot be fathomed. △ Four.
An analogy is drawn to illustrate this:
it is like a lamp whose flame is extinguished when both the oil and the light have been exhausted.

When the lamp is spent, the nature of the flame ceases; the exhaustion of the oil and grease is a metaphor for the cessation of the body; and the exhaustion of the light is a metaphor for the cessation of wisdom.
The names of the three fetters refer to this nirvana without remainder.
△ Second, citing scriptures to establish the proof.
The Sūtra says: "The five aggregates are forever exhausted, like the extinguishing of a lamp.

It is for this reason that the name "nirupadhiśeṣa" (without remainder) is established. △ Third, the double conclusion of the text on resolving the primary objections, in two parts. First, the double conclusion regarding existence and non-existence.
Thus, that which has a surplus may be designated, while that which is without surplus may be nameless;
both are said to be capable of establishing names based upon their respective characteristics.
When the nameless is established, those who cherish the void will delight in profound silence; when designations arise, those who harbor virtue will increasingly [revere it].

They look up to the sagely achievement, manifesting the benefit of establishing a name. Those who take emptiness as their principle are those who incline toward quiescence; thus they delight in profound silence.
Those who cherish virtue are those of great compassion; thus they admire the remaining traces of meritorious practice. Each follows what they esteem. And so...
There is indeed further cultivation.
This is that which has been transmitted in the texts of the canonical scriptures and the tracks left by the former sages.
These names appear in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and other sutras; hence they are called "canonical scriptures" (*diàngào*). As for "tracks," they refer to models and paths, all of which—
This is because one realizes these two types of nirvana. △ Second, the restatement of the previous formal refutation, which has four parts. First, restating the previous objection:
"Existence and non-existence are cut off within; names and designations sink away without. It is beyond the reach of sight and hearing, and is obscured even by the four formless realms."
This restates the preceding point. The following objection states:
"It would cause those who cherish virtue to cut themselves off from it, and those who take emptiness as their principle to have no place of reliance. "Mi" means "none.

Because one hears of *nirvāṇa* and thereby cuts off both existence and non-existence, those who cherish what remains [of existence] would cease their pursuit; and those who take... as their principle... [would likewise be left without support].
That which is empty and still has no place of refuge or reliance. △ Second, the refutation by means of an analogy:

It is like blocking one's ears and eyes within the shell of a womb, or concealing the profound celestial phenomena beyond the heavens, yet demanding to know the differences between the *gong* and *shang* musical notes.
This is to distinguish between the profound and the mundane.
When the ears and eyes are confined within the shell of the womb, then prior sight and hearing cannot reach them. When the profound celestial phenomena are shrouded beyond the mists of the heavens...

"The locations of the aforementioned four voids" refers to the four heavens of the *ākāśānantyāyatana* (Heaven of Infinite Space). "Obscure and dim celestial phenomena" refers to these four heavens of infinite space being shrouded and closed off from beyond the night sky;
thus, they are dark and not manifest. "The accuser" means the questioner. "Gong and Shang" are two of the five musical notes (*pañca-svara*).

"Dark" refers to black; "plain" refers to white. These are two of the five colors. One who examines the *gong* and *shang* tones must understand the distinction between the clarity and turbidity of the five notes;
one who distinguishes the dark and the plain must differentiate the five colors. Since black and white are distinct, there must necessarily be a basis for such perception and hearing.
This is precisely what was meant previously by the "convergence of the nine schools" and the "mysterious meeting of the various sages"—there must necessarily be [a source].

Regarding the place where they return and assemble: the intended meaning of this metaphor is that since Nirvāṇa transcends both sight and hearing, and is moreover not one of the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), how can it be that the various sages of the nine streams are made to take refuge and proceed toward it?

It is like blocking off the ears and eyes while wishing to inquire about the clarity or turbidity of the five musical notes, or to distinguish the differences between the five colors; how could such a principle exist? △ Third, the reprimand for the difficulty.

You merely know to distance yourself [from conventional categories], pushing the Perfected Person (zhiren) beyond the realm of existence and non-existence, and exalting his sublime resonance beyond the boundaries of form and name;
yet the ultimate intent of your discourse remains unknown, and thus its profound path naturally remains latent and unmanifested.

"Son" (zi) is a general term for a male, used here to address one whose name is unknown. "Tú" means emptiness. Because his understanding of principle was not yet precise, he possessed empty knowledge;
yet, by virtue of his exceptionally transcendent talent and style, he inferred *nirvāṇa* from existence and proclaimed the wondrous Way of non-existence.
Transcending form and name, one does not know its ultimate meaning and has nowhere to which it may return. The profound path of Nirvana is thereby concealed and remains unmanifest.
△ Fourth, the conclusion on the lack of benefit.
"Tranquil reflection and profound seeking leave the mind with no place of attachment.

As for "difficult," it refers to the tranquil mind and profound seeking mentioned in the preceding chapter. "Leaving the mind with no place of attachment" means that the mind is liberated and has nothing upon which to rely.
Is this not what is meant by "illuminating the great light within the dark chamber" and "producing the profound resonance where there is no hearing"?
The "great light" refers to the two marks; the "profound resonance" refers to the two names. The "dark chamber" is the failure to see the two marks;
"no hearing" is the failure to hear the two names. Since sentient beings thus lack the benefit of seeing and hearing, it is appropriate to manifest them so as to bring them forth.
Since the perfuming of the seeds of goodness has already extinguished names and marks, how could it manifest itself through true forms or be expressed by true names?
△ Second, the response concerning the differences and similarities between the True and the Responsive. This section contains two parts; first, the title of the chapter.

The third [aspect] is "position" (*vithi*), which refers to the stage. It consists of the manifestations of transformation, appearing to be born and appearing to perish; it is the stage from existence to non-existence.
Such is the basis for the essence. The wondrous nature of *nirvāṇa* is fundamentally without name or characteristic; that upon which all phenomena rely is called the "essence" (*tattva*).
However, because the state of the very essence arises as the totality of reality, there are stages of appearance and entry into extinction.
In these stages, the essence abides as the totality of response, yet it manifests the fundamental absence of the forms and names of coming and going.

As for the previous objection, it was based on grasping at the manifested marks (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) as the true Buddha, and thus used the existence or non-existence of names and marks to challenge [the teaching]. The preceding chapter negated the essence of names and marks; now...

First, it is shown that the provisional and the real are not the same; subsequently, the stage of transformation is revealed as being identical to the essence itself, hence it is called "the essence of the stage.

△ Second, the direct answer has three parts. First, the statement of the objection that [the transformation] is not real. Second, the reversal of the previous doubt. First, the refutation of the previous [objection].
Question:
As for the so-called "with remainder" and "without remainder," these are merely designations used outside of *nirvāṇa*; they are provisional names employed in accordance with worldly conditions.
The previous statement that returning to the origin is truly called the "mysterious name" (*shindo myōshō*) was merely due to a failure to understand the manifested appearance;
it is now directly refuted. △ Second, Dispelling Previous Attachments.
To preserve and cling to designations and verbal expressions is to be fettered by names; to set one's will upon vessels and forms is to be addicted to appearances.

"Preserve" (cún) implies clinging; "will" (zhì) implies longing; "fetter" (fēng) also implies clinging; and "addiction" (tān) implies attachment. Although these four terms differ in expression, their meaning is the same:
they all refer to failing to understand that the Sage manifests names and forms, yet instead clinging to those names and verbal expressions as being real.

To revere the forms, vessels, colors, and appearances as being real is to fail to understand that which is dependent upon others (paratantra), thereby giving rise to pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita).
This is merely a failure to realize that while phenomena have existence in name, they lack existence in reality.
Names are limited to titles; forms are exhausted by squares and circles. While squares and circles may be depicted, titles cannot be written.
Regarding the phrase "there is that which is not transmitted":

"titles" refers to written headings and names. Since the true essence of *nirvāṇa* is fundamentally beyond names and characteristics, it cannot be depicted by squares or circles, nor can it be transmitted through titles. The subsequent critique states:
How could it be named through the nameless, or manifested through the formless?
△ Second, showing the True and the Responsive. This section has two parts. First, clarifying that the responsive transformation is not the True.
The Preface to the *Nan* states: "Regarding 'with remainder' and 'without remainder,' this is surely the fundamental intent of the teachings that lead to provisional quiescence;
it is also the sincere manifestation of the Tathāgata’s concealment and appearance."

Regarding what the objector has stated: the two characteristics of nirvāṇa belong to the Tathāgata. For those who cling to non-existence, he manifests the provisional characteristic of having a remainder;
for those who cling to existence, he conceals the manifest characteristic of the quiescence of no-remainder. Thus, he establishes the intent of his teaching and transformation.
These are merely the traces of sincerity. This clarifies that while [the Buddha] responds to and transforms beings, it is revealed that he is not the ultimate reality.
However, this is not yet the profound and tranquil essence that transcends all words.

That which is the profound and tranquil essence is the realization of truth within phenomena; it is the simultaneous stillness of both existence and non-existence, manifesting the aforementioned provisional tranquility as being non-[ultimate].
This is profound stillness.
Furthermore, it is not merely the wondrous artifice within the "center of the ring" of the Perfected Person (*zhiren*).
The "center of the ring" refers to the place of emptiness; "artifice" refers to the method. It is the subtle and wondrous path of ultimate stillness realized by the Perfected Person.
Although it is detached from all marks, it is nonetheless identical to all dharmas; that the two aspects of concealment and manifestation are not distinct from this wondrous artifice.
△ Second, showing the true essence through correct contemplation.
"Do you alone not hear the teaching on 'Right Contemplation' (*samyag-darśana*)?
Summon those who are well-known and ask them: 'In your scriptures, there is a teaching on Right Contemplation; why do you alone not hear it?
Vimalakīrti said: 'I contemplate the Tathāgata.'"
In the "Chapter on Seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya," the World-Honored One asks: "By what means do you perceive the Tathāgata? This is the text of the response, which contains many phrases;
here, we shall briefly cite from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*: one perceives the Tathāgata of the true body (*dharmakāya*) through the Middle Way by means of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
"Suchness" (*tathatā*) refers to the True Suchness; because he comes while having no coming, he is called the Tathāgata.
It is without beginning and without end.
It is said that it does not come from the past limit (*pūrvānta*) and does not go to the future limit (*aparānta*), nor does it abide in the present.
Because the past limit is quiescent, it is without beginning; because the future limit is quiescent, it is without end; and because the middle is quiescent, it is without abiding. Thus, these three—
Because it reaches the limit where the three marks do not exist, it has neither beginning nor end.
The six sense bases have already been transcended and one has emerged from the three realms.
It is said that the six sense bases have no accumulation; eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind have all been passed beyond—this is called the vast emptiness of the true body.
It cannot be subsumed within the locus where the six—the faculties, consciousnesses, and objects—accumulate. Furthermore, it is not comprised within the realms of desire, form, or formlessness;
it does not abide in space, nor is it separate from space; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
It has no location; because the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) has no abiding, it does not exist [in a place]. It is nowhere incomplete, therefore it is not separate [from anything].
"To act" (*wei*) means the sense of fabrication. Its essence is not newly produced, as it is not attained through cultivation; thus it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Yet, because its form is not like that of empty space—where there is a distinct, vacuous substance external to it—it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It cannot be cognized by consciousness, nor can it be known by wisdom.
Because the sphere of conceptualization does not reach its essence, it cannot be cognized by consciousness; because the five eyes do not see its form, it cannot be known by wisdom.
It cannot be known by means of cognition;
it is without speech, without description, and the sphere of mental activity has ceased.
It is said that it cannot be displayed through any verbal expression or conceptual discrimination, for such expressions merely serve as conventional designations.

Because all conceptualizations of mind and consciousness fall short [of this], one who observes by means of this is said to possess right observation (*samyag-darśana*). One who observes by other means does not see the Buddha;
that is called wrong observation (*mithyā-darśana*). This refers to the various meanings mentioned previously. "Other" refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) from beginning to end.

Regarding the characteristics of existence and non-existence within the three realms, which are the true essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*), one should accord with them through the correct contemplation of the Middle Way;
it cannot be approached through the deviant contemplations of existence or non-existence. Thus, one knows that those who speak of "existence" have not yet rectified their deviant contemplation;

they merely recognize the empty marks of provisional manifestations, so how could they see the true and eternal Buddha-body? II. Correctly Clarifying the Essence of the Stages (three parts): 1. Establishing the Tenet and Revealing [the Truth]...
The meaning and the text consist of two parts. In the first part, the presentation of the thesis, there are three sections. First, citing a sutra:

*Prabhāsa* (the *Fàngguāng jīng*) refers to "Buddha" as "Awakening" (*jue*). According to the teachings on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the Buddha has three bodies, namely the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. In terms of principle, it is the Dharma-body.

Regarding the body (*kāya*): in terms of the function of wisdom, it is the *saṃbhogakāya*; in terms of the function of phenomena, it is the *nirmāṇakāya*. Furthermore, there are two types of *saṃbhogakāya*:
the self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*) and the other-enjoyment (*parasaṃbhoga*). In the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhāyāna*), these are combined into two:

the self-enjoyment *saṃbhogakāya* is identified with the *dharmakāya* as the true body (*tattvakāya*), while the other-enjoyment is identified with the transformation [body] as the responsive body (*pratibimbakāya*). Although these two bodies are spoken of, they are neither one nor two.
According to the reality of the teaching, the principle, and the wisdom—the essence and its function—although there are two aspects, they possess no dual substance.

The union of initial awakening with the fundamental [awakening] constitutes the True [Body], while the total arising of function from that Truth constitutes the Responsive [Body]. Those who previously raised objections merely clung to the six-foot transformation body as the true Buddha;
they did not yet know that one's own retributive body is a continuous succession without end, let alone the fact that the Dharma-nature True Body is profoundly still.

It is eternally abiding. Now, by merely citing the scriptures to establish the reality and clarify the true Buddha who is non-dual, the provisional meanings will naturally be dismantled and doubts and attachments will naturally be eliminated.
It is like space;
this is a metaphor. Space has three meanings: it is pervasive horizontally, it is exhaustive vertically, and it is all-encompassing.
The True Body (dharmakāya) is likewise pervasive in all places, exhaustive throughout the three periods of time, and endowed with pure merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

There is no going and no coming, for it is free from the characteristics of going and coming, whether with remainder or without remainder. The above clarifies the true essence; below, the stages are distinguished.
It manifests in response to conditions, yet has no fixed location or direction.
The response of the Perfect Truth (*zhēn*) manifests according to conditions. To those who should be saved by means of a Buddha-body, it manifests as a Buddha-body;

this extends to the various categories of the Three Vehicles, devas, humans, and the eight classes of beings. It has no fixed location, for it truly arises from the power of great compassion which accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Thus, in accordance with each individual faculty and condition, it manifests its boundless great function. △ Second.
Explanation of the meaning:
Now, therefore (this refers back to the preceding scriptural intent), "The Sage dwells in the world"—this phrase is a general restatement.
