Since it is said that he responds while remaining fully in the True, then in every encounter with phenomena, all is True; thus, the Sage has no...
The scope of this [state] is not limited. This phrase also employs the *Xici* (Appended Statements). It says: "Tranquil and unmoving, yet it responds and thereby penetrates the affairs of the world;
silent, empty, and void, without grasping or contention."
This explains the True Body (*dharmakāya*). The first phrase refers to principle (*tattva*). "Silent and still" means there is no sound or form, for it is originally void and non-existent.
If one seeks to see the Tathāgata through form or hear him through sound, one will not be able to see him. The second phrase refers to wisdom (*jñāna*).

"Contentious grasping" means that when ignorance moves delusively, the notions of self and phenomena (*ātman-dharma*) arise latently, leading to attachment and strife. Now, it is said that there is no such grasping.

As for "competing," it refers to the initial awakening (shijue) merging with the fundamental (ben). When both the coarse and subtle aspects of ignorance are abandoned, this is the time when the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is perfected following the stage of the Vajra.
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because one is far removed from even subtle thoughts, one attains the vision of the nature of the mind;
this mind is eternally abiding and is called ultimate awakening. This is taken as the True Body (*dharmakāya*). This wisdom and its principle—
Because they are neither identical nor distinct. It is said that the dimensions of the self-enjoyment body and its land pervade the entire Dharma-realm. As the aforementioned sutra states:
"The Buddha is like space; he neither comes nor goes."
"To guide without preceding and to respond only after being moved" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
"Guiding" means to lead and receive others. Because the conditions of their spiritual capacity (*indriya*) have not yet matured, there is no act of prior guidance.

When the capacity matures, it serves as the condition capable of evoking a response; at that point, the Sage will certainly manifest an appearance. This clarifies that the *nirmāṇakāya* is certain [to appear].

Arising from conditions: because each response is elicited according to its respective conditions, there are ten grades of bodies and lands, as well as distinctions such as those measuring one thousand feet or sixteen feet.
As the aforementioned sutra says: "Manifesting in accordance with conditions, they have no fixed location. This refers to that which possesses a name based on the preceding [explanation].
To pose a question based merely on the body of one *zhang* and six *chi* is still not yet to know the supreme; how much more so must this be true for the True Body (*dharmakāya*)?
△ Second, the explanation by way of analogy: It is like an echo in a deep valley or an image in a bright mirror.
This analogy illustrates the principle that the True Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Honored One is neither one nor two. A mountain valley is deep and remote, hence it is called "mysterious";
yet when summoned, an echo arises. A bright mirror stands upon its stand; when objects are reflected, their images appear. The valley is merely mysterious, and the mirror is merely bright.
Originally there is no sound or image; this is used as a metaphor for the True Body (*dharmakāya*), which possesses only the merit of intrinsically pure nature.

Originally there are no names or marks; yet when called upon, there is an echo, and when reflected upon, there is an image. This is used as a metaphor for the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) that manifests names and marks in accordance with conditions.

It is truly because the valley is deep that it can respond to an echo, and because the mirror is bright that it can manifest an image; thus, by means of these metaphors, [the principle is illustrated].

Wisdom that accords with principle is true; only then can it give rise to responsive manifestations. Furthermore, it is through the resonance of the response that one first knows the depth of the valley and the appearance of the image, and thus realizes the clarity of the mirror.
By means of this analogy, one understands that the transformations of the response are boundless, and only then does one reach the ultimate realization of wisdom and principle.
Using analogies to seek the Dharma allows for repeated reflection.
Facing it, one does not know whence it comes; following it, one is utterly unaware whither it goes. It appears vividly and vanishes in a mist.
This explains the analogy of the mirror-image:
it clarifies that not only is the True Body (dharmakāya) fundamentally without coming or going, but even the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya) likewise has no coming or going.
These marks are likewise not substantially existent. Like a reflection in a mirror, they appear when one faces it, yet have no place from which they come;

they manifest in accordance with conditions. When one seeks them by following these conditions, they are found to be non-existent. Since they are thus absent, what is there that goes? It is only through the encounter with external objects that they seem vaguely present;
this presence is not a fixed existence. When not encountered, they seem dimly non-existent; this non-existence is not a real non-existence. This is the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body).
The manifestation of these signs follows the same principle: they come from nowhere and go nowhere;
it is merely that, depending on whether the conditions of the faculties are met or not, one perceives arising and ceasing.
Moving yet ever more tranquil; hidden yet increasingly manifest. Emerging from the profound and entering the dark, its transformations are without constancy.
This explains the metaphor of the echo. It also clarifies that the names "going" and "coming" applied to the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) do not imply it is substantially real.

As for the one who calls: seeing the echo, they say it is "moving," yet the valley is fundamentally and eternally tranquil. That the valley is fundamentally without sound is called "hidden"; this refers to the response occurring within the call.

This is made even more manifest. It is simply because when the summoner rebukes it, it emerges from the darkness; when not rebuked, it enters the abyss. Therefore, it is called "the echo in the valley.
This is a name for the manifestation of the impermanent transformations of existence and non-existence. The principle is likewise so:

it is merely because the faculties have either a resonance or no resonance that one speaks of the Buddha having coming and going. △ Second, revealing the meaning, in three parts. First, regarding transformation.

The substance [of these names] is revealed through their designations. Furthermore, there are two [aspects]. First, the names manifest the meaning. As for these appellations (referring to the two names of *nirvāṇa*):

they are established according to conditions (*yīng*). Their establishment is the act of naming (*zuòzhě lì yě*). The manifestation of traces is called "arising" (*shēng*), and the cessation of traces is called "extinction" (*miè*).

Arising is termed "with remainder" (*yǒuyú*), and extinction is termed "without remainder" (*wúyú*). Thus, the designations "existence" and "non-existence" are fundamentally rooted in the nameless (*wúmíng*).
Because it is fundamentally and inherently true, there is the Way that is nameless; how could it not be named?
Because it is nameless, it can accord with all names; therefore it is said, "How could it not be named? △ Second, the aspect itself.
This clarifies the meaning.

Therefore, the Perfected Person (referring to the aforementioned Buddhas of Reality and Response) abides in the square and is square; stops at the circle and is circular; is in heaven and is heavenly;
dwells among humans and is human.
Previously it was said that "squareness and roundness are not transcribed"; now it is said that "according to squareness and roundness, one obtains the characteristics of squareness and roundness.

In the human and heavenly realms, one obtains the forms of humans and devas. This is because "squareness and roundness" are mentioned broadly to encompass humans and devas as the primary discussion. Furthermore, "squareness and roundness" refers to the land, while "humans and devas" refers to the body.
It is not only when the ultimate reality (dharmakāya) arises that it is complete; even when the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) arises, it is likewise complete.

Because it accords with the land (*bhūmi*). The ancestral teachings clarify that one approaches the nature (*dharmatā*) by means of conditions (*pratyaya*); thus, the essence of the body and the land are identical.

When approaching the nature by means of conditions, there is a distinction between subject and object. Now, because we clarify approaching the nature by means of conditions, the directions and shapes serve as the support (*āśraya*), while humans and devas constitute the primary [subject]. Therefore, this is so.
Originally, as for one who can act as both Heaven and man—how could this be something that Heaven and man are capable of?
It is a matter of reversal and illumination. How could there be anything that Heaven and man are capable of doing regarding the affairs of Heaven and man?
Because he is neither a deva nor a human, he is able to be both a deva and a human;
this accords with the principle of non-duality. Because his essence transcends devas and humans, he is able to respond to the conditions of devas and humans.
△ Second, the manifestation of his transformative activity is explained.
As for their governance:
when the ruler above issues a call, there are both the presence and absence of its application.
Therefore, they respond without acting, and follow along without imposing.

It was stated previously that while [the Buddha] acts in accordance with conditions, his essence is utterly devoid of the characteristics of fabrication (*prajñapti*) and activity (*kriyā*). "Fabrication" refers to conceptual designation;
"activity" refers to performance. Manifesting bodies and lands, being born, entering parinirvāṇa, dwelling in the world, and preaching the Dharma—all these are fabrications and activities.
Because there is no giving due to causes, giving is not expanded. Because there is no acting due to conditions, acting is not made great.
Although the traces of giving and acting are severed, giving and acting manifest through transformation; their vastness is unsurpassed.
That which is able to be so vast arises from the true source.
Because it is the greatest of all, it returns to the accomplishment of the small; because its application is the broadest of all, it reverts to the nameless.

To return to the accomplishment of the small means that, since the Great Function is without fixed direction, one turns back from the body of sixteen feet—the inferior function of a single Buddha’s small accomplishment—to accord with the vast assembly of the Truth, and from the conditioned functions of the Three Vehicles, one reverts to the Nameless.

The Source of Transformation (*huàyuán*). This refers to the Dharma-nature school (*fǎxìng zōng*), wherein the Responsive [Body] (*yìngshēn*) is identical to the True [Dharmakāya]. It subsumes the two preceding teachings.
As the Sūtra says, "the Way of Bodhi.
Here, *bodhi* refers to wisdom (*zhì*), while *nirvāṇa* refers to principle (*lǐ*). Since wisdom and principle are non-dual in essence, the Sūtra cited here speaks of *bodhi*.
The meaning of "ti" (提) is to realize the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.
It cannot be schematized or measured.
This phrase serves as a general negation of the characteristics of schematization and measurement found in the subsequent phrases.
High and unsurpassed; vast and boundless. Deep and bottomless; profound and unfathomable. Encompassing heaven and earth in its greatness;
penetrating the infinitesimal gaps in its subtlety.

It is "high" because it possesses the aspect of being unsurpassed; it cannot be measured or fathomed, which refers to the aspect of its limitlessness. "Deep abyss" (yuan) refers to the aspect of reaching the very bottom.
These two phrases constitute a single characteristic: namely, the aspect of being free from vertical extremes, meaning there is neither high nor low.

The absence of expansion is the characteristic of being free from horizontal pervasiveness; this is the characteristic of negation (*pratiṣedha-lakṣaṇa*). The latter two are the characteristics of affirmation (*vidhi-lakṣaṇa*).

To speak of "greatness," it encompasses heaven and earth; to speak of "subtlety," it enters into that which has no interval, such as a *paramāṇu* (infinitesimal atom), wherein there is no further intervening space.
Furthermore, because it fully possesses the essence of the Path (*mārga-dharmatā*), it enters into the state of no-interval (*anantara*).
Therefore, it is called the Way (*mārga*).
To summarize what has been clarified above: that which cannot be schematized or measured is called Bodhi.
△ Third, the conclusion: Thus, it is clear that the Way of Nirvana cannot be attained through existence or non-existence.
Since Bodhi transcends all scheming and calculation, by analogy, Nirvana likewise transcends all scheming and calculation;
thus, the principle that it cannot be attained through names, marks, existence, or non-existence is clear. △ Second, the conclusion and rebuke of deluded sentiments.

Yet those who are deluded—failing to understand the distinction between the True and the Responsive—behold a supernatural transformation and, because of it, claim [the Buddha] exists; seeing his entry into parinirvāṇa, they then claim he does not exist.
This was addressed previously: that which has a remainder may be designated as "existent," while that which has no remainder may be termed "non-existent. As for these supernatural transformations:
This demonstrates the unfathomable function of transcending the world.
How could the realms of existence and non-existence, or the domain of deluded thought, suffice to characterize the profound Way or to speak of the Sage’s mind?
"Deluded thought" (*vikalpa*) refers to the inverted mind. "Signboard" (*pang*) means to indicate. "Having names" refers to the attachment to names and forms (*nāma-rūpa*).

Because these are the wondrous designations for the divine Way that returns to the fundamental reality, they are now being scrutinized: existence and non-existence are merely what the deluded mind dwells upon.
How could these signs and marks be used to indicate *nirvāṇa*, or to speak of the sagely mind and wisdom?
Furthermore, since existence and non-existence cannot be used to mark the profound Way, how can deluded thoughts suffice to speak of the sage’s mind?

Increase cannot be made full; decrease cannot be made deficient.

thus, one may approximate the Right Path through a provisional understanding, resting the mind within the realm where the six sense-objects are severed. By grasping the underlying intent and discarding words of existence and non-existence, one can certainly seek the Way.
To realize that it is neither existent nor non-existent is to demonstrate correct understanding;

"realizing" (ti) means understanding (jie). The true and eternal Dharma-body is manifested through response and transformation, yet it cannot be sought through the categories of existence or non-existence, nor through sound or form;
only then does one truly realize and understand it.
How could it be said that, outside of existence and non-existence, there is a separate "existence" that can be designated?

This clarifies the meaning of non-separation. If the true is identical to the responsive, then because the true does not depart from the responsive, there is no reality-body of the True Buddha existing apart from the characteristics of existence and non-existence. △ Third, showing the intent of the preceding scripture.

The Sūtra says: "The three unconditioned [dharmas]" (this is a passage from the previously cited sūtra). Indeed, sentient beings are entangled in manifold complexities, giving rise to profound afflictions;
among these profound afflictions, none is more primary than existence (*bhava*).
This clarifies the intent of the sutra. "Entanglement" refers to the deluded mind flying about in confusion and being ensnared by a multitude of afflictions;
it denotes gravity and harm, namely the karma of good and evil. Because of deluded movement, one creates karma and undergoes retribution; hence it is called "grave affliction.
When one traces the fault back to its fundamental cause, it arises from the grasping at existence.
In the designation of "absolute transcendence" (*jueyou*), none precedes "non-being" (*wu*).
The Sūtras teach that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the truth, for they seek to transcend the delusions and karma of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

The provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles all state that by discernment one cuts off delusions and karma, eternally departing from the fruits of suffering and realizing the unconditioned; only then is it considered truly real.
Therefore, one borrows "non-existence" to clarify that things are not existent;
one provisionally adopts "non-existence" as the ultimate reality to refute existence as a delusion.
To clarify that things are not existent does not mean they are non-existent.
The sūtras clarify that these things are empty and illusory, not existing; this does not mean that their non-existence is itself the ultimate reality.

Furthermore, when followers of the Three Vehicles understand that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) do not exist, they must further realize that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is truly eternal; it does not mean a nihilistic non-existence.
Therefore, one must not cling to provisional sūtras while harboring doubts regarding the true intent.

△ Third, the two sections on "neither-nor" (ubhayānta-vinirmukta) are distinguished as follows: first, the question regarding "neither-nor" as identity or difference; second, the answer regarding the simultaneity of identity and difference.

Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, the title of the chapter; second, the actual question. Now, the first [part]: The title of the chapter. Second, the actual question. Now, the first:
"Sou Xuan" (Investigating the Profound), Part Six: "Seeking. This means to seek out the profound purport of the preceding chapter. Why is it that [the principle] is neither identical nor separate?
△ Second, the formal inquiry, in three parts: First, restating the previous section and setting forth the doubt.

The commentary states: "The purport of the treatise says that since nirvāṇa transcends both existence and non-existence, how could it be said—as was asked previously—that there exists some distinct 'existence' outside of existence and non-existence that can be so designated?"
Furthermore, it does not reside in existence or non-existence.
One who grasps the meaning forgets the words and realizes that its essence is neither existent nor non-existent.

Since it does not reside in existence or non-existence, it cannot be attained through existence or non-existence. Since it does not emerge from existence or non-existence, it cannot [be attained]... [therefore, it cannot be attained].
Seek it by departing from both existence and non-existence. When there is nowhere to seek it, it would seem that it must be entirely non-existent;
yet when one approaches it, it cannot be grasped, and when one departs from it, it cannot be left behind—fearing this, there may be no Way to be sought. △ Second, restating the intent of the doubt.
Nevertheless, it is not that there is no Way.
There are those who name it; yet others doubt this, saying: "The Way cannot be said to be non-existent.
Since the Way is not non-existent, the path to the profound realm can be sought."
Since one suspects that the Way exists, it must certainly be sought;
this is why the thousand sages have traveled the same path and have never returned empty-handed.

This explanation is not without reason. "Thousand" (*qian*) is a large number. "Path" (*che*) refers to a carriage track; it carries the meaning of transport and conveyance. Thus, the multitude [of sages]...
The Sages alike attained transcendence through *nirvāṇa*. There has never been one who failed to attain it and yet returned to the triple world;
thus we know that this Way is not non-existent. △ Third, seeking the profound purport.
If that Way truly exists, yet you say it is neither "not emerging" nor "not being within," there must be a profound and distinct meaning to this; may I hear it?
Although I know the Way resides in the interval between "not emerging" and "not being within," I have not yet fully grasped the purport of "not emerging" and "not being within";
therefore, I seek your instruction. In this, my understanding of the mind has already reached a state close to perfection.
Commentary on the *Zhao Lun* (Zhaolun shu),
Scroll Five,
Pronunciation Guide: Huang (hòuguāng qiè) Mǎng (mòlǎng qiè) Yǎo (yǎo yīn) Pǔ (bùgǔ qiè) Náo (nǚjiāo qiè) Jiāo (zǐyáo qiè) Ā (yúhé)
Qiè (lì [lì shì qiè]) kuí (qí guī qiè) liáo (lì diào qiè) huǐ (jū huǐ qiè) jué (gǔ xué qiè).
Commentary on the *Zhàolùn* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith), Fascicle Six.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Zūnshì of the Yáofēng Āranya in Gūsū.
△ Second, the response that identity and difference are simultaneous. This section has two parts. First, the title of the chapter:
*Miaocun* (Subtle Existence), the seventh.
"Miao" (subtle) means subtle, inconceivable, and wondrous. "Cun" (existence) means to abide. The Way of Nirvāṇa abides in...

It does not exist within the interval between non-emergence and existence, yet it cannot be categorized as emerging from either existence or non-existence, for it is conceived in terms of existence and non-existence;
thus it is called "subtle and wondrous. Why is this? The wondrous Way of Nirvana is neither existence nor non-existence, yet it is not separate from existence and non-existence.

Because it is neither existence nor non-existence, it is the unchanging true permanence; because it is [not separate from] existence and non-existence, it arises and ceases in accordance with conditions. Although it follows conditions...

Because it is eternally unchanging, it does not abide in existence or non-existence. Although it is unchanging, because it constantly follows conditions, it does not depart from existence or non-existence.
Because it does not depart from existence or non-existence, the manifested transformation is itself the truth. It does not abide in existence or non-existence, for arising and ceasing are not real.
It is said: "The subtle and wondrous Way exists in the interval between neither coinciding nor departing.

△ Second, the direct answer. This section has four parts. First, manifesting that which transcends words and thought. Third, first, describing the existence or non-existence of names and characteristics.
Wuming said: "Now, speech arises from names; names arise through mutual production; and these characteristics (lakṣaṇa) exist because of the characterized (lakṣya).

This describes existence. As for the 'characterized,' it is the grasping of characteristics. Because of this pervasive conceptualization and grasping, there is the appearance of both existence and non-existence."
Birth is established by means of characteristics; because words arise from names, one may seek names and characteristics through speech. Where there are no characteristics, there are no names;
where there are no names, there is no discourse; where there is no discourse, there is no hearing.
This describes non-existence. If one is detached from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), then appearances cease and names vanish;
there being no name that can be spoken, by what could one "hear"? Thus, those who possess names seek to hear of the Way as something distinct, yet they do not know that the Way is ineffable.
By what, then, could one hear it? II. Explaining the Transcendence of Nirvana. This section has two parts. First, citing the scripture.
The Sūtra says: "Nirvāṇa is not a dharma, because it does not exist as either being or non-being; it is not absent.
It is not a non-dharma."
It does not emerge because it is not apart from the existence or non-existence of phenomena;
it is without hearing and without speech, and is not known by the mind.

To summarize: there is no speech and no interval [of silence], for one grasps the text [as it is]. It cannot be characterized as being existent or non-existent, nor as neither existent nor non-existent.
Because it is spoken in this way, there are no sounds, names, or phrases that can be heard, nor is it something known by the discerning mind.
This is what is meant by "the path of language is cut off" and "the sphere of mental activity has ceased. △ Second, the statement of the intention.
"How would I dare speak of it? Yet you wish to hear it? When principle is perfect, words are partial;
when words express principle, principle is lost. Since the Master of the Treatise does not dare to utter a word, what could the objector possibly hear?
△ Third, revealing the ultimate meaning through provisional words.
Although the words used to describe it are provisional, its principle transcends verbal expression.
Subhūti has said: "If people can receive with a mindless mind and listen with a non-listening ear, I shall [teach them]."
"To speak by means of non-speaking" clarifies that this is an indication through provisional words. *Subhūti* in Sanskrit is commonly translated in three ways: first, "Śubhamati" (Good Fortune).
Regarding the phrase "receiving without a mind," "receiving" means being without attachment; "listening with the mind" means being without hearing. Those who are deluded regarding these two...
The phrases appear similar yet differ in meaning. "Hearing" belongs to the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), while "receiving" belongs to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Thus, it is the ear-consciousness and its simultaneous mental consciousness that hear the teaching; as for receiving the meaning, there is no grasping because one is not stalled by the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism.
Therefore, it is said: "to receive without a mind, and to listen without listening. When the recipient of the Dharma is free from delusion, the speaker of the Dharma may likewise proceed.

I offer these words: since it is taught by means of "speech that is no speech" and heard through "reception that is no reception," then both speaker and listener are in perfect accord with profound silence.
As Vimalakīrti also said: "The one who preaches the Dharma has nothing to say and nothing to show;
the one who hears the Dharma has no interval and no attainment. Is this not precisely what is meant?
"I hope to recount his words; thus it may be spoken. 'Shu' (庶) means 'to hope.
Since you desire to hear, I shall provisionally employ words within the realm of wordlessness. △ Second, the formal demonstration of the wondrous existence.
This section has three parts. First, citing the scripture to establish the fundamental tenet.
Vimalakīrti said, "One attains nirvana without departing from afflictions. The goddess said, "One enters the realm of the Buddha without exiting the realm of Māra.
These statements mark the essential tenets of the profound and subtle existence, both citing the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*; the former refers to Ārya Śāriputra.
The full text of the chapter follows, next of which is the meaning of the "Chapter on Observing Sentient Beings. It says:

The celestial maiden said, "The Buddha taught that the nature of lust, anger, and ignorance is itself liberation. As for afflictions (*kleśa*), there are six fundamental ones and twenty derivative ones. As for Māra..."
*Māra* is fully translated as "the Killer. This refers to lust, anger, and delusion, for they kill the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*).

*Dhātu* has the meaning of "nature" (*prakṛti*). *Buddha* here is translated as "Awakened. However, according to the teachings of the Three Vehicles, one must subdue and sever the root and secondary afflictions;

only when both seeds and habitual tendencies are abandoned does one realize the unconditioned truth (*asaṃskṛta-tattva*). Only by permanently severing the nature of lust, anger, and delusion does one enter Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
This constitutes taking the false as true; because one has not yet attained complete liberation, one now seeks to bring that person to ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
This involves realizing that the true nature of afflictions is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, and is therefore called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, since the essential nature of demons and deluded beings is no different from that of perfect awakening, one does not depart from the false natures of lust, anger, and ignorance to realize entry into true awakening.

"Right nature" (*samyaktva*)—this is because its nature is neither deviant nor correct. However, Vimalakīrti bases this on the non-duality of phenomena and principle, while the goddess bases it on the identity of the essence of the true and the deluded.
Thus, although these two passages differ in wording, they are identical in meaning. If one examines their essential purport, it lies precisely in the subtle existence [of reality]:
namely, that the realm of afflictions and demons is not subsumed under either existence or non-existence; now that [the practitioner] has attained nirvana, they enter the Buddha[-nature].
Because it is the fruit, it does not abide in existence or non-existence. Furthermore, nirvana is not separate from afflictions, and the Buddha-realm does not transcend the realm of Māra;
thus, it does not transcend existence or non-existence. Therefore, nirvana and the Buddha-realm are still the "true" as opposed to the "delusory."

Neither emerging nor remaining; when both truth and falsehood have perished, one may finally say that the wondrous Way of the profound mystery truly exists. △ Second, explaining the profound purport of the sutra:
Thus, the profound Way resides in wondrous awakening.
The profound Way should be realized through its subtle and wondrous nature; it cannot be fathomed by calculating with mundane emotions.
Subtle awakening lies in attaining the truth immediately;
to awaken to the subtle and wondrous is to find the truth within immediate phenomena.
When one realizes the ultimate truth, existence and non-existence are viewed with equanimity.
To view them with equanimity means that existence and non-existence are themselves the ultimate truth; thus, there is neither emergence nor non-abiding in this equanimous viewing.
When one views with equanimity, the distinction between "that" and "self" ceases to exist.
To emerge from existence and non-existence is called being "sacred" (the other); to remain within existence and non-existence is called being "profane" (the self).
Because one emerges while remaining, and remains while emerging, the "other" and the "self" are not two.
Therefore, heaven and earth share the same root as I, and the myriad things constitute one body with me.
Heaven, earth, and the myriad things are all encompassed within the non-existent. As for "I," it is the wondrous principle of *nirvāṇa*, which is neither existent nor non-existent.
Because the profound Way lies in the interval between non-emergence and not being [within], heaven, earth, the myriad things, and my nirvāṇa are identical.
This is the essence of the root of non-duality:
to be identical with me means they are no longer subject to existence or non-existence; to differ from me means they deviate from harmonious penetration.

When all things share the same reality, existence and non-existence naturally exhaust themselves; for existence and non-existence do not differ from "neither existence nor non-existence," and thus they deviate from the Way of universal integration.
Thus, although there is neither emergence nor non-existence, the Way resides within this interval.
This explains the perfect existence; herein, the principles and phenomena exist and vanish simultaneously, which constitutes the correct understanding.
△ Third, the re-explanation following the inquiry.
Why is this so? What is meant by "not emerging and not abiding"? It is because the Way exists within that which lies between them.

Now, the Perfected Person (the ultimate person who, by dwelling among others, manifests the Dharma) possesses a vacuous mind that reflects in profound stillness; thus, there is no principle that they do not encompass.
Although there is a person capable of realization, because there is no separate essence to be realized, the illuminating mind is empty, profound, and tranquil;
this is precisely the principle of realization. This principle of non-duality encompasses and subsumes all things without exception.

He embraces the six directions within his breast, yet his spiritual discernment remains more than sufficient; he mirrors the myriad existences within his square-inch mind, yet his spirit is ever void.

"Embraces" means to hold within; "within the breast" refers to the interior. As for "the six directions," they are the four cardinal points along with above and below. "Spiritual discernment" refers to the mind.
Furthermore, regarding "having a surplus," Zhuangzi said: "How vast it is! It still has ground left over. This is intended to praise the boundlessness of the Way.

Moreover, although the six realms of existence have no boundaries, they are concealed within the wondrous mind of spiritual discernment; yet even this mind of spiritual discernment still possesses a surplus.
This is the absolute, non-dependent essence that pervades everywhere—it is not merely a matter of... [the text here implies a negation of a limited definition].
The Great One is a single entity that encompasses the six realms of existence and yet has something remaining beyond them; this is further illustrated by the metaphor of the mirror.
The physical heart and the spirit are both the mind. While a mirror manifests the myriad phenomena yet remains eternally pure, the mind manifests all existence yet remains eternally empty.
The former sentence explains that heaven and earth share the same root; this sentence explains that the myriad things are of one body.

One who is capable of uprooting the profound roots from the very beginning immediately employs the multitude of movements to still the mind; tranquil and serene, profoundly silent, they wondrously accord with spontaneity (*tathatā*).
This marks the Supreme Person (*uttama-puruṣa*) and reveals the capacity for such realization. "Uprooting" means to extract. *Nirvāṇa* is profound.

The Root has neither beginning nor end; only the Sage attains it. As for "the multitudes of movement," these refer to the two deaths and the two obstructions—these are things agitated by manifold phenomena.
Because this [Root] accords with the wondrous mind of quiescence, the principle of profound stillness is inherently as it is;
only then can it be called "wondrous accord" (miaoqi), and thus it is called "wondrously abiding" (miaocun).
Therefore, it abides in non-being yet does not fail to be; it dwells in being yet does not fail to be non-being.
This means that while it does not emerge from [the ultimate], it does not reside within being or non-being.
Because it dwells in non-being yet does not fail to be, it is not non-existent in the state of non-being. Because it abides in being yet does not fail to be, it is not existent in the state of being.
This is precisely not being [in anything], yet it does not depart from existence and non-existence.

Therefore, it is able to not depart from existence and non-existence—because existence and non-existence are themselves the truth—while not being in existence and non-existence—because the truth is not existence or non-existence.
This concludes the summary. △ Third, the exposition of the perfected ultimate meaning.
Thus, phenomena possess neither the characteristic of existence nor non-existence; the Sage possesses neither the cognition of existence nor non-existence.
Principle and phenomenon are equal, serving as the object to be realized; truth and conventionality are non-dual, serving as the wisdom that realizes. Therefore, wisdom is without...

There is non-knowing. The object is the object characterized by neither existence nor non-existence; this is precisely the aforementioned wisdom of the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is simply the aforementioned *prajñā* as non-knowing.

The Sage possesses no knowledge of existence or non-existence, thus having no mental activity within (for the essence of wisdom is fundamentally free from conceptual construction); phenomena possess no characteristics of existence or non-existence.

Thus, there is no reckoning of the external (for in the ultimate truth, names and marks are fundamentally non-existent); externally there is no reckoning (names and marks are themselves non-dual suchness);
internally there is no mind (delusive thought is itself right wisdom). This and that are quiescent; things and self are merged in one.

Correct wisdom is suchness; it is the non-dual unity of principle and wisdom. Because they are darkly merged as a single essence, there is no wisdom outside of suchness that can realize suchness, nor is there a suchness outside of wisdom that serves as the object realized by wisdom. Therefore, it is said that things and the self are darkly unified.
"Fear that there is no trace" is what is called *nirvāṇa*.
"Fear" refers to quiescence; it means that there are no traces of intellectual activity or principle. Being equal and non-dual, it is therefore called unconditioned *nirvāṇa*.
This is the correct understanding of namelessness, perfected herein.
If nirvāṇa is such as this, all conceptual plotting and calculation are utterly severed.
"Plotting" (*tu*) refers to measurement and estimation. Whether it exists or does not exist, whether it transcends existence and non-existence—none of these can be measured or estimated.
This is where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases. 4. Concluding by Reprimanding Previous Errors.
How could it be permissible to seek reproof within the realm of existence and non-existence?

Previously, in examining the essence, we used the names and characteristics of existence and non-existence to investigate and challenge the true essence of Nirvana; now, we shall challenge it once more.
Furthermore, may it not also be verified beyond existence and non-existence?
Previously, having established the "Middle" (madhyama), one sought the true essence of Nirvana by departing from existence and non-existence; now that same point is being questioned.

Moreover, within the "Investigation of the Profound" (Sōgen), the principle of neither emerging nor remaining was asked about in a dual manner; therefore, it is now dismissed in a dual manner. Thus, we know the wondrous Way.
Existence does not lie outside of "not being present" (*avasthāna*); yet, one cannot seek it by means of that which is "not being present. Therefore, it is said:
"The wondrous existence resides herein. This concludes the clarification of the equal understanding through the True and the Responsive.
△ Next, four pairs clarify equal practice in relation to the Three Vehicles. The text has two parts: first, a general correlation with the practices of the Three Vehicles;

second, a specific correlation with the practices of Bodhisattvas. Within the first part, there are three sections. The first is the correlation with the three assemblies as one. This section has two parts: first, the resolution of the single doubt regarding the three.
There are two further questions. The title of the first chapter is "Difficulties.

The eighth difficulty is termed *nan* (difficult question), where *nan* means to question or challenge. *Cha* (difference) refers to differentiation; that is, the various distinctions among the stages of the three vehicles and the bodhisattvas.
It is distinct. Since it was stated above that the self and phenomena are merged into one, this is called *nirvāṇa*, which is equal and of a single flavor, with no higher or lower.
For what reason, then, do people cultivate and realize this Dharma? Among people there are three vehicles (*triyāna*), and their stages have degrees of high and low.
This refers to the differences among people within the difficult practice of the Dharma of understanding.
△ Two texts. Part three: First, restating the preceding principle (1).
It is said: Since Nirvāṇa transcends the realm of conceptualization and calculation, it lies beyond the six sense objects;

neither emerging nor remaining, the profound Way alone endures (this restates what preceded). This is the ultimate exhaustion of principle and fulfillment of nature—the wondrous oneness of the final path.
There is no difference; the principle is indeed so.
This constitutes the unity of the Dharma. The *Book of Changes* says: "To exhaust principle and fully realize one's nature is to reach the mandate.

Now, regarding the various phenomena of mind and objects, one exhausts the principles of conditions and nature until reaching the ultimate true nature. True nature is equal; when person and phenomena are non-dual, only then does one [attain it].

Because the ultimate, wondrously singular Way and the principle that object and wisdom are without distinction must necessarily be so, it was previously stated that the profound merging of self and objects is called *nirvāṇa*.
△ Second, the specific narration of the three types of persons has two parts. First, the general doubt regarding the Three Vehicles.
Yet, from the clouds of radiance it emits, it is said: "The paths of the Three Vehicles all arise because of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), yet they possess distinctions.
This sutra is likewise so. The *Vajracchedikā* states: "All worthy sages (*ārya*) have distinctions based on the dharma of the unconditioned.
Because Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas realize the unconditioned to varying degrees of depth, there are thus the Three Vehicles.
Distinction. △ Second, specifically addressing the doubts of Bodhisattvas.
The Buddha said: "In the past, when I was a Bodhisattva, my name was Māṇava. At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I had already entered *nirvāṇa*.

During the time I was the Bodhisattva Māṇava, I attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) at the beginning of the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), and subsequently cultivated the three stages."

In Sanskrit it is called Maṇibhadra; here it is translated as "Child of the Sages" (Māṇava). The sūtras state that during the causal stage of Śākyamuni, he actually passed through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
At the completion of the first kalpa, when he encountered the Buddha Ratnaśikhin, his station was the first bhūmi.

At the completion of the second kalpa, when he encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, his station was the seventh bhūmi. At the completion of the final kalpa, when he encountered the Buddha Vipaśyin, his station was the tenth bhūmi.

Regarding the stage: according to the time when the subsequent kalpa is completed, it is called the "Seventh Abode" (*saptamī vihāra*). Initially, he was at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha. The Seventh Abode is equivalent to the Seventh Ground (*bhūmi*);

there have been many such translations in the past. If one takes the Seventh Abode as referring to the seventh of the lower stages of worthiness (*pṛthagjana*), then it would be appropriate to speak of "advancing through and cultivating thirty-three stages.
Furthermore, at that time, the first kalpa had not yet been completed; it was not the occasion of meeting Dīpaṃkara.
Therefore, it is known that this refers to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, in the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra), the five patiences (*kṣānti*) are assigned to the stages;

since the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is attained within the seventh stage, it is said that one has "already entered nirvāṇa," which signifies the realization of the principle of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

If categorized according to the Initial Teaching (*śāstra*), from the first stage onward there is a partial realization of the unconditioned. If categorized according to the Final Teaching, true reality is realized at the first dwelling (*vihāra*). Now, regarding this [text], it is based on...
Regarding the statement that "the realization is taught at the seventh stage," this refers to the attainment of the profound realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

It does not mean that the preceding stages have not realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is because prior to the seventh stage, one has not yet attained the exclusive contemplation of the signless (*animitta*), whereas from the seventh stage onward, signs and conditioned phenomena never again manifest before one;
therefore, it is said that from the seventh stage onward, one enters the exclusive contemplation of the signless. Regarding...

Through the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*), one advances through the three stages of the eighth, ninth, and tenth [bhūmis], like a boat sailing with the current, naturally flowing into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

Based on this profound realization, it is said that one has "already entered nirvāṇa. Regarding the statement "attaining the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the section on the seventh bhūmi, states:
"When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, their immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental actions are thoroughly purified."
Because they practice the signless, they attain the radiance of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Now, I cite the Buddha’s intention:

it is merely to clarify that for one who realizes the Dharma, having realized the Dharma of a single flavor (*eka-rasa*), how could there be any distinctions between various stages? △ Third, using one to question three.
If nirvana were one, there should not be three;
those who attain the equal Dharma should not have three vehicles, nor should there be the distinctions of high and low among the three stages.
If there were three [distinct natures], it would not be ultimate.
Since people have attained the Dharma as being threefold, they know that the Dharma is not ultimately of a single flavor;
thus, within the ultimate Way, there would be distinctions of ascent and descent.
Ascending and descending are simply high and low. If all have attained the ultimate single flavor (*ekarasa*), why are there such differences as ascending and descending?
Since various sūtras present divergent teachings, by what standard is the "middle" to be grasped?
This is the central and correct principle. If the explanations in the various sutras differ from the tenets of this treatise, which should be taken as the definitive meaning?
Below, the author first answers regarding the three vehicles, and then, reaching the fourteenth chapter, asks again about the three stages.
△ Second, opening one [topic] to form three answers. The text has two parts. First, the chapter title:
"Discriminating Differences, Chapter Nine.
By means of the single dharma of *nirvāṇa*, it discriminates the differences among the persons of the three vehicles; all are three while being one, and all three are [one].

It is precisely one; therefore, it is called "discerning the differences. Nevertheless, the meaning of "one yet three" is precisely to reveal and manifest that the three vehicles are identical to the one Buddha-vehicle, while not obstructing the preservation of the three vehicles' aspects of practice, realization, and attainment. Eliminating the two attachments, severing the two obstacles simultaneously, and practicing the two benefits simultaneously is called the Mahāyāna. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:

the three carts emerging from the burning house is precisely what this refers to.

because all emerge from birth-and-death, they are equally termed "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).

This reveals that difference is itself non-difference. It is like the three carts within the house; they are all intended as gifts of the white ox-cart.

Removing one inch of wood results in the absence of that one inch; this is a metaphor for the śrāvakas who suppress and sever afflictions, attaining only the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

"The Twelfth Interrogation on Gradual Progression.
"Gradual progression" refers to successive stages. Because [the interlocutor] heard that the aforementioned Dharma is identical while persons are different, he now raises this interrogation.
Since we have equally realized the one Dharma, why is it that there are three types of gradual progression for people?
△ Second, the formal inquiry has three parts. First, clarifying that the severance and realization are identical. This section has two parts. First, a general discussion of delusion and awakening.
It is said: "The myriad entanglements flourish and manifest; they are rooted in deluded thought (*vikalpa*).
'Delusion' refers to the fact that the obstacles of confusion are not uniform, hence the term 'myriad. That these are all capable of binding sentient beings is called 'entanglement.

'Flourish' means to increase; 'manifest' means to become evident. 'Deluded thought' is ignorance (*avidyā*); because one is deluded regarding the ultimate principle, delusive thoughts suddenly stir. Thus there are myriads [of afflictions]."
Delusion arises together with [the mind].
Once false thoughts are dispelled, then all myriad burdens are entirely stilled; this is awakening.
When the three vehicles equally realize the unconditioned (*asamskrta*), shatter delusion, and emerge from the entanglements, they ought to be equal without distinction of high or low. This—

Since all three vehicles equally destroy delusions and achieve liberation, they realize the same principle. It is suspected that those of the three vehicles have not yet exhausted the gradual process of the unconditioned (*asamskrta*).
△ Second, the formal narration of what is common, in three parts: First, the identity of wisdom.
The followers of the two vehicles attain the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*),
which is the wisdom of the emptiness of self (*pudgalanairātmyajñāna*), because they realize, "My births are exhausted.
Bodhisattvas attain the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

This refers to the wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*). By investigating and examining the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*), one finds that all four [conditions] are non-arising—namely, not from themselves, not from another, not from both, and not without cause.
Thus, because arising and phenomena are non-arising, they are empty. Furthermore, the *Wu-di shu* (Commentary on the Fifth Ground) by Qingliang states:

Regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*): non-arising is cessation. The exhaustion of causes is called "exhaustion," which is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).

That subsequent effects do not arise is termed "non-arising," which is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). This exhaustion and non-arising constitute the essence of cessation. Such is the knowledge of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The intent [of this teaching] is to take the attainment of cessation as the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) within the Path (*mārga*). According to this explanation:

Thus, for the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), the extinction resulting from the elimination of causes is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣaya-jñāna). For the bodhisattvas, the extinction resulting from the simultaneous abandonment of both cause and effect is called the "knowledge of non-arising" (anutpāda-jñāna).
Consequently, within the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya), there are superior and inferior levels of wisdom, and differences in depth regarding the attainment of extinction;
therefore, these two names are distinguished. △ Second, the identity of abandonment.
At this time, delusive thoughts are entirely exhausted (originally removed), and the fetters are forever eliminated;

this refers to the end of life. "At this time" means the time when those of the Three Vehicles have reached the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*). To say that "delusive thoughts are entirely exhausted" means that afflictions have been removed.
Since those of the Three Vehicles at the stage of No-More-Learning no longer initiate karma or provide the moisture for rebirth, it is said that the fetters are forever eliminated.
Elimination. △ Third, the proof of identity:
Since the fetters have been eliminated, the mind is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Since the three vehicles are free from the bondage of the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*), obstructions are exhausted and wisdom is perfected; thus, they equally accord with the unconditioned true principle.
The followers of the Two Vehicles realize the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-nairātmya*), whereas Bodhisattvas realize the emptiness of both [self and phenomena] (*dharma-nairātmya*).

However, the bondage of the three realms resides precisely in the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), for they are capable of initiating karma and moistening rebirth; the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) lack this capacity.

Nevertheless, because Bodhisattvas enter into conventional reality to benefit sentient beings, they fear that these [cognitive hindrances] might obstruct the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*); therefore, they must simultaneously suppress and simultaneously sever both. Now, with respect to this...

The three vehicles’ departure from suffering and realization of truth both concern the afflictive hindrances; thus it is said that when bonds and fetters are eternally removed, the mind is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Since the mind is unconditioned, there is no further obscuration regarding principle.

The minds of those of the three vehicles are in accord with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); regarding this principle, there are no further obstructions. △ Second, citing scriptures to corroborate this same meaning:
The Sūtra says, "These various noble wisdoms do not contradict one another; they neither emerge nor abide. In reality, both are empty."

This citation serves as proof that their wisdom is identical. Although the emptiness of beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) realized [by the Bodhisattvas] differs from the twofold emptiness (*dharma-pudgala-śūnyatā*) [realized by the Śrāvakas], the wisdom capable of such realization is not contradictory.
Because Bodhisattvas of Great Compassion have thoroughly understood the three realms, they do not depart from them;

because all those of the Two Vehicles have detached from the three realms, they do not remain within them. In reality, however, they are identical because both have realized the principle of emptiness.
It is further said: "The unconditioned Great Way is equal and non-dual.
This is because the principle being cited as proof is identical to the principle being proven.
Since it is said to be non-dual, it cannot admit of duality.
Reaffirming the meaning of the identity of wisdom and principle: since it is said that the principle realized is non-dual, one knows that the mind which realizes it cannot be said to be different.
△ Third, the formal refutation of gradualism.

If one does not realize it, that is the end of it. But if one realizes it, one ought to exhaust its subtleties. To say that one has realized it yet not fully is what I have not yet understood. "Realization" means comprehension.
Since the three vehicles are identical in their arising of wisdom, their abandonment of afflictions, and their realization, they equally realize the principle of emptiness;

fundamentally, they should converge into one. If there is no comprehension, then one simply stops and says nothing more. But if there is comprehension, one must necessarily reach the subtle and wondrous. Why, then, did you previously say that it was not yet [realized]?
Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is exhausted, there are only three [vehicles]. This point has not yet been understood.

This chapter is for those who, having just heard the teachings of ultimate reality (*tattva*), speak of the non-differentiation of the single principle, yet do not understand the meaning of the distinctions within the provisional [teachings].

They thus wish to abolish the three and establish the one, failing to realize that the teaching of ultimate reality accommodates the provisional by subsuming the three into the one, rather than merely identifying the three as one.
Yet they are one; nor does this preclude being three within that very oneness. Those who do not understand this have not yet grasped the essential meaning.
△ Second, the answer manifesting the person through the Dharma. This section has two parts. First, the title of the chapter.

The Tenth [Chapter], "Clarifying the Gradual," elucidates the process of discernment. It distinguishes those who, though their ultimate destination is the same—the One Vehicle—enter the reality from provisional means.

Since there is originally a gradual progression through the three vehicles, and because one now knows that the One Vehicle manifests as three, this chapter clarifies the gradual sequence of the three vehicles.
△ Second, the direct answer in three parts. First, acknowledging the preceding teaching (1):
It is called "nameless" because it is unconditioned and non-dual; this is already established.
Although people may have partiality or completeness regarding the principle, the principle itself is fundamentally non-dual. Therefore, ultimate reality returns to the same source.
The Dharma of the One Vehicle, which is non-dual, is logically thus.
△ Second, [the author] reproaches the predecessor for being equally [in error], concluding that this is a grave delusion; yet, to claim it can be "suddenly exhausted" remains incomprehensible.
This is clearly based on the three vehicles within the provisional teachings, as the capacities of sentient beings are not equal. "Knots" refers to the two obstructions;

the discriminative and innate [obstructions] are their function. "Delusions" refers to ignorance, which is their essence. Because these are successive knots upon the essence of ignorance, they are called "heavy delusions.
The followers of the Two Vehicles merely suppress and sever afflictions (*kleśa*), whereas Bodhisattvas suppress and sever both [the afflictive and cognitive obstructions].

Regarding the obstructions of the five stages of the three vehicles, these are gradually eliminated stage by stage. Yet, when it was previously stated that "delusive thoughts are entirely exhausted" and "fetters and bonds are forever removed," this intent was not yet understood.
Thus we know that if one realizes the provisional within the real, the three vehicles become manifest; if one realizes the real within the provisional, the principle is of a single flavor.
To claim that because the single principle is without differentiation, one should therefore obliterate the cultivation and realization of the three vehicles, is a misconception.

Regarding "gradual progression": this does not yet constitute true knowledge and awakening. △ Third, the direct answer concerning gradual progression, in four parts. First, the direct answer using both teaching and analogy.
This section has two parts. First, the citation of the analogy.
The Sūtra says: "Hitting the mark with three arrows.
"Mark" refers to the bullseye. The metaphor of three arrows hitting one and the same target illustrates how the three vehicles (triyāna) equally realize the single principle.
The Three Beasts Crossing the River:

An elephant, a horse, and a rabbit—these three beasts cross the same river together. This is a metaphor for the three vehicles (triyāna) collectively severing the fetters and delusions of the three realms;
while their crossing of the middle [of the river] is no different, there are distinctions in the depth of their attainment.

They are one and the same. Just as crossing the same river leaves no difference between them, it is a metaphor for the simultaneous severing of fetters and afflictions and the simultaneous realization of ultimate truth.
Yet, there are differences in the depth to which the three arrows reach; the three animals entering the river each have their own distinct depths.
This is a metaphor for the varying degrees of depth in the severance of afflictions among the three vehicles, and the gradual nature of their realization of the ultimate truth.
This is because their respective powers are not the same.

"Because" (*wei*) means "due to" (*you*). It is due to the fact that the three arrows and the three beasts have varying degrees of strength that there are three levels of depth for those entering the water;
it is not that the river itself possesses any difference. △ Second, the application to the Dharma.
Sentient beings of the three vehicles (the three arrows and three beasts combined) are all ferried across the ford of dependent origination.

"To ferry across" means to cross over; "ford" refers to a river crossing. "Dependent origination" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). This combines the Dharma with a metaphor. It corresponds to the aforementioned "crossing the river."
Together they reflect the mark of the Four Noble Truths and accord with the central meaning.
However, the four truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the three vehicles are taught separately and do not mutually interpenetrate.
As previously cited from the *Lotus Sūtra*: "For those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka, he teaches the four truths, and so forth. If one considers them in mutual relation...
"Universal" (*tong*) has two meanings. First, the meaning of universal contemplation. As the Sūtra says: "Those of superior wisdom contemplate suffering and attain the bodhi of a Bodhisattva;
those of middling wisdom contemplate suffering and attain the bodhi of a Pratyekabuddha; those of inferior wisdom contemplate suffering and attain the bodhi of a Śrāvaka;

those of the highest-superior wisdom contemplate suffering and attain the bodhi of a Buddha. Thus, one knows that the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) equally contemplate the Four Noble Truths. This is the sense of "universal."
Apart from the twelve links of dependent origination and the causality of the three periods of time, there is merely a difference in the sharpness or dullness of the application of wisdom.

Regarding the meaning of mutual observation between these two [vehicles], it is taught within the context of the twelve links of dependent origination that the five causal links of the past and present constitute the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*), while the seven resultant links of the present and future constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Thus, when a Śrāvaka observes suffering and accumulation, they have already fully understood the twelve links of dependent origination. As for a Pratyekabuddha...

Contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, one fully understands suffering and its accumulation, realizes cessation, and cultivates the path; this is true for both vehicles of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
However, they do not equal the Bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion and vows, which long cultivates the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

While the Bodhisattva cultivates the five and six perfections in tandem and perfectly realizes the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividhaśūnyatā*), how could they fail to penetrate the causes and effects of the three periods of time and be endowed with the path and cessation? This, then, is the practice of the Three Vehicles.

The two gates are mutually complete; therefore, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*) are common to the realization and abandonment of all three vehicles (*triyāna*). The fundamental intent of this treatise specifically concerns these two gates of abandonment and realization.

Since dependent origination consists of the causes and effects of the three periods of time and does not transcend the three categories of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*), it is abandoned by all three vehicles.
Thus, it is said that they "jointly cross the ferry of dependent origination. The Four Noble Truths involve the thorough investigation of both the mundane and the supramundane.
The causal relationship between the world and its fruits is the reality as it truly is; it does not exceed the two kinds of emptiness, which are universally realized by the three vehicles.

Therefore, it is said that they "jointly contemplate the core of the Four Noble Truths. Since the three vehicles are collectively termed "transcending the world" and "realizing the truth," this does not refer to their distinct individual modes of practice.
Cutting off the false to realize the true (merging with the preceding "crossing over" is no different); together ascending to the unconditioned (merging with the preceding "middle" is no different).
Those of the Three Vehicles alike leave the birth and death of the triple world behind and together reach the other shore of the unconditioned.
However, the reason why those who ride upon them are not uniform is also due to the differences in their powers of wisdom (*jñāna*).

"Those who ride upon them are not uniform" refers to the differences in the wisdom and practice of the three vehicles (*triyāna*): the Śrāvaka vehicle emerges from the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the Four Noble Truths;

the Pratyekabuddha vehicle emerges from the emptiness of self and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*); and the Bodhisattva vehicle [emerges] from the two types of emptiness and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
[The text] concludes. Why is this so? As stated below: "It is because there are differences in the magnitude of their intellectual power.

This combines with the aforementioned distinctions of shallow and deep to constitute the difference in power. Thus we know that the original intent of all Buddhas is to universally desire that others be no different from themselves;
however, because their intellectual power has not yet reached that level, the teachings are established with gradual stages. △ Second, the comparison of the two.
Riding upon the measure of wisdom:
although the multitude of existents is vast, their measure is finite.
"The multitude" refers to that which is not one; it refers to the ten thousand existents (*sattva*). To speak of these ten thousand existents is to encompass all objective domains of existence.
